Query--If the keeper of a jail be a jailor, why is not the keeper of the prison a prisoner? A patient electric clothes-line has been invented. Upon an attempt to remove the clothes an alarm if sounded, four dogs set loose, a gun fired, and the thief , drops. • I They were discussing the subject of man's vitality at Eberle's Grand Hotel, and after relating several remark- able recoveries of people who had been what was sup- posed fatally, shot, a quiet Irishman who evidently didn't -intend to be outdone in relating remarkable stories, remarked—"l once knew a man who was all shot away but one arm, and yet he got well." All fur- ther discussion on the subject was postponed. • An Irish labourer going to buy a pair of shoes asked the tradesman if he could tell him what would preirent them going down on the sides. The shoemaker answered that he must change them every morning. Pat left the shop after purchasing a pair, and on the following Morn- ing returned and asked for a pair of shoes, tried them on, and (leaving the pair he bought the day before) was proceeding out of the shop. He was asked what. he was doing. "And is it what lam doing, you ask? Didn't you say I must change my shoes every morning ?" A CANiNi/ Gurnr.—A Lincelnshire farmer has a dog that for practical wisdom wilicompare favourably with most men. Should its master leave anything—such as a stick or gloves—on the farm, he has but to make known by a sign the fact of his loss, when off the dog will trudge, and not come home till it has found the missing article. It will permit a well-dressed man to enter the farm-yard by day, but should a beggar put in an appearance, this respecter of persons will gently seize him hy Ws clothes and see him safely off the premises. By night, however, all strangers approach at their peril. The farmer's sister lives on the adjoining farm, communication between the two farms being obtained by means of a single plank across the deep ditch that separates them. Sometimes the farmer's children want to visit their aunt, and they are always entrusted to the care of the dog. It marshals them in a small troop, conducts theth to the bridge, where a halt is called. The bairns are then taken., over one by one, doggie seizing hold from behind of the child's dress. It then waits for the return journey, and escorts them in the same way.—" Little Folks" Magazine. RHENISH ROMANCIL—On the right bank of the Rhine, between Linz and Unkel, a range of isolated bergs are hi view at some distance from the river. These form no part of the famous Seven Mountains, which dO not come into sight until we reach the island of Nonnen- werth, in the middle of the stream. Here we touch a great centre of Rhenish, romance and tradition, , First appears the ruined- castle of Rolandseck, on the left bank. There is little more than a shattered arch and , one or two towers;• but, in Longfellow's words, "the ruined tower still looks down upon the Kloster Nonnen- werth, as if the sound of the funeral-bell had changed the faithful paladin to stone, and he were watching still to see the form of his beloved one come forth not from , her cloister, but from her grave?; •The story; is thus briefly told by Bulwer :—" Roland the paladin, nephew of the great Emperor Karl, goes to the wars. A else report of his death readies his ,betrothed. She retires to the convent in the Isle of Nonnenwerth, and takes the irrevocable veil. Roland returns home, flushed with glory and hope, to find that the very, fidelity of his affianced had placed an eternal barrier between theta. He built the castle which bears his name, and which overlooks the monastery, and dwelt there to his death, happy in the power at least to gaze, even to the last, upon those walls which held the treasure he had lost." —"Picturesque Europe." LEGENDS OF THE FLOWERS. THE SCARLET PIMPERNEL. When skies are bright and winter's o'er, And leaves and flowers return once more, A little blossom 'mongst the grass Peeps at wayfarers as they pass. llongst gayer buds of larger size ‘, It modest opes its purple eyes; And those who love the flowers know well r The little Scarlet Pimpernel. , It hath a story of its own, That unto country-folk is known; For Nature's hand bath given it strange Perception of the weather's change. If clear will be the day, and fair, It opens wide its petals rare; But if the clouds should threaten rain, It shuts them up quite close again. *** The shepherds love the little flower That tells them of the changeful hour, And many a one asks, "Tell me, pray, What weather there will be to-day." And so in, time another name, In honour of its rare gift, came; And the wee blossom 'mongst the grass Was called the "Shepherd's Weather-glass." r,+" Little Folks" -Magazine.
MY STAFF OF AGE My staff of age ! 1 lean upon you, and, sighing, seethe fern leaves red and sere, - And the yellow water-flags wave on the edge of the gray,

cold mere: The blood of niy heart is chilled with the breath of the waning year. My staff of age! I lean upon you when Winter lights the ruddy tavern pane. While gallant roisterers quaff their ale and raise the joy- ous strain, I creep to my lonely bed with no mirth in my heart or brain. _ .
My staff of age! I lean upon you when the cuckoo darts siuging through
the air, - When the white foam sparkles on the wave and the hills
are green and fair, - And Summer brings a deeper pain with love I cannot share.
My staff of age! am saddest of all this May of the long, brown furrow's fine, When the early corn is green and the tendrils curl on
the vine, - And I have to lean on a crutch where once I could sing
and shine.
My staff of age! """"' ' • The woes of eld are upon me, and my locks are thin and
gTaY 111 y eyes, that a woman loved, are; sad and dull to the light of day, And my lips, so often kissed, can but mutter and groan and pray.

My staff of age ! It is sad to be bent and old, to be cold in limb and heart, To be without mirth or love, and to losethe breath of my art, But saddest to remember of my life how great was their part. —From the Celtic of Llytearch lien.

rHE EXAMINER, SATURD AY. SEPTEMBER 27, 1884.

eider the fact that "America (United States and Canada), Holland, and France continue to supply this country with an enormous quantity of cheese, which is constanly on the increase. Last year, as is shown bra Parliamentary return, we imported 1,799,704 cwts. of cheese from the four countries named, the aggregate value being £4,890,400; while for 1882 the respective, figures were 1,694,623 cwts., and the value £4,749,870. It is worthy of note that the cost to the wholesale im- porter was under sixpence per pound, showing, as most people will think who can seldom get a good article under tenpence, an exceedingly high proportion of profit for the importer and retailer. • Last year there was'a falling off as compared with the previous year in the imports of cheese from the United States, but a large increase from the Dominion, which now sends us more than 25 per cent, of the total quantity imported. Then there is the butter supply. About £12,000,000 was spent by our people in,1883 for imported butter and its substitutes, concerning the manufacture of which in the United States Mr. Tollemache, M.P., remarked at the meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society the other day, that the statistics were simply appalling. The real i problem dairy farmers have to solve s to supply abetter article at as cheap a rate. They are on the spot, they are provided with many facilities for its production, they may easily imitate the example of co-operative cheese and butter making. It is really the result of their own supineness, to a very considerable extent, if foreigners are making such inroads with inferior pro- ducts.'

THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT. The Mark Lane Expos continues its remarks on the operation of the Agricultural Holdings Act. The replies received by that journal to the queries it has issued show that landlords, its a rule, have not given that consent to the execution of permanent improvements by tenants, without which the latter cannot claim compensation under the Act. So far as permanent improvements are concerned, the .A.ct is little better than waste paper. The answers to the question whether tenants who have contracted olit id the Act have done so of their own free will are many of them particularly satisfactory, testify- ing to an independence of spirit among tenants that was but little known a few years ago. The lesson has been learned of a stern schoolmaster—Adversity; but, having been learned, it will not be entirely forgotten if Pros- perity ever returns. One writer says that he has heard of many attempts to induce tenants to sign agreements in lieu of the Act, but he has not, heard ef one succeeding, and other correspondents give similar testimony. A Wiltshire writer goes so far as to declare that 4‘ under the present state, of agricul- ture the tenant seems to have all in his power," and there are several replies to the effect that tenants can now make their own agreements. On the other hand, there are such replies as this The tenants have never been consulted. :The usual practice is for the landlord to send a notice that the Agricultural Hold- ings Act is not in any way to interfere with .their leases." Now a notice to that effect is simply a piece of impertinence, and nothing more. It has nO validity whatever, as the signature of the tenant is required to any agreement, setting the Act aside in any way. There is a very general opinion among our correspondents that tenants will not contract out of the Act of their own free will, and: that where they have signed substitu- tional agreements they have had unfair pressure put upon them. A case 'of undue pressure is cited by a Montgomery correspondent. The tenants on two estates were asked to sign away their rights under the Act. On one estate the majority of the tenants resisted in a manly manner, and gained the day;' on the other, out of three tenants who had notice to quit, one has come to terms with the landlord, one has died, and the third holds out. Tenants should resolutely refuse to sign any • contract by which they give up compensation under the Act, and get very little instead. With the Act at their backs, and plenty of vacant farms all over the country • too, they should have strength to drive a satisfactory bargain if they consent to set aside any of the provi- sions of the Act. In the replies to the last question, asking whether tenants are satisfied with the Act, and if not, 'why not, there is much to amuse as well as instruct. A few strong party men declare that farmers are not • satisfied with the Act because it was passed by Mr. Gladstone's Government The majority of the correspondents are not satisfied with the Act. Take a few representative samples :—" It gives no protection against the loss caused by arbitrary eject- ment." "Too complicated for the agricultural mind," and "considered a lawyer's Bill." "The conditions of the Act lead or are open to expensive litigation." "Not at all. For permanent improvements private agreements on fair terms cannot be obtained. For temporary impreve- ments the Act is troublesome to work." Certainly not, and accept it only as a stepping stone to a more just measure. "Too complicated," and "too much trouble to obtain the sanction of landlords." Several object that no security against rent being raised on tenants' improvements is given." A very signifi- cant reply is this :—" The Act is too permissive. It gives compensation for only some improvements, and it gives that in such a way that it is not worth while to take the trouble of getting it." Equally good' is this as a reason for dissatisfaction with the Act:—" Because, after grudgingly admittingt he principle of compensation, 'it bristles wfth landlords' safeguards and vexatious con- ditions, altabst to choking point; and it will never sur- vive the first popularly-elected Parliament." Another, good reply is as follows:—" Because there is no security. against rent being raised on your own improvements, and the landlord's consent is so largely required." One particularly frank gentleman says, in reply to the first part of the last question, "I do not think farmers know what they want and what they don't want ;" and in reply to the second part, " Becanse they are stupid fools, with few exceptions. Among the other answers calling for notice are some stating that farmers are not now in a position to make improvements. There is too_ much truth in this, and the Act is not calculated to help them. If they had real and palpable security—if their improve- ments were their own to sell, many capitalists who now hold aloof might be disposed to help capable and enter- prising tenants to carry out manifestly advantageous improvements. One thing is certain—if English farmers are to hold their own at all in such times as these, it will not be•by the old humdrum method' of •growing half crops of corn at half the old prices; and every new de- parture in farming means outlay, which is not safe at present. There never was a time when security for capita/ invested in improvements was more needed than it is now.

Lord Tollemache does not seem to have as much suc- cess with his maize as Lord Walsingham. His crop, which was siloed on Tuesday, in Cheshire, only yielded 18 tons per acre. Mr. Woods, at Merton, siloed maize 'last week that, as weighed in the field, averaged 33 tons to tge acre. FIFESHIRE HONEY Henvzsr.—Not for many years has the harvest of honey been so heavy as that now being secured. In those districts where heather abounds the gathering season has not been completed; swarms have iust been put upon such straths, and they are expected to add much to their store before the close of autumn. PROFIT OR Loss ON WHEAT.—A Kentish landowner having stated that the present selling price of wheat shows a clear profit of only 7s. 9d. per quarter, some tenant farmers have issued a statement 'giving the cost of growing eight bushels of wheat per acre, taking that ' as an average for the sake.of example. The total cost Is set down at £2 12s. 6d.:and putting the sale price at £1 14s.—the value quoted last week—and allowing 10s. for the straw and chaff, there is shown to be a loss of Bs. 6d. per quarter, instead of 7s. 9d. profit. These cal- culation § are based upon a rental for land at 255. per acre. _ . _

HORSES AND CATTLE IN NEW'. SOUTH WALES.--:At the close of .1883 there were in the colony 66,413 ordinary draught horses and 10,403 thoroughbreds, together with 86,702 harness horses and 163,448 saddle horses. The total number of horses, exclusive of those running wild, was 326,964, Sh i orhorns are the most numerous n the colony, where they number 796,560, as against 150,386 Herefords, 12,348 Devons, 573 Black-polled, 1,559 Ayr- shire, and 473 Alderneys. The crossbreds are—Short- horns and Herefords, 405,847; Shorthorns and Devons, 65,439; Herefords and Devons, 30,140; Shorthorns and Black-polled, 152. There are also 156,324 head of cross- bred cattle which cannot be: rec,ognised. Tse ONION PLY.—Miss E. A. Ormerod, honorary ento- mologist of the Royal Agricultural Society of England writes :—" The amount of -damage to onion crops from the maggot is frequently so great that for some years I have been experimenting on the subject. Lfound that the fly (when it could) laid Its eggs on some exposed part of the bulb, often almost beneath it, which in common practice the exposed state of the onion bulb allows. On noticing this, about three years ago, I covered a plant up to the neck of the bulbs. and next morning found fly eggs deposited on the onion leaves, and dropped at haphazard on the ground—where they perished, and the onions, being saved from attack, did well. The following year I had some part of the crop ,in rows earthed up with success. The .onions were firm and sweet, and though not as thoroughly protected by the rough earthing up as by my own hand, dressing it answered to some extent, and the onions in many cases were not injured or grew past attack from being ,in favourable condition. This year I had a trench prepared as if for celery, and had the onions sown along the bottom, and as they grew the sides of the trench :were filled in on the bulbs. They grow extremely well, notably better than those in the bed alongside, and on raising them to-day I find them ionnd and fine bulbs, very free from any mark of insect injury. PROFESSOR SHELDON ON BRITISH AND CANADIAN AG- RICULTURE.—At the British Association meeting at Mon- treal, ,Professor Sheldon read a paper on British and Canadian agriculture. He said :—The competition of the old and new countries is growing keener, and con- • tains _ certain elements which were never expected by our fathers. The export of cheese 'from Canada has greatly increased, while that in butter has decreased, of late years. The competition of Canada with England in the future will be more in the form of animals and their products than in that of grain; her exports of wheat prove already that she is deviating herself More to live stock and dairying. The competition of India in the domain of wheat raising will be more serious to Canada than ever that of Canada was to England, and prices of breadstuffs are destined to contract still more. India, with her suitable climate and abundance of cheap labour, can produce wheat at a very low cost. The lay- ing down of land to grass in England is still going on, and the number of live stock is increasing. Wet seasons have, impoverished British farmers' who, however, are better shielded now by law, against confiscation of im- provements. Agricultural tuition is improving, and it Cis by improved practice that the English farmer may hope to meet foreign competition.—Professor Fream de- scribed the position and prospect of British agriculture. VILLAGE CO-OPERATIVE Soar:rms.—A remarkable in- stance of successful distributive co-operation in a small village is given ,by a correspondent of 77ze Times. In 1873 the society, consisting of ten members, was formed and: duly registered, the capital being only I£lB. Since, the first year, down to the end of 1883, the profits have amounted t0R1,166, equal to 4s. 7d. in the pound on the purchases of members, besides five per cent. interest on paid-up shares. The writer, in conclusion, says,— With two exceptions, the shareholders are exclusively agricultural labourers and married domestic servants, the wife of one being the present storekeeper, who re- ceives a shilling in the pound on the sales for selling and agency. The society has received not one penny from so-called charity or benevolence; it stands on its own bottom, which ,is ready money and concerted perse- verance. The goods sold' are groceries, tobacco, beer, I drapery, some hardware, and now clothes are supplied, of an excellent quality, to measure, from a Manchester house. There has never been a wrangle or quarrel among the committee, and fresh. shareholders are com- ing in from the shepherds' lodges, one two, and three miles away. Coal and clothing clubs have disappeared, and their place has been taken by a self-supporting medical club on co-operative principles, with the doc- tor's fee paid for the year in advance. The county court bailiff never visits us now, and we are absolutely free from pauperism. &LING THE Arranmarn.—ls it toe late to reccoramend farmers who have aftermath to attempt for once in their lives to preserve it, not, on this occasion, as hay, but in the form of ensilage? A capital letter has re- cently appeared in the Live Stock Journal, written by a practical farmer. If his readers are short of fodder for I the winter he advises them, if they use their produce I for fattening their cattle, to elat a portion green and pit it. More stock can be kept, they will thrive better upon it, and three out of four prefer it to the best hay. Such at least has been his experience. Last year he fed a hundred and thirty head upon oats and meadow grass pitted green. He advises too, that no one should object to pay 5 per cent, upon the cost of a cheap silo built by the landlord. Now that silos can be built so cheaply however—for the paper-lined wooden silo at the end of a barn answers very well-there is scarcely any need to call in the landlords assistance. The writer only used a few common boards on the top of his fodder, weighted with 561 b. of stone to the foot. Ensilage undoubtedly in- creases the flow of milk, and is readily eaten by pigs as well as cattle. It has been said that it affects the flavour, of butter in a similar manner to turnips, but the latter do not affect flavour if they are properly managed, as almost every farmer knows, nor will ensilage unless it is given in a most improper state. Not only can the farmer preserve his aftermath at the present time, but, he should think about spring crops such as rye, green I oats, and vetches, all of which he may grew, in the future in larger quantities thou heretofore, for what his stock are unable to consume he can put in the silo for winter consumption. =MN THE INDIAN WHEAT HARVEST.—The Revenue and Agri- cultural Department of the Government -of ladia in March last attempted to determine the area ordinarily placed under wheat in British India and the Native States, and to estimate the outturn in an average year. The broad conclusions arrived at were that the total wheat area in India is about 26,000,000 acres, of which 20,000,000 acres are in British India and 4,000,000 in Native States. The total yield in a fairly good year was put at 135,000,000 cwt., or 34 million quarters, giving an average outturn of 9 1-3-bushels per °ere. Since the conclusion of the year's harvest, reports have been re- ceived from the chief wheat-growing provinces as to the comparative area and outturn of the crop of /884. In the Punjab the harvest in the south-eastern division, known as the Delhi and Hissai territory, has been very different. Batt in the central and northern portions of the province, both the acreage and yield have been above the average, and this has more than counter- balanced the deficiency in the south-east. In the North- Western Provinces and Oude the area under wheat in 1884 appears to have been fully up to the average, but the yield was somewhat short owing to the deficiency of the autumn and winter rains. In,the Bombay Presi- dency the yield per acre this year is reported to be generally above the average, and in the Central Pro- vinces the harvest has been excellent, and the outturu is put fully 15 per cent, above the average. The four provinces from which reports have been received should yield a total of 24 million quarters. All the reports have not been received, but enough is known to antici- pate that the total wheat outturn of India this year comes up to the average of 30-1! million quarters. It is difficult, perhaps impossible, to estimate how much of this is available for export. In the calendar year 1882 the export was 15,000,000 cwt., and in' 1883 it was 22f million, and this without any effect in raising prices. It may, therefore, be inferred that with a good rainy sea- son following an average wheat crop, so as to secure the autumn harvest, at least one-fifth of the wheat harvest can be spared for export without materially enhancing prices. - - • THE DAIRY CONFERENCE -ASSOCINITON.—This associa- • tion, which has been founded in furtherance of the movement, commenced at the conference held at. div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

if there is a small frame or hand-glass to plve over them. Phloxes are perfect4+ hardy, and may ba propa- gated now i or if the roots are sufficiently strong they may be divided in spring. The general work n the front garden is to remove decayed portions of branches andfloweys, securing to stakes all subjects that require I it, as well as hand weeding and hoeing every available piece of unoccupied ground, and where it has a solid,.l and crusty. appearance it should be broken up with the point of the fork.

- THE Wninovr.—The raising of seedling farms is a most interesting pastime; and costing really nothing, as the articles required to carry it on are limited and cheap. The Germans, we have been told by one of themselves, are in the habit of sowing the seed on a piece of peat earth, which has been previously soaked in boiling watar with the view of destroying the germs of any an animal matter that it may contain. This they surround with stones, or in some instances mix them together, still pre- serving the lumpy condition of the peat. Mrs. Helen Watney advocates the use of fresh cinders mixed with a small quantity of peat, which she considers it safeguard against fungus growth. This ladY also states that spores (fern seed) which have been kept two or three years will come up quicker than those newly gathered. That spores will germinate after being collected more than half-a-dozen years we have proved over and over again, but whether they do so quicker we are not prepared to say, as we have not made the comparison. It is satis- factory to know that in our wanderings we may see a choice fern, and as it may not be convenient to carry that one away, it may be possible to bring the germs of scores of it in our waistcoat pocket if we are only pro- vided with some clean paper to wrap it in. Most peo- ple make a journey from home at this season of the year, and if they are lovers of ferns and are anxious to add to their collections we would advise them to secure spores of the objects of their admiration, which are now matured on most ferns, or will be during the next month.

The removal of exhausted crops is a heavy item of labour-in the garden at the present time. Now that there is diminished daylight and the sun less powerful, it is of the greatest importance that all objects be removed that are likely to interfere with their beneficial influence. Peas, for instance, should not remain on the ground a day after the last dish is gathered, for the haulm, though withered, will cast a shadow over its neighbours to the extent of its own heiglit The' same may be said of Broad Beans. Between tie latter we have Broccoli, and Celery between the Peas, two crops that require all the light and air they can be exposed to. The refuse of the garden may be burned, and the trim- mings of hedges and weeds should be collected to be consumed at the same time. The ashes from burnt vegetables and the prunings of trees are highly esteemed by gardeners, and as evidence of their fertilising effect we have only :to observe a corn field on which the farmer has been burning heaps of weeds. The, corn grows so rank on the spaces where the fire has been that it is easy to point them out some distance off. The farmer may have distributed the ashes to the ground level, but the influence of the fire has reached a few inches lower, and acted on the roots of the grasses and the soil; and made them highly manurial, so that the straw will be so exuberant that the grain will fail to ripen; and to render these patches like the other part of the field a few inches may with advantage be thrown out and re- placed by some of the surrounding soil. We have observed similar results in a garden where burning has been conducted and the ground not dug previous to sowing the next crop. When preserved in a dry plaee these ashes are invaluable to the cottager to scatter over seedling plants to thwart the movements of the slugs, and in some instances they have been the means of sav- ing a crop of turnips attacked by the turnip fly. Where it is not convenient to burn the refuse of the garden, it is best to excavate a hole in one corner, and if the soil thrown out fs placed neatly round, the depth wily be increased without the labour of digging. Into this hole all should be wheeled except sticks. An occasional sprinkling of fine cinder ashes may be placed over as well as all the slops from the house, and if at any time an offensive smell arises from it, cover the whole with the finest of the soil that has been thrown out of the hole. • FALLING APPLES.—To attempt to preserve these in the fruit store will only end in disappointment, for they are not many days before they show symptoms of decay at the part that came in contact with the ground. To convert all of them into puddings and tarts may not be possible, nor yet desirable. We would therefore recom- mend that they should be converted into jam in con- junction with Blackberries. The two fruits may be of equal proportions, weight for Weight, or there may be less of one or the other, and we think sour apples are preferable to sweet ones. This is one of the cheapest conserves that can be made, where the Blackberries are procurable for gathering. So much is the Blackberry appreciated by the Americans that the plant is culti- vated with the same care as we do our Raspberries, The , State of New Jersey is particularly favourable to its growth. Mr. Hendricks, of New York, writing in The , Garden, states that one year in a single township the amount of the crop was 15,625 bushels, and the valne would be about £6,200. One night in July this season , 76,000 quarts were shipped. FRONT GARDEN,Penstemone. are elegant plants in Ithe front garden, and their Foxglove-like flowers are' produced in succession most of the season. It is to be regretted that they are not sufficiently hardy to stand out most winters, but last seasons fair percentage did.' so. Gardeners, therefore, make it a rule to insert a few cuttings about this time of the year. Others take some of the old plants and preserve them in boxes containing sand. A 6-inch pot would contain as many cuttings as the cottager would require if he could only insure their rooting. They are best in pots on account of being readily moved, and there is no difficulty in rooting them

THE NOMTHERNMOST POINT OP EURGPM—Hitherto it has been always taken for granted that the North Cape,l on the Island of Mageroe, at the extremity of Norway, was the most northern point of Europe. But observa- tions lately made by Captain Sorenson go to show that Cape Knivsjaerodden, on the same island, to the west of North Cape, lies still more to the north. The latitude of North Cape is set down at 70 deg. 10 min. 45 sec., and that of its rival at 71 deg. 40 mm. 15 sec., being a differ- ence of nearly 30 minutes in favour of the•new claimant of extreme northern honours. FIREDAMP DETECTOR.—MI'. W. E. Garforth, of Nor- manton, has perfected a simple invention for the detec- tion of firedamp in collieries, which promises to be very efficient. The arrangement consists of a small india- I rubber hand-ball fitted with a protected tube. By corn- pressing the ball and then allowing it to expand in a suspected atmosphere it becomes filled with the air. The sample thus obtained—as the apparatus can be carried hi the pocket—can be taken to a safe place, and the air forced through the tube into the flame of a safety lamp. The elongation of the *flame and the well-known blue cap will at once indicate if firedamp exists in the sus- pected place. This detector has been tried in several collieries with very satisfactory results. A Nrw THERMO-ELECTRO GENEnaron.—Mr. L. G. Woolley, the patentee of an plectric,lead light fortlocomo- tives, is stated to have invented a thermo-electric gene- rator, which is to revolutionise applied electricity. The generator is like a copper boiler, and is operated by a lamp. The flame of a lamp, used to give light in a sick room, furnished a supply of electricity which ran a one-horse engine and illuminated four in- candescent lamps—at least so it is stated, and there is an air of truth about the "sick-room" lamp. Mr. Wool- ley is understood to claim that he will be able to furnish motive power at about one-twentieth of the present cost with stationary steam engines. It does not appear, how- ever, that he uses this thermo-electric generator for his locomotive head light, which is being tried on the Chi- cago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway. In that case the dynamo is driven by a rotary engine, and both are pieced on the left-hand side of the footplace of the loco- motive.—Eng4sh Mechanic. THE HYGIENE OF GLASS-BLOWERS.—GIass-blowers are peculiarly susceptible to various diseases of the lips and cheeks, besides having a predisposition to tumours and rupture, which are the more serious as boys are fre- quently employed, when the system is weakened by rapid growth, and is liable to he injuriously acted upon by the high temperature and dry' atmosphere. A pro- cess, however, has been brolight into use hy Messrs. Ap- pert, of Clichy, in. which they employ air stored under great pressure, so as ,to dispense altogether with the blowing by the mouth, except in a few cases. Not only is an unwholesome practice put an end to, but the manu- facture of the glass is considerably improved, both *OM the increased rapidity-ofexecution and the larger sizes of the pieces produced. Although Messrs. Apperts' pro-1 c,ess is the first one-that has come into practical develep- ment,-it is not the .first invention of the kind, a workman of Baccarat, so far back as 1824, having invented what was known as the Robinet piston with the same object of dispensing with the ordinary blowing. It was net successful, for the reason that it held so little air that only small pieces conld be-turned out. PHOTOGRAPHING LIGHTNING.—The Rev. Dr. C. Michie Smith, of Madras, sends the following interesting note to Nature :—" By papers received by last mail Fsee that , Mr. W. C. Gurley claims to have shown, by photo-1 graphing a flash of lightning, that the ordinary ;lotion, of forked lightning must be given up.. Ido not know whether this conclusion has been drawn from the photo, graph of a single flash or not, but you will see from the. enclosed photographs that the conclusion is an entirely false one. An examination of my photographs will show that all the flashes except one had the zigzag form; and that some of them are-magnificently forked. They resemble very closely the photographs of sparks from a Holtz electrical machine, taken by Mr. A. Matheson in Professor Tait's laboratory; and published in volume 27, part 3, of the 'Transactions' of the Royal Society'of Edinburgh. The amount of detail shown in the photo- graph of the tree illuminated by- the flash gives one a very good idea of the brightness, when we consider-that exposure cannot have exceeded' the millionth part-Of a second. I may add that my -first photograph was taken on , October 16th, 1883, and was circulated amongst friends immediately afterwards." THE BLENHEIM . PORTRAIT OF' CHARLES I. The. Athenalan gives the following micount of Van Dyck's. portrait of Charles I. lately bought for the National. Gallery from Blenheim Phlace‘ for £17,500. It was originally, ho doubt, painted for the king, and was sold' during the Commonwealth for £l5O. Another portrait of the king on a white horse passing under an arch, which is now at Windsor, was sold on the same occasion for £2OO. A third equestrian portrait, probably a copy, was sold for £4O. The great' Duke of Marlborough bought the Blenheim portrait at Munich. In the British Museum is a fine sketch for the trees in the background, The painting is on canvas, in excellent condition, and' shows the king bareheaded, otherwise in complete shining black armour, mounted an a dun-coloured horse, seen in profile, advancing to tha-left, and attended' by- his equerry, Sir Thomas Morten,. on foot, and holding• the royal helmet. On a richly-framed tablet suspended from a tree is written Carolvs. r: Rex. Megrim. Britairke. In the king's hear hangs the large pearl it was his cus- tom to wear, which, after his execution, was given to the' Princess Royal. Mr. Scharf tells us that Queen Mary of Orange authenticated this jewel in her own writing-1. William 111. gave it to the Earl of Portland; it is now' in the possession of the Duke orFortland. BORIC ACID AND INFECTION.—W. M. Williams writes in' the Gentleman's Magazine:—ln one of my notes ("Cholera Germs and Boric Acid"); I suggested that by taking boric acid in' small quantities daily with our food we may be "rendering ourselves antiseptic like the mutton" described in another note; that we may avail OurselVes of the wonderful properties of this nearly tasteless sub- stance by using it to preserve 'ourselves against all dis- eases that really are propagated by agencies analogous to those which induce putrefaction, whether they- be' bacilli, bacteria, micrococci, or thechemical disturbancest of old-fashioned pathology. Oa July 21' M. de .Cyon read a paper to the Academy of Sciences in Paris, show- ing that he had asked himself the same question, and, being more industrious than myself, was not content with the mere asking, but set to work laboriously to answer it. He describes the Desalts of experiments-that have extended over a period of six years. He finds that common borax is' a powerful antiseptic, and that itmay be taken internally in sufficient 'quantity to preserve' the body from all contagions caused by parasites or mi- crobes without producing any functional' dtturbanee. For the prevention of cholera he recornmendathat boric acid or a solution of borax be applied to allthe- external mucous membranes, and about six grains :of borax to Ibe taken every 24 hours with. the food and drink; His experiments indicate that it' not only acts directly on the Microbes that may have e,stablithed colenies in the intestinal canal, but that it also attacks the bacilli that are breeding in the blood. I, THE LARGEST COLOSSUS IN THE WORLD.—Mt• FIiTICTSFS 'Petrie, who has long been engaged in excavating at San Tanis, the ancient Zoan, in Lower Egypt; has dis- covered further portions of the cut-up colossus of Mimeses 11. These fragments, viz., an ear,. atoe; pieces of an arm, &c.—mere chips of a few tons each—though they represent but a very small portion of the whole, hade enabled Mr. Petrie to measure, de,scribey,and weigh the shattered giant with absolute certainty. He proves it to have been the mostmtupendous colossus known to have been sculptured by-the hand of ' man. Those statues which approach nearest to him id-site' are the colossi of Aboo-Simbel; the torse of the Ramesseum, and the collosi of the. Plain. These, however; are all seated figures, and, with the ereception of the•torso, are executed in comparatively soft- materiala. But- the Rameses of Tanis is not only sculptured bathe. obdurate red granite of Assouan and designed uponar mach larger scale than any of these, but he stood ereet and crowned 100 ft. high,from top to toe, or 115 ft. high Mcluding his pedestal. div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
CROSS-BRED FOWLS.

We have often in this column spoken in favour of i cross-bred fowls, and many readers of The Examiner ' have spoken well of the crosses recommended by us. But as we like to allow both sides of a story being heard, we give the following extract from an American con- temporary showing the opposite view : " I have frequently (says the writer) been led to speak 1, of the injudicious crossing of fowls, as I have had some experience in former years. Long since I arrived at the conclusion that there is nothing like a pure-bred fowl for all purposes. My business with poultry has been the production of eggs). and to obtain that breed that would give the greatest amount with the least expendi- ture of food, or numbers. I have found a breed that at present answers the purpose; after having been regard- less of outlay. This breed is the Brown Leghorn. Some ten or fifteen years ago this variety was comparatively little known, consequently prices were high. I procured a trio, however, from a breeder of fancy fowisoit a price that would have bought three good sheep, and to this day have never found cause to regret it.. The fotvls were very small, and the first season I was unfortunate in not raising any chicks from them. The trio con- sisted of an old hen that did not lay more than two sit- , tings of eggs, and a young, very immature cock and ' pullet, to all appearances full brother and sister. They were very finely plumed, and thoroughly pure, but poorly kept. In the autumn I purchased nine more equally as fine, and possessing more size. The ,next season I raised as fine broods as to size and number as I have ever met with. Being the first to introduce the fowls into the county, a humber of egg were sold for hatching purposes at prices that might be termed fancy. The first winter the hens last bought laid eggstnough to pay their express charges, even at com- mon market rates, and when the hatching season opened they soon paid for themselves. At one time there were no Leghorns in the county of this variety, but those descended or directly procured from these fowls, I have never abandoned this breed, and consider it one of the very best for egg production. They are quiet, tract- able, and easily managed. When r hear complaints about brown Leghorns I know that the fowls are not managed rightly. My birds are of good size for the breed, are constantly confined, and never know what it is to be hungry or thirsty. The consequence is I have eggs the whole year round, of uniform colour, quantity, quality, and size. My eggs are now commanding six cents per &men more than market price, sold side by side with other eggs. For the table the fowls are small, but of unexceptional quality. They are uniform in size and quality. This is the reason why I like thoroughbred fowls and object to crosses. I have, however, a few cross-bred fowls that have been raised from the sitters which I have to keep. A Leghorn crossed on a Brahma may and may not make a good fowl. There might be obtained some good.layers, but such would be the ex- ception, not the ride. For culinary purposes, while the amount of flesh is increased the quality is reduced. Where a regular busines of raising eggs is maintained, aa with the writer, thdroughbred fowls, and non-sitters at that, are by far the best. I only raise sufficient chicks annually- to keep the stock good, and dispose of the old birds."

With much that is said about the Leghoms our rea- ders will be aware that we cordially agree, and there- fore no more need be said on that score. But we may be allowed to give another letter that recently appeared in an American journal, which bears out what we have indicated, for, be it remarked, we have never suggested indiscriminate, bur systematic crossing. This writer says:—" While the several pure-bred fowls that we have kept have all been good layers, we, must say that none have equalled the laying record of some of the many crosses we haVe made. This is nothing strange, as the new life that such crosses give to the fowls should be shown in their extra ptolificness. This has been our pleasing results of each cross, almost regardless of what material is used in the formation of the fowls, and, ac- cording to our experiments, the good effects did not cease with the first cross, as most writers assert it will, but was fully as strong in the chicks reared from these cross-bred fowls as in the first progeny. And even when these crosses were used to cross again with common fowls or with other pure breeds the results were about the same—a fowl of splendid laying qualities. Some fine Houdan hens mated with a Brown Leghorn cock gave a fine lot or jot black hens, cocks dark breasts and red' backs and hackles. For great laying qualities we have rarely seen the equal of these hens. Some were quite large, too; one, we-remember, weighed over 71b5. But they were usually about the size of Brown Leghorn hens. Eggs were white as could be, and as large as large Houdan eggs. These hens crossed with,Plyrciouth Rocks gave a larger Dominique-coloured fowl, hut; were not quite as good layers in summer, being inclined to sit occasionally. They were good winter layers, hew- ever; had light-coloured legs, and Were a fair market fowl, dressing rather more flesh than Black Spanish. The fifth toe and crest had very nearly disappeared, showing only in a few specimens, and very slightly at that. ' A few feathers at the base of the slmll and as slight bifurcation of the hind toe were all the ex- ternal traces of Houdan blood, but the eggs skewed plainly, and the fowls when cooked showed.by the fine quality of flesh that the French fowl bleed was still alive. Some of these fowls, left to themselves on alarm near by, soon reverted to the jetty black of the first cross, The blood appeared to be very strong. We were shown a few hens the other day, which, said the farmer, with pride, 'are some, of the old Houdan-Leghorn cross. I never saw the beat of these hens for laying. Every morning, when I come to the barn therare on the nest.' 'But they are very small,' we remarked. 'But they lay a larger egg than any of your Brahmas or Cochins,' said our friend enthusiastically. One of the- best crosses we have lately seen was produced by- mating a Lang- shan cock with some brown-colouredhens of no parti- cular breed, as far as we could learn. They were mostly dark-coloured fowls, their only weak point being their dark and sometimes slightly feathered; /bgs. They were immense as winter layers, and as hatchers and mothers I think they ;would have' been hard to beat. However, this rather light-coloured skin and dark legs and beaks were fashionable in the eyes of farmers and others selling live poultry, and for that reason; this crosa is not to be recommended. Light Brahmas and any medium-sized fowl are suitable for general purposes. and when crossed give us a good fowl for all farm pur- poses. We have crossed this fowl with several other breeds and the common fowls, and have never failed to get a good practical every-day fowl. They wer,-; in every case good winter layers, and; unusually good hatchers too. Occasionally a hen or pullet would be found that was as strictly a non-sitter as any Leghorn or liam.hurgh. But while, if wanted only eggs and flesh for market, we might go, on crossing, we would, if we owned a farm, keep some breed in its purity, as we could then have the fancier's pleasures as well as his profits,"

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

So long as the— weather keeps and open, the chickens may be allowed' to roost in the trees, or wlrrever they like; but the nights and mornings are just now and again beginning to feel a little chilly, so that careful watch must be kept in orderto check at the very first all colds or other diseases. For this rea- son it is most important that the stock should be con- stantly looked over, as probably if roup gets a firm hold on a yard at this season, of the year it will be very diffi- cult indeed to get it out again. One of the best pre- ventives is to mix in, the soft food every morning a small quantity of stimulating powder, such as the ;aromatic compound' we have occasionally referred to, :and to give the soft food hot as soon after daylight as possible. This prevents the birds getting their stomachs chilled, and attention to so small a matter as this will be found to have a vionderful effect in keepingtbs birds free from disease.

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.

SATURDAY. This court was again opened on Saturday, the revieing' barrister being Mr Millis, Coventry, of the Inner Temple. The Liberals were represented by Mr Henry Roberts (secre- tary to the Liberal Association), and the Conservatives by Mr E J Nicholson, solicitor, andl Mr John Hampson (Con- aervative agent). A BONK EMPLOYE'S VOTE.—Samuel Loy, a porter, &c., at Parr's Bank, Warrington, claimed a vote in respect of the house he lived in. The vote was ol*cted to by the Liberal" In answer to Mr Roberts, he stated that the house be °ma' pied was situated within the gates of the bank. Re did not know whether any person other than the porter would be allowed to live in that house.-..Mr Roberts: Does not your arrangement with the bank compel you to live at this house? No; Icould live outside if I thought proper.--Mr Roberts: Will you, swear you could still retain your situa- tion at the bank if you gave up that house? I think so:* Loy then stated that he bad formerly lived outside the bank premises and performed the same duties,. bat in answer tre Mr Roberts be admitted that that was prior to his present' house being built.—Ultimately, the consideration of the' claim was adjourned for the production of further evidence to show as to whether or not Loy was compelled to live in his present house.—On Monday the case was further coo' sidered, and the vote disallowed. CLAIM BY A GEHMAN.—A German, named William Freidank, claimed a vote. This was opposed by the Con- servatives. He had, he said, been in England three Years and three months. When asked in English if he bad been legally nationalised, he said he could not tell; but on being questioneel in German by Mr Nicholson, he replied that be was still a German. The vote was not allowed. A MONTH IN Bickley, a labourer, resid. ing in Morris's Court, off Silver.street, claimed a vote, but was objected to by the Liberals on the ground that he bad been in prison during the qualifying year. On being Pea. tioned, Bickley said that he had been fined for being drunk, and in default of paying the fine had gone to prh;on for a mcnth.—Mr icholson held that in the present ease the man's residence could not be said to have been severed. When in gaol he had simply been in the position of a man away on a holiday or a visit. If be had been committed to pri,,on without the option of a Sne it would have been a different thing; it could then have been said that his occu- pancy was severed.—The Revising Barrister withheld his decision, but afterwards the vote was allowed on the ground that Bickley had had the option of a one. MONDAT.

The court was again openea en Monday. THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL MASTER'S VOTE. Mr Rbert Davies appeared to claim a vote for the Rev E J Wilcock, o headmaster of the Warrington Grammar School.—The claim wee objected to by the Liberals, and Mr Roberts called at- tention to the following item contained in the rules of the school, viz:—" Every future headmaster, previously to entering into office, shall be required to sign a declaration, to be entered in the minute book of the governors, to the following effect :—‘l,-- declare that I will always to the best of my ability discharge the duties of headmaster of the Warrington Grammar School during my tenure et the office, and that if I am removed by the governors, I Will acquiesce in such removal and will thereupon relinquish an claim to the mastership and its future emoluments, and de- liver up to the governors, or as they direct, possession of all the property of the school then in my possession or occupa- tion.'— The headmaster shall dwell in the residence ro- signed for him. He shall have the oacupation and use ot such residence and of any other property of the school of whieh he becomes the occupant as such headmaster, in re- spect of his official character and duties, and not as ten- ant, and shall, if removed from his office, de- liver up possession of such residence and other , property to the governors, or as they direct. He shall not, except with the permission of the governors, permit- ' any person not being a member of his family to occapr such residence or any part thereof.' "—lt was in cOO5O queues of these clauses, Mr Roberts said, that he objected to Mr Wilcock's claim.—Mr Nicholson contended that it was a ease in which the vote ought to be allowed. If Mr cooks was not a tenant he must be something.—Mr Daviesaid that many schoolmasters were in the position of Mr Wilcock, and he could not think that the Legislature in- tended to disfranchise them all.—The 13.1.1vieter said he 80- posed this state of things would be revised in the new bill. butat present he must disallow the vote.

A DION-RESIDENT'S VoTa.---eMr R Davies also appeared to claim a vote for Benjamin Sharp, Sankey-street. The Liberals objected to this claim, and in answer to questions, Mr Davies said that Mr Sharp lived a::,Bath, and bad a' manager to look after his business in Warrington. There were several furnished rooms belonging to Mr Sharp in Sankey-street, bat Mr Davies could not say whether or not Mr Sharp had slept in them for years past. The vote not allowed.

Mr TM PAMPISON'S VCY6.—A vote was claimed by T M Pattison in respect of a bed-room and sitting-room at 10, Bold-street, but objected to by the Liberals—Mr Pattisou stated that he lived at Waterloo, but as his business caused him frequently to stay at nights in Warrington be retained these two rooms He had not slept in them for more than twelve months back, but would have done so if he had not stayed with friend% During the coming winter he would probably have to use them frequently.—The Barrister re- served his decision, but on Tuesday he said he would allow the vote. A QUESTION. SOP COMPULSORY Rustramm—Mr Watson. timekeeper at Messrs P Stubbs and Co., file manufacturers, Scotland-road,.claimed a vote in respect ot his residence. Be t was objected to by the Liberals on the ground that his resi- ,dence in the house at Messrs Stubbs's premises was corn- ' pulsory. It was stated in evidence that the house Watson lived in had been built at the same time as the rest of the premises, and that he had gone to live in it on his being SP' pointed timekeeper, the previous timekeeper having al3° Jived in the same house. The vete was net allowed. TUESDAY. The Court was again held on Tneada7.. A PECULTAO NANE.—Sam tael Robert Fredeux, of Orford,

was objected to by tha Liberals, and it appeared that his name was down on the list as Robert Samuel Perdue Re had not, he said, made that claim of his own accord, but had been urged to do so by a man who came to his house.—Mr Nicholson contended that it was clear that the wrong name was intended to belong to the claimant, but the Barrister held that the vote mild not be allowed under the circum- stances; DIS4II7AZIFIED Br BANKRUPTCY.-A, claim bv Thomas

Owen, Sankey-street, was again hear d 4 its consideration having been adjourned because of the Liberals objecting tn. Mr Owen on the ground of his having been bankrupt and his business having been placed in the hands of trusteeo- during the qualifying period. This objection was not ad- mitted, but on Tuesday Mr Roberts produced the managing clerk oft Mr Percy Davies, who stated that he had searched, the file in reference to the proceedings ,re William Owen and Sons. The file oy the 17th October, 1883, showed that an appointment of the receivers was made, and on the 18th October Mr Voisey was appointed a trustee, and the tree -- tees wore released on the 11th June, 18841.—The vote waa. not allowed. At the close of the court the Barrister expressed big thanka for the help he had received from the party adlo- catespand Mr Roberts, in reply, stated that he felt person- ally deeply indebted to his Honour fer the patience he laad displayed throughout the Revision, and the uniform cour- tesy/which had marked his cond-.mtof the proceedings.

The jury found that the child "Died from blood,poisoninff following vaccination," but acquitted of blame the medic" men concerned. FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.
NEWS FROM GORDON.-THE SIEGE OF KHIR-
TOUNI RAISED.

- Cam, SAMIDAY.—The Mudir of pongsle. telegraphs from Ambnkol that Gordon Pasha's messenger brought alto- gether eighteen despatches, including two or the Sheikhs of Kabbalish, which have been delivered, and two for his son-in-law, who, however, had been previously executed in public by one of the Vain Prophet's Ameers to overawe the people and compel them to join him. This Ameer and many chiefs fell in the battle of Korti. Gordon's messenger reports that on Atgust 24th the Anteer Abu Khanga and an army coming from Kordofan were slaughtered by Gor- don's troops, and that another fight took place on the night of the 30th ef August, in which the siege of Khartoum was raised, and the Sheikhs Sidi, his son, and followers were 'killed. The Mudir adds that this news is confirmed by a letter from Elmoos Bey, who Rays he has occupied and is bolding rfalEeyeh with Egyptian soldiers. The Shaggiet tribe and others had come in and tendered their submission. Samar was in perfect safety. The population of Berber have recovered their fright at the anticipated descent of Gordon. The chiefs have all voluntarily submitted, asking for mercy, and have made a compact swearing on the Koran that they will no longer follow the False Prophet—a com- pact which they have eince observed. The first battalion of the 'loyal Sussex Regiment has arrived at Tangour. Two hundred men of the mounted infantry have left Wady Haifa for Dongola with six months' provisions. The Sphinx left for Agig this morning for the purpose of communicating with the Beniawer tribe. Major Cherraside to-day sent the Sheikhs ot Ashraff to the Governor of Massowah, at &mit, on a mission concerning the evacuation of Kassala. The attacks upon Suakim have ceased. The Atnarars have re-occupied the Berber road, driving back the Haded-Haden- dowas as far as Stnkat, but they experience difficulty in the commissariat. Four Amarar hostages, who were released by the Governor, are reported to have been killed while on their way to rejoin their tribe. CAIRO, MONDAY.—A telegram received here from the Trench Consul at Khartoum confirms the news that the siege at that place had been raised, and that the neighbour- hood had aeon freed from the rebels. The Consul states that the victualling of Khartoum is comparatively easy, and ' further announces that he is going with General Stewart and Mr Power to Dongola. The Mandi is reported to have sent messengers to the neighbourhood of Suakim. He has heard of General Gordon's recent successes against the rebels, and intends, it is said, to despatch troops to Khar- toum. In accordance with Lord Wolseley's recommenda- tion, the movement of two battalions of infantry to Egypt has been suspended for the present. WADY HALF:I, SUNDAY.—The mounted infantry em- barked to-day at Sarras, and sailed for Dongola. One com- pany of Egyptian troops leaves Sutras for Dal, and three other companies leave here for Sevres to assist in the con- struction of the railway. The steamer Gin.* with a steam launch, left here this morning to ascend the cataract. Small native boats are being rapidly pushed up the second cataract. _

.ALEXANDRIA, MONDAY.—The hired transport Pelican ar- rived here to-day with a cargo of Vile' boats. &TAMIL MONDAY —The Amarars have gained a further victory over the Hadendowa tribes, with the less, however, of 30 killed. It is reported that the Hadendowas have an- pealed to Osman Digma for assistance. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Temp publishes a telegram from Men stating that Harm, Berbeira, and Zeila have been evacuated by the Egyptian garrisons, the two latter places being subsequently occupied by British troops. WADY HALFA, WEDNESDAY, E?.M.—A telegram has been received here from the Mudir of Dongola. dated yesterday. stating that the country was quiet and safe. The Mudir has passed through all the districts of the Mudiriah and ex- horted the people to remain quiet, assuring them that the time of the False Mandi was over. 'The telegraph line is now complete as far as Ambukol, near Debbeh. MALTA, TIIIIRSDAY.—The hired transport Bulimba has arrived here from Plymnuth, and will sail to-day for Alexandria with 248 officers and men of the Royal Marines.

The detachments of men from each battalion of the Guards forming the Camel Corps were invented on Thurs- day morning at Wellington Barracks, London, by General Gipps, commanding the home district. The men appeared in high spirits. The Duke of Cambridge afterwards ad- dressed the men, saying he was sure they would do their duty, and upheld the honour of the Guards. His Royal Highness then left for Aldershot.

div.head: EXPEDITION PREPARATIONS.
div.p: THE EXPEDITION PREPARATIONS.

The transport Schelat, which arrived at Portsmouth on Friday, sailed on Saturday evening for Egypt, after having embarked 24 Nile boats and several hundred tons of stores. In consequence of a telegram from Lord Welseley, fresh orders respecting the reinforcements for Egypt were tele- graphed in various directions from the War Office and Admiralty on Monday. Lord Wolseley did not at present require the two battalions ordered on horn Malta—the let Shropshire and the 2nd South Yorkshire will not go out for their relief. Instead of the 11.400 camel troops and 500 drafts being conveyed in the National Company's steamer Erin, they will embark in the Deccan and Anstralia. A telegram was received at the Albert Docks, on Monday, stating that the fitting of these two ships was to cease, and later a telegram to the Erin cleared the workmen from her decks. Later in the day the Deccan and the Australia were directed to go round to Portsmouth to embark the camel troops next Friday. Orders have been received at Chatham garrison directing a detachment of the,Army Hospital Corps Lobe held in readiness for embarkation. It is reported that Lord Wolseley will proceed to the•base of his operatioss at Wady Haifa almost immediately., 'January 15th was the date mentioned by Lord Wolseley for reaching Khartoum, but many military men are of opinion that Major Kitchener will arrange a meeting of General Gordon's force with that of Lord Wolseley's midwaybetween Berber and Ehartoum, which would bring the date of meeting to about Christmas. A large draft of the let Battalion of the Berkshire Regiment was to have left Chatham on Tuesday morn- ing for Egypt, but the order bas•been countermanded forth present. Forty more boats for the Nile expedition were despatched on Tuesday evening from Portsmouth in the transport St. Louis. The troopship Orontes took on board on Tuesday afternoon the Staffordshire Regiment, with whom she was to have sailed at once for the West Indies, but her de- parture has been delayed owing to the non-arrival of cer- tain baggage which was despatched from London on Satur- day. _

, CAIRO, TUESDAY MORNING —Lord Wolseley and staff start for Wady Haifa on Saturday, where they will probably remain three or four weeks. Egyptian troops will probably garrison Wady Haifa and Ltongola after the British forces advance. A merchant who has arrived from Obeid reports that the Mandi has 25,0 N followers, 10,000 being armed with Remingtons. He has2o Krupp guns. There are 20 Europeans still at Obeid. On Wednesday afternoon a detachment of the Royal Horse Guards and Life Guards, selected to form part of the camel corps on the Nile Expedition, proceeded to Aldershot, one detachment travelling from Windsor, and the other fro m Wellington Barracks, London. 'ri'he men were in their Eght- ing dress, with isandoliers far ,cartridges slung over their shoulders. On their march from the barracks to the Water- loo railway station they were loudly cheered. The som of one hundred thousand pounds ha gold wassent to Lord Wolseley On Wednesday. The money was shipped in the steamer Australia, which left the Royal Albert Itooks with the Deccan to receive tke Camel Corps and other troops at Portsmouth. MOVEMENTS OF THE MAHOL

CAIRO, TUESDAY.—Major Cherrnside telegraphs that sin of the Mandi's special envoys have arrived at Tamai, and distributed the Mandi's letter inciting the tribss to revolt. It is reported that the Mandi on hearing of Gordon's ac- tivity sent reinforcements aboat the middle of August te prosecute the Khartoum seige with vigour. WADY HALFA, SUNDAY. Maor Kitchener telegraphs from El Debbah that everything is .quiet there. At Me-- rawi and Berber the people are much frightecad by news of the British expedition, and some of the inhabitants are leaving WADY HALFA. TUESDAY. General Earle sad Colonel Stewart have arrived here. General Stewart wilt proceed to Dongola, where he will take up his command. A cmall store boat has struck upon a rock at Samucla.

div.head: EGYPTIAN DEBT.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN DEBT.

- - CAIRO, SIINDAY.—The members of the Caisse of the Pub- lic Debt yesterday protested against theeriolation,et the Law ••cf Liquidation. The Consuls-General have not vet protes- ted, as several of them are awaiting instrzctions *item their ,zespective Governments. CAIRO, Moster.—lt is stated that the French Diplo- matic Agent has been instructed to demandl the withdrawal ,of the letter addressed by the Minister oI Finance to the ,Caisse of Public Debt suspending the sinking fund. The acting representatives of Germany and Austria have been instructed to enter a vigorous protest againet the suspension, but the latter -las applied for farther instructions. Lord Northbrook will leave here to-morrow for Mor.andria. CABao. WEDNESDAY —The acting Russian Consul-G en- oral has been instructed to join In the protest of the other Powers against the suspension of the Sinking -Fend. In I:4- lomatic circles it is stated that an Identical Note protesting Limply, but strongly, against the action of the Egyptic.n Government will to-morrow be forwarded to Nubar Pasha by the Consuls-General of France, Germany, Russia, and Aus- tria. The proposal of the French Government that the withdrawal of Nubar Pasha's letter should be demanded will be left fcr subsequent diplomatic action. Meanwhile, the European administration of the Egyptian railways and ee the Customs have, in compliance with eke ministerial order, paid into the Ministry of Finance, the fcrmer £ESPXO and the latter £512,000- OFFICIAL PROTEST. CAIRO, TRVRSDAV.--The diplomatic representatives of G-ermany, Austria, France, and Russia visited Nubar Paella separately at a late hour this afternoon, and presented to him an identical Note protesting against the anepension of the Sinking Fund. FRANCE AND CHINA. SAIGON, SATDIZDAY.—Tbe French transports Saone and Nive have left here for the north of China with troops and ammunition. PARES, SATURDAY.—Tbe Catholic Missions in Paris have received a despatch from Hong Kong, dated the 13th inst., announcing that the Chinese have destroyed the Catholic chapels in the province of Canton, and that 8,000 Christians are homeless. Snexcinar, MONDAY,.—In addition to the previous cumuli- Cations caused by the Puma, tb.9 destruction of the fleet of

police junks in the Min has removed the mackinery for the suppression of piracy wherever it is pursued, and will neces- sitate the performance of police functions by the neutral fleets. The Russian Consuls have been ordered, wherevev the French Consuls leave, to protect French interests. Tke Russian fleet numbers one ironclad, three cruisers, two cor- vettes, six gunboats, and the announced reinforcement is three ironclads. This strength, considering the smallness of Russian interests, is significant. TIENTSIN, WEDNESDAY.—Li Hung Chang has been re- instated in all the offices he formerly held. TIENTSIN, MONDAT.—The Governor-General of Fukien has been dismissed and degraded. Chang Thou Tung, Governor of Tukien, and Mu Tartar, General of Fukien, have not only been excused for the success attending the French arms in the Min river, but have also been praised for their own action, and permitted to retain their appoint- ments. .

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

ROME, BAVETRDAY.—The Pope has addressed a letter to Cardinal Jacobin', in which his Holiness, after applauding the measures taken by the authorities in Rome against the cholera. says that should the epidemic break out in Rome, he would, as a mark of affection for the Roman people, establish a hospital in the neighbourhood of the Vatican, the management of which would be intrusted to his Major Dome and to his physicians, Signori Ceddarelli and Valen- tione. For this purpose the Pope has set aside the sum of a million francs. The hospital, which his Holiness has pro- mised to visit in person, is destined for the inhabitants of the -suburbs of Bourgo and Trastevere. HOME, MONDA.Y.—The official bulletin reports that during the last forty-eight hours there have been 410 cases of cholera and 209 deaths in the province of Naples. In the province of Aguila, 5 cease; Bergamo, 30 cases and 21 deaths • Caserta, 13 cases, 3 deaths; Cremona, 9 cases.; Cuneo;24 cases, 23 deaths; Genoa, 60 cases, 29 deaths, of which 37 cases and 18 deaths were at Spezia; in the pro-1 ,vince of Parma there were 10 cases and 6 deaths; Regg4o d'Emilia, 8 cases, 4 deaths. There were several isolated cases in other provinces. MADRID, MONDAY.—Several fresh cases were reported yesterday, and to-day it is reported that eleven new cases and five deaths have occurred in the province of Alicante, and six cases and three deaths in the province of Tarragona. PARIS, MONDAY.—SiX deaths from cholera have occurred in the department of the Pyrenees Orientales. There was one fetal case yesterday. TOnLox, MONDAY.—No deaths from cholera have oc- curred here during the last twenty-four hours. There are still eight persons affected. ROME, TIIESDAY.—ro-day's official bulletin states that from midnight of the 21st to midnight of the 22ad 251 eases of cholera and 82 deaths occurred, in addition to 70 deaths among patients previously under treatment. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—To-day's official bulletin reports that during the lee twenty-four hours four fresh cases of cholera and two deaths have occurred in the province of Alicante. No returns have been received to-day from the provinces of Lerida and Tarragona. Roma. WEntrEsoaar.—To-day's official bulletin 'reports that 264 cases and 75 deaths have occurred in the town of Naples, exelusive of 51 deaths among patients previously under treatment, and that 47 cases and eight deaths, exclu- sive of 17 fatal cases among patients previously attacked, have occurred in the remainder of the province. AUSTRIA.—THE NEW ALPINE TUNNEL. BERGENZ, SATURDAY.—The Arlberg Railway was to-day opened by the Emperor Francis Joseph with much cere- mony. His Majesty, accompanied by the Ministers Count Taafe and Baron, and most of the leading monitors of Par- liament, went over the new line and through the tunnel in a special train. THE EARTHQUAKE IN AMERICA. NEW YORK, SATURDAY.-*AO earthquake was felt in many points in Indiana, Ohio, and Ontario, and in some parts of Kentucky. The shock was also perceptible at De- troit, Cincinnati, and at Fortwayne, Indiana. No damage was done. The shock was very slight at Cincinnati an% Fortwavne. NEW YORK, Sr/lawn—The car works of the Granl Trunk Railway at London, Ontario, have been destroyed by fire. The loss is estimated at 400,606 dollars. THE AFGHAN FRONTIER COMMISSION. QUETTA, SATURDAY.—The Afghan agents have arrived at the Helmand, and are comtnunic sting with Col. Ridge- way, at Mushki. They are collecting supplies and co-opera- ting heartily. ARREST OF ANARCHISTS.

VIENNA, To Esney.L-The arrest i; officially announced of 21 persons charged with being accomplices of the five pro- prietors of the secret anarchist printing ,establishment, who were arrested some time ago. Burglaries have been committed at some gunpowdr and dynamite stores near Vienna.
RIOTS BETWEEN GERMANS AND P.USSIANS. 10 PERSONS KILLED, 30 WOUNDED.

BEnus, WMNESDLY.—lntelligeoce from St Petersburg states that sanguinary riots recently occurred at Rownv, in the Government of Saratow, between some C ermans resident at that place and Russian peasants. Ten persons, including a police officer, were killed, and thirty others severely in- jured in the encounter, which asmuned the character of a band-to-hand fight. On the despatch of the news' order had not entirely been re-established. The Governor of Saratow had left for the scene of the disturbance. RIOT IN A. BURMESE GAOL.—RUNDREDS OF CONVICTS KILLED.

CALcurri, THURSDAY.—A serious outbreak has occurred at Mandalay gaol, and was only suppressed after great bloodshed. Several hundred convicts are reported to have been killed. THE MITRE BLACK SEA, I'LEET.

ST. PETERSEMMG, THDREDAY.—The keels of two new ironclads will be laid down next week at Cebastopol. These vessels, to be named Sinope and Tschesine respectively, will Form the nucleus of the future Black Sea fleet.
THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION IN CA-NADA.-THEIR
nal ER BURNED.

NEW YORK, THURSDAY.--A number of members of the British Association had a narrow escape of death last night. They were on their way to Quebec in a steamer, when it ctught fire near Toint an Pie, and was burned to the water's edge. The crew and .passengers were fortunately saved.—Daily News.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

HARVEST THAMIESGIVING.— The harvest thanksgiv ng services were held at the Parish Church on Sunday, when two sermons werefreached by the Rev F W Willis, vicar of All Saints', Wellingborough; Mr. Stammers presided at the organ with his usual ability. Collections were made in aid of the choir fund, and amounted to £l4 de 91d. LICENSIXG SESEMNS.—The adjourned licensing sessions for Prescot were held on Thursday, the sitting magistrates being Mr F W Earle and Mr W Pilkington. Six Widnes publicans were reported by Mr Superintendent Barker as having been convicted during the past year. These publicans were now called forward and admonished by the bench, and their licenses renewed. The offenders were—Alark Wright, Commercial inn; William W Lewis, Bridge Hotel ; Joseph Bell, Ship Ina:; John Gill, Manchester House; Tnomas Bradshaw. Church llotel : and William Ince, Stonemasons' Arms.

div.head: GOL BORNE.
div.p: GOL BORNE.

SINGERS' TA& NIDEVING.—The members of the Goltorne Wesleyan choir were on Wednesday night entertained to tea in the chapel by the kindness of several members of the congregation as an acknowledgment of the choir's gratuit- ous and efficient Services. A pleasant evening was spent. CATHOLIC CHAIPEL.—The annual charity sermons were preached in the Golborne Catholic Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev Father Byrne, of Golborne, and the Rev Father Melling, of Wigan. Notwithstanding the unfavourable weather there were large congregations. lhe singing was of the highest order. Collections were made in aid of the mission.

FIRE AT GOLF:LORNE PAPER MILL —A fire was discovered at Messrs Mitchell Arnott and Co., Paper staining Works, .on Wednesday. A boy employed by the firm had beet. -smoking during the dinner hour, and carelessly left his pipe on a boiler containing turpentine and resin. The liquid ignited and a large flame burst forth. Fortunately assis- tance was at hand, and the outbreak was a:romptly sup- pressed. Miss Urrsworan's MARRIAGE:GO Tuesday evening abent 50 young ladies connected with the GrolLorne Catho- lk Schools sat down to an excellent tea in the ochoolrooni, Worslev-street, at the invitation of Mrs Joseph Unsworth (late Miss Unswortla Park View), Who was recently mart:ed. A pleasing incident was the presentation of a very-handsome dinner service by the young ladies, as a wedding present to their late tpacher (Mrs Unswcrth). A pleasant evening was spent in games and dancing. A GCLLBORNE FARLIER NCPED.—A glaring piece of im- position has just been made known in Gelborne which is specially interesting to farmers. It appears that about ten weeks ago a travelling gipsy called upon a Golborne farmer and left ,a couple of horses to be put oat to grass "for a few days," under the preterribat they were lame. The animals continued in the farmer's possession until the night of the 12th inst. when they were missed from the field. In- formation was given to the Golborne police, who, on St-mclair last, traced•the Gipsy to Pemberton and there found the animals in his possession. The amen acknowledged that the horses had been in the care of the Golborne farmer, and stated that he sent a man with a erevereign to release them. Unfortunately tor the farmer the animals were released while he stept, and as a consequence he is very wrath. ,Q3l course his only redress is in the county court, and there ,he intends shortly to figure. Of late the practice has been been quite common in the Golborne district, but this is the , fist time a case has been successfully traced. During Rol incestigation it transpired a similar trick had been played at Pemberton, as many as 20 horses having been secretly re- moved from a farm there last Sunday. The same game has, been successfully played at Hindley, free pasture for horses' having been secured in every instance.

THRfFT.—The latest official returns of Provident Societies in England and Wales show a membership of six millions and funds amounting to thirtv-aight minions of pounds. The ROYAL eLOTHING CLUB, of 57. South Jobn-street, Liver- pool, is one of the institutions for the encouragement of thrift, whereby Oicthing may be obtained by egsy payments of is and 2s per week. This club has ben an enormous success in bane• fitting the middle and working elasses, the economies( system upon which it is conducted enabling it to supply Clothing of exceptional quality at moderate prices. The public should send for prospectus and join at once, as nothing is to be gained by delay in matters a thrlftiness.—"ldet,

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27, 1884.
THE REFORM AGITATION.

An open-air meeting was held at Salford on Saturday, to 'protest against the action of the Peers in rejecting the Fran- chise Bill and urging the abolition of the House of Lords. There were over a thousand persons present, including a strong section adverse to the object of the gathering. The principal speaker was Dr Pankhurst: The House of Peers, he said, was a mere body of Crown officials, whose only right to sit an vote was given to them by the Royal writs. If the Crown refused to issue writs the Lords had no remedy, and he certainly hoped the Crown would refuse to issue a writ again to Lord Salisbury. There were several other speakers who were frequently interrupted. In the end, how- ever, a resolution was carried by an overwhelming majority te the effect that the House of Lords was useless and dan- gerous, and ought, therefore, to be abolished. Sir Mathew Wilson, M.P., addressing his constituents at Wibsey, Bradford, on Saturday, said that the Peers had ex- hibited the height of folly in rejecting the Franchise Bill Bonld the Lords suppose that the two millions who were. thereby deprived of the franchise would not be angry and regard them with scorn? The Lords represented nothing but themselves, and if they repeated their almost incredible folly in the autumn session they would not only have the of the people, but their execration. The meeting was well attended, and the vote supporting the Government was gamed unanimously. Lord Houghton, who presided over a large assemblage which met in Pontefract Park in support of the Franchise sill, asked why it was that the Tories, if they gave towntnen the privilege of voting, stood in the way of the passing of the bill? It was because Lord Salisbury and his followers believed that they could make a party use out of this delay that they were doing it in the teeth of the will of the people, and even of their own prejudices.—Sir J WT Rams- den, M.P. said the Tories were all for reform in the ab- stract. The moment the Liberals proposed any practicable moans by which that reform could be carried into practice the Tories said " Oh, no, but that will not suit us at all— (laughter)—you want to separate the franchise and redis- tribution. We are so hot for redistribution that we cannot wait for that. We must have them both, and we are so de- termined to have them both together that rattier than not have the whole thing we will do without it altogether." (Laughter.) The Liberals bad not perhaps such a tremen- dous zeal about it as these new converts.
