If they could get the franchise and redistribution in one, so much the better, but if they could only get the franchise, let them be thankful for it, trusting next year for a further instal- ment.

A meeting. addressed by Mr R-nnie Wilkinson, of Ad- dington, Mr Charles Pollard, of Kettering, and other well- known local Liberals, was held. Resolutions condem- natory of the action of tho House of Lords and calling for a reintroduction of the Franchise Bill were passed. A meet- law of South Northamptonshire Liberals was held at liar- lestown, not far from Earl Spencer's residence at Althorn Several prominent members of the party from Northamp- ton were present, and here, too, res3lutions were carried with acclamation. . . . .

A large andlinthasiastic demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill was held at Ladibank, Fifeshire, and was at- tended by several thousands drawn frotse the surrounding villages. Resolutions were moved and supported by Mr R P Preston Bruce, MP. Mr Williamson, MP, Mr Dick Pod- die, NI P. Mr .1 Boyd Kinnear, and others, and were carried amidst great enthusiasm, calling upon Parliament to pass the Franchise Bill, but to supplement it with such other measures as were necessary to the full end equal represen- tation of the people, and declaring that the long-continued obstruction of useful legislation by the House of Lords was injurious to the prosperity of the country; and that the legislative functions of the hereditary Chamber ought fobs adjus,ed /SG as to bring it into harntony with the national sentiment. The meeting further expressed its continued ap- prova, of the policy of the present Government, and its en- tire conddence in its illustrious leader, Mr Gladstone. After the demonstration a meeting was held, at which Mr Boyd Kinnear, of Kinloch. proposed that the legislative authority of the !Ruse of Lords was hurtful to the nation, and that the existence of a second Chamber was inconsistent with the free government of the country as carried on through its selected representatives. The motion was carried unani- mously. Demonstrations in support of the Government were also held atHawick, Consett, Stirling, And Denby Dale, where speeches were delivered by many Liberal members of Par- liament.

A great demonstration was held at Duty lee. The proces- sion nambe.ed about 20,000, and was composed of 3,000 members of the Liberal Association, '12.000 representatives of every trade in the town, and 5;330 mill operatives. Ex- cursion trains were run to Dundee,and there were vast crowds in the -streets and on Magdalen Green, where speeches were delivered from five platforms.—Mr W E Baxter, M.P., said he was there because he was a veteran reformer of 1632, and because he had voted for every measure for the extension of the franchise in the House of Commons for nearly 30 years. (Cheers.) He believed that the Tories knew quite well that they had no chance of success in their present policy, but whatever they might do the Franchise Bill must be passed, and that very speedily. (Cheers.) One of the series of Conservative picnics was on Satur- day held in Charlton Park, the seat of Sir S M Marvon Wilson. About 25,000 tickets were said to have been issued., and something like one-fifth of that number of per- sons responded. There were tte usual sports—cricket, quoits, and lawn tennis; a band, .and refreshments under "special arrangements" in regard to moderation in price. Mr D R Plunket, M.P., proposed the first resolution, de- manding that the Franchise Bill should be ac- companied by a satisfactory measure for redistribu- tion. The reading of the resolution sufficed to show that there was a strong infusion of Liberals in the audience, for the names of the party leaders were met with groans of disapproval as well as with the cheers of their supporters, and the proceedings were subsequently con- ducted amid much noise, though with excellent temper. The right bon gentleman said they had met to give support to the-action of the House of Lords. (Cries of " Never.'l) He had found all over the country unanimity and enthu- siastnin support of the action of the Conservative leader. (Cheers and ironical laughter.)—Sir John Ellis supported the resolution, which was ultimately put amid much conk- sion, and declared to be carried zieor.. eon.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman was being moved, when there were cries raised to have the opportunity of voting against the resolu- tion. The dissentients, however, did not press their de- mand. The vote of thanks was carried. A demonstration in favour of a complete Reform Bill, and in approval of the action of the House of Lords, took place at Oldham. About 4,003 walted in procession, accom- panied by bands of music. The meetings were held at ClarksEeld, where there were three platforms. The Marquis of Waterford was the chief speaker, and be declared that it was all nonsense to say that the House of Lords was op- posed to the people. They were with the people upon the question of the franchise. If the (;,"overnment brought in complete Reform Bill there was scarcely a member of the House of Lords who would oppose it. It would be highly dangeroLs to give Mr Gladstone power to bring in such e Redistribution Bill as would please him, and it would be all the more,dangerous as regarded Ireland, because redistribu- tion would be made such as would increase the power of the Nationalists and decrease the representation of the Loyal- ists. A. resolution in favour of a complete Reform Bill was passed, but there was considerable opposition. Mr Houle's- worth, M.P.. spoke at another platform. A Conservative meeting was held on Tuesday night, in Dublin, which was attended by from '3,000 to 4,000 persons. The Hon. David Plunkett, M:P., wrote regretting his in- ability to attend, and urging special attention to the regi- ster, as a general election was almost certain to occur before next year. Mr J T Hamilton, M.P., said the present crisis had been brought on not by the House of Lords, but by the arrogant obstinacy of that self-willed dictator—Gladstone. 'The present Government had patronaged, encouraged, and most certainly had utilised, the Nationalists. Mr Osborne Morgan, M.P., at a meeting held at Wrex- ham, on Wednesday, in support of the'Franchise Bill, said that surely some among the two hundred Peers who followed Lora Cairns into the lobby were patriotic men, who at a great crisis in their country's history were not prepared to see their great ancestral Chamber turned into a mere ap- panage of the Carlton Club. MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.

On Saturday Mr Gladstone left Breehin Castle, the man- sion of the Earl of Dalhousie. At ridge of Dun and Forfar addresses were presented. At Glamis station the Premier was received by Lord Strathmore and driven off to •Glamis Castle. On Monday the Premier concluded bis visit here and proceeded to St. Martin's Abbey., where he will remain until Wednesday the guest of Eir Andrew Clark. Alt several stations there were demonstrations, and at Caper Angus Mr Gladstone 4343 received by Sir Donald Currie and S:r Andrew Clark. at. brass band was in attendance and accompanied the right bon gentleman to the Cross ia the centre of the town, where a platform had been erected and a large crowd had assembled. Mr Gladstone was enthusias- tically received. In response to several addresses, Mr GrAnsrowe maid the address pointed to theurgencv of careying the bill that was presented to Parliament during thellast session. (Oheers4 It was most urgent on more grounds than one. The,queation which he hoped would be settled the next month or the month after was the question of the franchise, but if unfortunately that question should not be promptly settled, the controversy would not fall to the ground. (Great cheering.) It would raise wider issues. Its 1834.,,f0r the ftrst time, reform was seriously proposed, and it created the utmost alarm in the weaker-minded por- tion of the community. Liam was not altogether unreason- able, although it was undeubtectly condemned by the results which were not only most beneficial to the country but abso- lutely eesential to its welfare and its good. (Cheers.) In 1887 and 1868 the same experiment was again tried, and the Tory party themselves did not venture to deny that the extension of the franchise bad been highly advantageone. This was the third time, and there wan this difference-: that whereas there was great novelty in the Act of 1832, and whereas there was considerable novelty in the adoption of the household suffrage, in what was now proposed there was I,no novelty at all. Therefore he contended that opposition to such a measure was divested of all appezrance of reason. and that not a plaueible argument could be urged in its de- fence. (Cheers.) Their opponents disclaim opposition to the measure. (Laughter.) That disclaimer was tolerably well understood. The Home of Lords had said, "We are quite willing to pass your Franchise Bill, provided you will join with it another bill which will so increase its complica- tion and its difficulty that an attempt to pass both together will be absolutely fatal to them, and we shall remain where we are." (Cheers.) Under those circumstances they assure you they have not rejected the bill. (Cheers.) They said also that it was contended that the House of Lords is no longer to have any independent term lie would not enter

upon the question how far the House of Lords had exer- cised with wisdom its legislative functions, but it was most ) unfair to say that they sought to extinguish independence ' because on the occasion of a Darticular bill they contend • that the House ought not to enter into conflict with the nation. (Loud cheers.) Mr Gladstone continued: For the ' last fifty years there has hardly passed a session in which the House of Lords has not interfered—materially interfered • —with the proceedings of the House of Commons; and yet, • although these interferences have in every case been adverse to Liberal Governments, and although the country has al- most always demanded to have and has had a Liberal Government, yet all those interferences have been borne with patience, and no one has attempted to circumscribe that very large province within which the House of Lords has followed its own will. But we do say that there are limits to those proceedings—(cheers)—and that whatever may be said about the manner in which a hereditary assembly may be of use for certain purposes, yet the best and wisest friends of the hereditary principle will say that it never can be safe when it is brought into con- flict with the representatives of the power of the country. We want this bill settled, and then we want to go on to give a more just distribution of seats, so that political power may be distributed over the country in a manner as equitable as possible. (Cheers.) They tell us that they, forsooth, are the people who are anxious for redistribution. That is, I tell you, they are proposing to us a proceeding which we know to be utterly impracticable. (Cheers.) But I want to know is it not natural that we should wish for re- distribution? Why, what will be one of the features of any possible Redistribution Bill ? Why, it will be that ten or twelve—possibly more—additional members will be given to Scotland. (Cheers.) And is it to be dreamed of for a mo- ment that I, or that any one of those who are acting with me in the Government, should be ether vise than eager to give more members, compatibly with justice, to a country where we are received, wherever we go, by meetings such as these? (Cheers,) These local meetings afford a proof that ' it is not only in those places where political intelligence circulates rapidly and powerfully, that there is a feeling on this matter' bat that it pervades the whole of the land. (Cheers.) You cannot touch the soil of the country at any point where there do not come up manifestations of this sentiment. You have conferred upon me a great honour; you have strengthened my hands by the manifesta- tion you have made. (Cheers.) The part that falls to us yon may rely upon it we shall endeavour to perform. The country will likewise, I believe, do its part so as to bring about the speedy, safe, and benefi- cial consummation which we all heartily desire. (Loud sheers). The party then drove off to St. Martin's Abbey. On the , terrace an address was presented from the non-electors and electers of the parish of Scone.—ln replying, Mr Gladstone mentioned the state to which his voice was reduced in re- plying to such addresses as testimony of the feeling of the people. The people of Scotland met wherever he had gone in such unreasonable and outrageous number for the purpose of testifying, that be had been comnelled to use his vocal organs in a manner that had left them in a mutilated condi- tion, and fit only to be sent into hospital. He continued: I , The nation, in my -opinion, has said, and is saying, that it , must have this measure. The question is not whether it , shall have the measure, but whether it shall have it at once, , and without the raising of other and wider controversies, or ' whether, in consequence of a more prolonged struggle, those and larger questions are also to be raised. Gentlemen, lam a man of peace. (Cheers.) I wish to see progressive legis- lation advance with rapidity, if we can have it. but with security and solidity, and with the general contentment and union of the people. (Cheers.) I rejoice to observe in Scotland that whole classes are united in regard ta this ex- i tension of the franchise. The other day a considerable l farmer, in reading an address to me, said, "We farmers have I no jealousy of the extension to those whom we employ." That is the right spirit in which to approach this question. There can be no doubt as to the issue of this conflict. God grant it may be speedy; God grant it may not disturb the harmony of this country, but may continue to place the concord of all orders on a yet more stable basis, and may contribute yet further to the strength, the union, and the prosperity of this great Empire. (Loud cheers.) Mr, Gladstone, acting on the advice of Sir Andrew Clark, spent Tuesday quietly. After luncheon, Mr., Mrs., and Miss Gladstone drove to Rosie Priory, the seat of Lord Kin- naird, where company had been invited to meet the Premier at dinner. _ . .

On Wednesday, the Premier, accompanied by Mrs and Miss Gladstone, and his medical adviser, Sir Andrew Clark, whose guest he has been, left St. Martin's Abbey on his return to Hawarden, via Dalawny. His progress south- wards was quite as demonstrativs as that northwards. At Perth the right hon. gentleman attended a public meeting, held in the Town Hall, where he was presented with addresses from the Perth Corporation, and from the Liberal Associations of Perth and Perthshire. In reply, the right hon. gentleman delivered a most important speech on the Franchise Bill, and the conflict which the House of Lords has provoked. The right hon. gentleman observed that the , manifestations of popular feeling In Scotland and England must convince the most incredulous that the representative Chamber was supported by the nation, and he hoped that the Opposition leader, who had been travelling in Scotland, 'having noticed the feeling which prevailed, would use his influence with the House of Lords to be wise while there s•was yet time. He asked if, under these circumstances, it was unreasonable for the House of Lords to recede from the —for them—illstarred, and, if continued, most menacing conflict which they had forced upon the country. if they per- severed in their rash and reckless course an enormous responsibility would rest upon them. They had to do with people who, whenever they said ." No," meant what they said. Enthusiastic as were the people of Scotland in the year 1880, he believed that now it was greater, purer, stronger, in favour of the Franchise Bill. Mr. Gladstone pointed out that he had done his best during the past half century to prevent the question of the power of the House of Lords being raised, bat if they re- fused the demand, the constitutional question would be raised, and the Lords would be the persons who had con- tributed to bring themselves and their authority into diffi- culty. The irresponsible Chamber could not always be coming into conflict with the power of the Representative Chamber, or the question would arise whether its power should be resisted. In conclusion be appealed to the Upper House to give way with grace and dignity and honour to the expressed will of the nation, which was backed by.the strength of immutable and eternal justice. An address was presented to Mr. Gladstone at Stirling. The weavers of Alva presented Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone each with a plaid. Addresses were presented to the right hon. gentleman at Harbert, Graharuston, Polmont Junction, and at Rattio, and he was loudly cheered as he drove to Dal- meny House. the residence of Lord Roseberrv. SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE AT NEWCASTLE.

Sir Stafford Northcote journeyed smith from Birnam to Newcastle on Monday. The right hon. gentleman, who jtas been the guest of Lord John Manners at St Mary's Towers, travelled by ordinary train to Edinburgh. At the Waver. ley Station he was recognised by a large amber of passen- gers on the platfarm, and was most respectfully saluted. Sir Stafford, without any demonstration whatever on the part of the porde, walked towards the Newcastle train, where be was shown into an engaged carriage. As the train slowly steamed out of the station the right hen, gentleman was loudly cheered, and bowed his acknowledgments. Sir Staf- ford appeared to be in good health. He drove into New. castle at half-past one on Taesday afternoon, and was en- tertained at a public luncheon in St George's Hall. The weather was bright, and at several points where he was re- cognised the right hon. gentleman was cheered. At luncheon which was attended by about SOO gentlemen, the Duke of Northumberland presided. Among the guests present were:— Earl Ravensworth, Earl Percy, Viscount Lumley, Sir Geo. Elliot, and Colonel Milne Holme. M.P. After luncheon the Chairman proposed the health of Sir Staff )rd Northcot2, to whom addresses were presented from 80 Conservative asso- ciations in Northumberland and Durham. This ceremony •concluded, 'Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTS rose to respond to the toast. After thanking those present for the cordial reception that had been accorded him, the right honourable gentleman proceeded to say they had before them just now the most important and critical straggle which this country had witnessed since the passing of the great Reform Bill of 1832, and it behove those who took part in the struggle to give themselves up to the work. Whatever might be the position of the Conservative party in the northern counties, whether they were in the majority or minority, they at all events wetedoing their work in a sound business-like way. What wauthe Franchise Bill going to do? It would not touch. or stall events hardly touch, the metropolitan or large or small boroughs, but it would the counties. There would be a large addition to the electorate, and if it was not joined with a Redistribution Bill they would find the effect of the intro:action of that large element would be to entirely des- treythe counties, which were at present the representatives of the Conservative party. He said that the effect of such a measure as the Franchise Bill, if not accompanied by re- distribution, would be of a most serious character to them. The remainder of the right honourable gentleman's speech was devoted to impressing on his followers the necessity of orgsnisation, and on taking his seat he was loudly cheered.

In the evening Sir Stafford addressed a meeting in the Circus. The building, although it accommodates 4,000 or 5,000 persons, was filled before the proceedings began. Mr W D Cruddas, the chairman of the Newcastle Conservative Association, occupied the chair, and amongst those present on the platform were Bid Percy, M.P., Sir M W Ridley, M.P., Colonel Milne Home, M.P., and others. Sir STAMFORD NORTHCOTE, who was cheered on rising, after thanking those present for the warmth of the recep- tion, said the mass of the working-men in England, as in Scotland, had displayed an intelligence and a desire to take their part in politics and in the discussion of the great ques- tions of the day., which was highly to their honour, and upon the whole highly advantageous to the country. (Cheers.)l All the Conservatives wanted was that any new Franchise Bill should be a measure for strengthening, and not over- throwing the constitution. Both parties desired the exten- sion of the suffrage; but one wished to go on in the dark and the other in the light. (Cheers.) What was to be done (Several voices," Pass the Bill," aad cries of "No.") He would say also pass the Bill, but do it in a rational manner. (Ckeers.) If they wished the Bill they had now the opportunity, because they would have a clear gassier) before them, and no other measures neces- sary to take up, because they had already made considerable progress by the discussion which took place last session on the Franchise Bill, and because it was quite in their power by bringing forward such a measure in a readable manner to abridge considerably the discussion that would take place. (Hear, hear.) He believed the Govern- ment rOuldsury the question through if they were disposed

to deal with it in the spirit of men who had their hearts and minds bent upon its settlement, but he did not think they would be able to if they took the course they did last session. (Cheers.) If they passed the Franchise Bill alone, they would have no power to compel the Radictls and extreme people to pass a fair Redistribution 'Bill. Sir Stafford proceeded to give some figures to show that the strength of the Liberal party lay in the small boroughs, and that unless something reasonable was done in regard to them the Conservative body would be entirely outvoted there, and practically disfranchised ; and also that the Sill, by pouring large numbers of really urban voters into the counties, would swamp and destroy the agricultural element. This was not fair, and it could not be tolerated by any rational people. There were many other questions upon which, if he had time, he could touch, and amongst them the administration of our finance. On that subject he would remark that it would be a very dangerous thing if by any changes they made they threw the whole power of spending money into the handset a differ- ent class from those who had to pay it. (Hear, hear.) That was a danger which threatened, not only the asses who had the money, but also the whole community. for they might depend upon it, if it was to go on, and if they were to have a strong administrative House of Com- mons unchecked by an independent House of Lords, they would find that matters would not rest there. They should not allow themselves to be misled by demagogues or people with crotchets and nostrums, or to be overcome by mere prejudice, but they should carry on the business of the em- pire, so far as it was in their power to do se, open the lines which their ancestors worked, and through which the great- ness of the empire had been made. (Cheers). Subsequently a res)lution was carried expressing contin- ued confidence in the right honourable gentleman, and ap- proving of the policy of the Opposition. Sir Stafford Northcote left Newcastle on Wednesday. At Derby he was met by a deputation from a Conservative club. The right hon. gentleman expressed his gratification at the success of the meetings he had attended in the North, and urged the Conservatives to get their arms ready, as he was convinced there would be a dissolution before very long.

div.head: AN ASHTON GENTLEMAN KILLED BY
div.p: AN ASHTON GENTLEMAN KILLED BY
LIGHTNING ON SNOWDON.

The coroner for Carnarvonshire' on Monday afternoon, held an inquiry at Llanberis as to the death of Mr Thomas Live- sley, Ashton-in-Makerfield, who was killed by lightning on Sunday afternoon. From the evidence it appeared that the deceased bad been staving at Prince Llewelyn Hotel, Beddgelert, on Friday, and left on Sunday, intending to cross Snowdon and make the descent on the Llanberis side, his luggage being sent on per road to the Padarn Villa Hotel, Llanberis. The ascent was safely made through a thick driving mist ; and soon after the summit was reached the rain, which com- menced falling heavily, drove Mr Livesley and others who had ascended the mountain into the two wooden huts which have been erected for the accommodation of travellers. These huts are bound with strong bands of iron, which are clamped into the rocks—a necessary precaution in such an exposed place against being blown over. Mr Livesley and two ladies, who bad also ascended from Beddgelert, sought refuge in the but on the left side of the cairn of stones which marks the summit, the fourth occupant being Mr Thomas Roberts, the proprietor. They had only just en- tered, when a flash of lightning struck the cairn, dislodging several heavy stones and making a clean passage through it. Then it struck the hut, and the electric fluid passing over one of the ladies who was seated at the table, and singeing her hair, struck Mr Livesley, who was standing in the door- way watching the efects of the storin. The second but, in which there were three gentlemen who had made the ascent that morning from the Llanberis side, and who but a few moments previously had been in conversation with Mr Live- slay, who remarked to them that although he had frequently ascended the mountain during the past 16 years, the present was the first occasion he had been upon the summit during a thunderstorm' was struck by the same flash, which, enter- ing under the doorway, ripped up the flooring, rendering exit impossible, overturned the tables, and made its passage Out by the window, which was smashed to atoms. A small metal gong bell, which was on the table, was melted by the fuid, and the place was wrecked. The keeper, finding Mr Divesley eras unconscious, and that the two ladies were too terrified to be of any assistance, ran to the second hut, which is but a few yards distant, and made his way in by the win- dow. A gentleman who was in the hut accompanied him, and found Mr Livesley reclining against the side of a bed. He was placed upon it, and life was found to be extinct, death apparently having been instantaneous. In company with the two ladies, the occupants of the second hut left for Llanberis on the abatement of the storm, and news of the disaster reaching Llanberis, Dr:Lloyd Williams, with a party of guides who volunteered their services, at once as- cended the mountain, brought down the body on an extem- porized bier, and deposited it in the mortuary attached to Mr Assfaiston Smith's slate quarries. The jury returned a verdict of " Killed by lightning." This, it is stated, is the first fatality from lightning which has occurred on Snowdon for a great many years. The late Mr Thomas Livesley was a gentleman who was well known and highly respected in Ashton, and in the various positions which he filled he gained the esteem of all by his uniform kindness and courtesy. Though only about 35 years of age, he had for something like 14 years been prominently connected with many of the public movements in Ashton. His father, the late Mr Mark Livesley, belonged to an old Ashton family, and was regarded as the principal boot and shoe maker in the township. Mr Thomas Livesley was the youngest at four sons and two daughters, and was born on the 18th May, 1849. He joined, some 16 years ago, the Lancashire Hussars, and rose from the rank of private to that of Quarter-Master Sergeant-Major, in which office he was indefatigable in promoting the success of the A troop to which be belonged. At the troop dinners he was invariably present, and his geniality combined with the kindness of his disposition rendered him a warm favourite, and when he was promoted to the rank he held at the time of his death the circumstance was accepted with general favour. Besides being connected with the Hussars, Mr Livesley held various public appointments. Shortly after the elec- tion of Mr J E Fairless as clerk of the Ashton Local Board in 1874, Mr Liveslev succeeded him' as assistant overseer; on the 25th July, 1877, he was appointed school attendance officer and inquiry officer te the School Attendance Com- mittee of the Caine Board, and no later since than the 11th Jane in the present yea', on a re-arrangement of the offices of the Board, he was selected as collector of the rates. The deceased, who was not married, took a leading position in the formation of St Thomas's brass band, and was its con- ductor at the time of his death. • As soon as the sad news of his decease was made known many expressions of sorrow were manifested towards his relatives. The body arrived from Wales on Tuesday evening at Newton Bridge, and was conveyed from thence to the family residence in Gerard- street, where it remained until the interment, which took 'place on Wednesday in the family vault in St Thomas's Church. The members of the A Troop of the Lancashire Hussars and St Thomas's band were present and took part in the funeral obsequies, and though Mr Livesley's late friends in parochial work have not, owing to the sudden- ness of the event and the short time at the disposal of the relatives, been apprised of the occurrence, many were present in order to show their respect for one who was anxious and willing to support their just rights. Mr 'Liveslev's last public appearance was at the Wigan County Police Court on Friday week, and it was anticipated that on the following Friday he would have presented the jury list for the township of Ashton.

GREAT WATCH ROBBERY.-JA gentleman named Hesse, member of a London firm of watch manufacturers, has been robbed in Birmingham of a bag containing 120 gold and silver watches. He had been calling upon customers, and •on returning to his hotel deposited his sample-bag in the dining-room, from which it disappeared during his tempor- ary absence. A Docroa KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.—On Thursday morning Dr Thomas Williams, of Woodlands, Mold, was killed on the railway between Mold Station and his resi- dence. He was knocked down by an engine and carried along the line for 30 or 40 yards, his body being frightfully muti- lated. The deceased, who was between 70 and 80 years of age, had retired from a large medical practice. DESPERATE Gwyn FIGHT IN LIVERPO3L.—A prize-fight of a determined description has taken place in Liverpool between Jack Stewart, of Liverpool, and a well-known pu- gilist named Ellis, of Birmingham. For the first hour the fight was most stubbornly contested, but Stewart then began to get the best of his opponent, and a draw was suggested. The Liverpool man objected to this, and it is alleged the Birmingham man's backers called in the police, who put an ead to the fight. The fight was with gloves under the Queensbury rules. THE CLAIMANT.—A Portsmouth correspondent says the Tithborne claimant will be released on ticket of leave from Portsmouth Convict Prison on October 24th, special means being taken by his friends to prevent any public demonstra- tion. For the benefit of his health he will live in retire- ment during the remainder of the year at a private mansion ar,Kempton Park, handsomely furnished for his personal use. Next year the claimant will attend gatherings in all parts of the country, and will probably become a Parliamen- tary candidate, invitations from nine constituencies having been received. Fusaaar, OF MR. Taoatas Cop.—The funeral of Mr Cope, who died on Thurdaay night, took place on Tuesday afternoon in the presence of an assembly of 2,000 persons, including many who were either present or former employes of the de- ceased's firm. About half-past twelve the funeral cortege left Parkside Cottage, Huyton. It consisted of the hearse, several mourning coaches, and a large number of private carriages. Asa mark of respect, the blinds in the houses in the village were drawn, and many sympathisers watched the departure trona the house. The principal mourners were Mr Thomas Henry Cope (son), Mr George Cope (brother), Mr B Sharpe, Mr John Hignett, Mr J A Willoar, Mr Castle Spencely, Mr Henry Tate, Rev G J Banner, Mr Wm Tate, and Dr Packer. The University College in which Mr Cope , took a warm interest, was represented by Princi- pal Rendall, Professor Campbell Brown, Rev C Beard, Mr M Guthrie, and Signor Londini. The interment took place in the family vault, in the Church of England portion of the burial ground, and the service was read by the Rev U J Banner, of Roby. The coffin was literally covered with beautiful wreaths, sent by relatives and friends, and the sides of the vault were deco- rated with ferns and choice flowers. Besides the workpeople in the employ of the firm (who closed the place of business for the day) there was a large contingent from Messrs Big- nett Bros. establishment, and also many belonging to the werking classes, who remembered the many kind acts of the late Mr Cope.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

".* Secretaries of Football Ohms are requested to note that rep9rts of matches played ou Saturday must be sent to the head office. Bearsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON TRUE BLUE (2ND TEAM) V. WIDNES Ex- CELSloll.—Played on Saturday on the grouod of the latter, and resulted in a win for the visitors by two goals, two trys, and one minor point to two minor points and one touch in goal. HAYDOCK TEMPERANCE V. KEARSLEY (2ND TEAMS.)— These teams met at Haydock, on Saturday, for the first time. A very pleasant game was witnessed. Although the Tem- perance men pressed the Keatsley men very much, the visi- tors succeeded in scoring four coals to the Temperance men two, owing to the home team not having an efficient goal- keeper, the person acting in that position lacking expe- rience.

EARLESTOWN 2ND y BOOTLE WANDERERS 2ND. The Earlestown 2ad Eleven journeyed to Bootle on Saturday after- noon, and met the 2nd team of the Bootle Wanderers on the ground of the last named club. The visitors were very strong and soon showed their superiority over their oppo- nents. The Bootle team scored the first goal, soon after the game had commenced; the subsequent play was all in favour of the Earlestonians. At half time the score was Earlestown two goals, Booths one; and after the change of ends the visitors scored four additional goals while their opponents failed to secure a single point. Earlestown thus won by six goals (Harrison four and Ferguson two), to one. J Gray (captain), goal; J Plant and A Clayton backs, J Pennington and T Feirclough half-backs, H Holcroft and H Rich rightwing, .1 Appleton and J Harrison centre, T Fergu- son and J Ogden left wing. NEWTON HEATH L. AND Y. R v. HAYDOCK TEMPER- ANCE.—The above teams having beeb drawn to compete with each other in the first round of the Lmcashire Chal- lenge Cup competition, it was agreed to play the game on Saturday, and took place at Newton Heath, Manchester. The ball was kicked off at about 3-45, and at the commence- ment the home team began to press the Temperance men. The Heath men played a very strong, combined game, hav- ing an excellent team upon the field. The Temperance men also made some splendid shots, but they failed to prove to any effect. Hatton played a splendid game at fall back for the Temperance, as well as Knowles, in the goal, who was cheered by the spectators for the manner in which he defended the Temperance goal. Result of the game : Newton Heath four goals to Haydock Temperance nil. EARLESTOWN v. BOOTLE WANDERERS.—The first meeting of the Earlestown and Bootle Wanderers clubs took place on Saturday afternoon, at Wargrave, Earlestown. The weather waa beautifully fine, but there was not a very large attend- ance of spectators. The home club turned out a fairly strong eleven, while the visitors had their best team in the field. The Earlestown captain won the toss, and during the first half chose to play with the ground and wind in his favour. Guy kicked off for the visitors about half-past four, and a visit was at once paid to the Earlestown quarters Green was early called upon to defend his charge, but three minutes had only elapsed when J Tebay (one of the crack players of Liverpool) made a shot from the right wing which sent the leather flying through the uprights. Im- mediately after the game had been resumed, Cameron while dribbling the ball towards the Bootle goal was charged by one of the Bootle players, with the result that his right leg was brogan above the ankle, as reported elsewhere. The play was stopped for several minutes, after which it was resumed. The Earlestonians, however, appeared to have lost heart by the mishap to one of their players, and conse- quently they did not exert themselves as they usually do. After about 15 minutes' play the visitors secured a second goal after a scrimmage in front of the Earlestown goal, but shortly afterwards Dagnall with a capital shot scored the first goal for Earlestown. No other point was made up to half-time. After the change of ends the home team severely pressed their opponents, and not many minutes had elapsed before Dagnall equalised the scores, bringing forth hearty cheers. The subsequent play was of a very exciting char- acter. The Bootle team was compelled to act on the defen- sive, but the home players were very unlucky in their attempts to score, the ball several times striking the cross bar. A few minutes before time was called the visitors' forwards secured the leather, and for the first time in the second half seriously endangered the home goal. One of the Earlestown backs made a mis-kick, with the result that the ball rolled through the posts, and Bootle thus secured a leading point. No other score being made, the Earlestown men retired defeated by three goals to two. Teams:— Earlestown: J Green, goal; J Whalley and R Green, backs ; J Duxbury and R Bowker, bait-backs; J Sims and W Rich, right wing; A Dagnall and J Ellison, centre; J Cameron (whose leg was broken) and W Thompson, left wing. 'Bootle Wanderers: T Tebay, goal; J Francis and W Reade, backs; J Cotton and T Fogg, half-backs; J Tebay and E Thomas right wing; J Guy and G Griffiths, centre; G Jones land W Bailiff, left wing.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday, in the first round of the Scottish Challenge Cup competition, the Vale of Leven beat Jamestown (after a drawn game, one goal each) by four to one • Kilmarnock beat Hurford by six to one: Kilmarnock Athletic beat Cun- ningham (Stewarton) by 14 to none ; and Greenock Mor- ton defeated Paisley Abercorn by four to three. At Pat- rick, Queen's Park beat Patric!: Thistle by five to one ; Dumbarton beat Renfrew, at Dumbarton, by three to none; at Hamilton' the Hamilton Academicals beat Fossil Park I (Glasgow) by eight to one ; at Kinning Park, Glasgow, the Rangers beat St Mirrens's by two to one; at Bolton, the Wanderers beat Walsall by five to one; at Birmingham Sheffield Wednesday beat Aston Villa by three to two; at Smallheatb, the Alliance and Aston Unity played a drawn game, two goals each; at Birmingham, St George's beat Northwich Victoria by four to one ; Stoke and Walsall Swifts played a drawn game, two goals each Stafford-road (Wolver ampton) defeated Wednesbury by three to one ; Pollokshields Athletic defeated Port Glasgow Athletic by two to one.

_ _ The Blackburn Olympic have in the space of eight days played three matches in which they have secured 40 goals without a single point being recorded against them. The Etrlestown club sustained a great loss on Saturday in its match with the Bootle Wanderers, when " Joe Cameron had his leg smashed early in the game. At no other period could the club so ill aff 3rd to lose so brilliant a player on the left wing, and it will be greatly felt in future engagements. After his retirement, need it cause surprise when it is stated that the Earlestown team were defeated bv three goals to two. The opponents of the Earlestown Club, the Bootle Wanderers, were spoken of as a rough set of players, by a sporting contempory on Wednesday week, but no one expected that such a striking illustratiox of the fact would be afforded. It is, however, to be hoped that " Joe "will soon recover from the sad accident which befel him.

The second "string "of the Earlestown Club smartly dis- posed of the Bootle Wanderers second at Liverpool. The latter, after the first ten minutes, never had a chance of win- ning, as the Earlestown lads sat upon them to the tune of six goals to one. On Saturday next the two crack clubs of South-West Lancashire—Everton and Earlestown—meet on the ground of the former. The teams are old opponents, and it will be remembered tnat last season Everton just managed to beat Earlestown by one goal in the final tie of the competition for the Liverpool and District Challenge CUP. The defeat of Haydock Temperance by Newton Heath in the first round of the competition for the Lancashire Cap Ties was a surprise and disappointment to the supporters of the Haydock team. In Earlestown and Haydock everyone expected that Newton Heath would be beaten, and there was scarcely a thought that they would win. However, they did win by four goals to none. St. Helens (Rugby) were represented at Walton on Satur- day with only a moderate team, but the latter displayed considerable skill, with the result that they won the match. The first half of the game was very even, but in the second half the St. Helens men completely over-matched their opponents. Securing a victory over the Rovers in a match that pre- ceded the fixtures of the season, the Blackburn Park Road were led to expect that a series of successes unparalleled in the history of the club would be secured. Since then,' however, secession from their ranks have had an effect upon the players, and on Saturday, instead of decisively defeating the Wanderers' team at Burnley in the County Cap compe- tition, they had to content themselves with a draw—the scoring being heavier than usual in such circumstances. Preston Zingari visited Clitheroe on Saturday, and con- tinued their victories by defeating their opponents by four goals to none. Up to the present they have scored 14 goals to two, the only club who so far has been able to score against them being Rossendale. It is stated, on the authority of a leading member of the Association Committee, that football will this season be played under the same conditions as last year, leaving pro- fessionalism against clubs to be dealt with upon objection. The same authority also says that by next season profes- sionalism will have been legalised.

On Wednesday the miners employed in the Silkstone and Parkgate seams of the Barrow Colliery,near Barnsley, struck work, with the view of resisting the new terms which the employers wish to impose. About 1,000 men are idle. THE RIBBLE SCHEME.—ResOlutions Were passed by the Preston Town Council on Thursday morning extending the time within which awards will be given in the arbitrations as to compulsory acquirement of lands required for the development of the Ribble. Corx.isrow us Tim CHANNEL.—On Thursday the steamer Wiltshire, of Newcastle, was in collision with the barque Santa Margarita, of Genoa, in the English Channel. The barque foundered, and two of her crew were drowned. The schooner Three Brothers, of Runcorn, in ballast, was wrecked on Thursday morning off Bantry Bay. The crew escaped. TER " ANTIQUARY " HOTEL.—The Auchmathie Hotel. which was situated in a romantic Spot close by the sea, and about 30 miles from Dundee,was totally destroyed by fire on 1 Monday. This hotel is well known to many Scotch and English tourists, and has gained world-wide *fame as being the scene of Sir Walter Scott's novel of "The Antiquary." The origin of the fire is unknown.

_ DEATH OF AN ENGLISH M.P. IN AMFAlCA.—lnformation has reached this country of the death of the Hon Gilbert H C Leigh, M.P. for South Warwickshire, whose body has been found at the foot of a precipice among the Big Horn Mountains, Wyoming territory. The deceased was the eldest son of Lord Leigh, and left Eegland early in August for a hunting expedition in the north-west. It is supposed that during a chase he accidentally fell over a cliff and was fatally injured.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Lord Dufferin has arrived in London. His departure for India will not, it is understood, take place until the betin- ning of November. On Monday Mr Walter Farthing, the well-known Devon cattle breeder, drowned himself, and the inquest on Tuesday resulted in a verdict of suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity. A CYCLIST KILLED.—A bicyclist named James Heard, of ' Harley Villa, Victoria Park-road, London, was on Monday crossing over the river Lea by a bridge at Waltham Abbey, when his bicycle swerved, precipitating him under the wheel of a timber carriage. The front wheel passed over his chest, and the injured man was removed to an adjacent Inn. Two doctors quickly attended him, but be died within a few minutes.

A MANUFACTURER CHARGED WITH FORGERY.—Joseph Meir Watkin' brick and tile manufacturer, of Burslem, was remanded, charged at Hanley, on Saturday, with forgery and fraud, chiefly in regard to bills of exchange on the Cheshire Banking Company, of sums amounting in the aggregate to over £5,000. The prisoner was arrested at Trentham station on Friday night while returning to the Potteries.

MINING ROYALTIES.—Mr Bright writes, regarding the movement in Lanarkshire to abolish royalties on mines : "If you mean you can honestly propose to seize the minerals beneath the earth's surface and abolish the present owner's rights, I cannot support the league for such a per- pose."-Lord Aberdare also writes that as his income largely depends on royalties he cannot give a disinterested opinion ion the subject.—Mr Broadhurst thinks royalties should be abolished. SCANDALOUS CONDUCT OF A Sow.—At the Central Crimi- nal Court, on Tuesday, William Augustus Nash was sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude for sending threatening letters to his father, a Limerick magistrate. Prisoner lest his appointment, and when his father did not remit to him as often as he wished, he sent letters threatening to charoe him with horrible offences. Statements of these charges he also sent to the Lord Lieatenant of Ireland. In court he confessed that the charges were unfounded. A RECLUSE —An extraordinary di,covery was .made in Edinburgh on Saturday. Two medical men were called in to see a patient, when they found the mart had been living for seven years in a bed closet, holding communication with no one, not even his sister, who lived in the same house the whole of the time. His hair was about two feet long, and be had armed himself with an axe, with which be attacked the doctors when they approached him. The unfortunate men was conveyed to an asylum. IMPUDENT FRAUDS ON PuntacAtes.—Several Liverpeol publicans have been victimised in an impudent manner by a fellow in military uniform representing himself as nay sergeant of some soldiers who would be billeted in Liverpool on the way from Manchester to Egypt. He obtained bed. board, refreshments, and money, and then disappeared. One publican, who advanced £2, became suspicious, and commu- nicating with the authorities, discovered the fraud. It is be- lieved that the fellow, who is still at large, has been carry- ing on swindles in other towns. A CLERGYMAN ON " QUIET TIPPLING" BY LADIES.—The Hereford branch of the Church of England Temperance Society has just been holding its annual meeting. The Rev W B Wilkins m (vicar of St Luke's, Birmingham), is re- ported to have said "he was sorry to say that be knew of many ladies from the western suburbs of Birmingham who went in their carriages to one confectioner's, where thev had a glass of sherry or something stronger, then to another, and then to another, and their coachman had to assist them into their carriages. Shame on them !"

SHORT flnfa IN THE SPINNING TRADE.---On TueSclay night an important meeting of limited companies and private spinners was held at Oldham, Mr Robert Whitaker presiding. Several million spindles were represented. It was resolved that it was desirable to continue the short time movament another month, and that a circular be sent out to all private firms and limited companies in Oldham. Ashton, Mossley, Stalybridge, and districts, asking if thy were favourable to adopt short time on condition that too.- thirds of trade do so. A strong opinion was expressed th,..t other towns were leaving Oldham to tight the battle. and that short time should be continued until there was better trade.

COLLIERY WARNING.—Since the previous warning.. at- mospheric pressure has, with slight variation, continued very high, the average height of the barometer over central England in the past twelve days being 30.25 inches. This being somewhat unusual for September, it seems very de- sirable that the special attention of miners should be drawn to the fact, as it may indicate the earlier arrival of the colliery explosion reason. So far the explosions this year have been comparatively. unimportant. Seventeen explo- sions, nine fatal, and about 30 lives lost, the average annual loss being 240, and the lowest in the past 24 years being nearly 100. It will be seen that censiderable care must be exercised during the remainder of the year; if even the lowest number of past years is not to be exceeded. CONFESSION OF AN IRISH "APPROVER."—We have tiOnle ' more" disclosnres " by an Irish informer of a sort which cannot fail to assist the efforts which are being so per- sistently made in certain quarters to discredit the adminise tration of justice in the eyes of the masses. Patrick Cole, of Kilpatrick, Westmeath, who figured as " approver " in the Barbavilla conspiracy trials, now "seeking peace of conscience and pardon from Almighty God," has made in • presence of three Roman Catholic priests a statement in which he declares that his evidence was false, and was given under coercion and in the fear that he himself would be - convicted. Cole is careful to include in his present de- claration an assertion that he had no connection with the conspiracy. The rev, gentleman who communicates Cole's disclosures to the press makes an appeal for an investigation on behalf of his "incarcerated parishioners." MORDERS.—A Russian sailor named Ernest Ewarstaldt. on Saturday night murdered a woman named Elizabeth Ed- wards. by stabbing her in the breast with a dagger, at a house in Anson-place, Pembroke-place, Liverpool. The murderer was arrested immediately. Jealousy is supposed to have instigated the crime —A murder has been commit- ted at Odibam, near Aldershot, on a farm belonging to Sir Henry Mildmay. A cowman named Ayles and a carter named Ferguson had an altercation on Friday. At ten o'clock that night Ferguson went out of his house, and half an hour afterwards was found dead in the yard, his brains having been beaten out. An iron door hinge, with blood and hair upon it, was found near, and Ayles, who was arres- ted, had blood upon his clothes.—At the inquest, on Satur day. on the remains of the girl, Ann Pollard, whose naked body was found in the Leeds and Liverpool Canal last week, the medical testimony was to the effect that she had been subjected to shameful treatment and then drowned, and that afterwards both her legs had been broken. The police have offered a reward of £5O for information that will lead to the conviction of the child's murderer and a reward of £5 for her clothes. Owen, the flatman, on whose flat the girl was seen the night before the body was found, and who was taken to the Detective Office and there detained, has been liberated, there being no evidence against him. SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS.—On Saturday, Mr. Beres- ford Hope, M.P., who presides in the Art Department, deli- vered the departmental address. There was a good attend- dance. Mr T C Horsfall c died attention to the need that exists for beautifying towns and for providing parks, plat- grounds, and other facilities for public recreation. His views on these subjects were generally endorsed. The ques- tion of open spaces was also discussed. In the course of a debate upon the utilisation of waterways ass means of reduc- ing the cost of inland transit for goods, reference wae made to the proposed Ship Canal bstween Manchester and Liver- pool, and it was pointed out that already the agitation had brought about a reduction iu the railway charges between Liverpool and certaie manufacturing towns.—On Monday, Professor Leone Levi read a paper on "The social condition of the working classes now, as compared with a quarter of a century ago." The three great hindrances to progress he regeaded as being density of population, overcrowding, and intemperance. Some were degraded, ignorant, and miser- able; but all things considered, he thought a distinct im- provetnent had been made, and be hoped for a greater im- provement in the future. Mr. Miller, Q.C.,LL.D., argued in favour of the amendment of the lunacy laws, and the abolition of all private lunatic asylums. In the Economic and Trade Section, Lord Lymington, as president, delivered an address on "State Socialism ;" Commander Cameroa, RN., C 8., read a paper on "Commercial Geography," and urged that in these competitive times it was eaeential for our merchants to understand the commercial requirements of other countries. On Wednesday the proceedings were brought to a conclusion at Birmingham. The report of the council stated that the meeting had been a succese, not only as regarded the papers read and the interest evoked by them, but also as regards the attendence.

, ERRIBLE STORY OF EASTERN REVENGE.--Letters from Sofia, published in the Vienna newspapers, report that the Bulgarian population of Macedonia have been greatly exci- ted by the murder of the Archimandrite Theophilus;Legate in Macedonia of the Exarch of Bulgaria. Public opinion amoqg the Bulgarians has pointed to the Metropolitan An- thimus as at least the indirect instigator of the crime. There was a long-standing feud between the two dignitaries, i and t was the general belief that neither would shrink from any means of overthrowing his rival. The Archimandrite had brought forward serious charges against the Metropoli- tan, and last winter he placed in the Grand Vizier's hands aformel memorial on the part of the Bulgarians of Macedo- nia against Anthimus. Returning to his residence at Debra he forced the Metropolitan to quit the province, but after a few months' exile he returned, and was able to expel hi s enemy from Macedonia, having kept him in prison. Theo- philus went last July to Lazaropol, but he received a sum- 'none i i purporting to be from Turkish authorities asking him to return. He went back and found the summons was !‘ forgery, and he learnt at the same time that the Metropol!- tan had gone to Lazaropol. He at once resolved to quit Debra, declining the offer of the Turkish authorities of an escort, and taking with him only two Albanians. Next day his i body was found about six mites from Debra n anarr.ow pass between two rocks. He had been shot. The Albanians had disappeared, but the prevailing impression as that they also i were murdered and their bodies concealed n order to direct suspicion towards. them. The news of the assassination caned viol ent exci Cement at Lazaropol, and thqeoule, setting down the Metropolitan as the author of the crime, resolved to have his life. It was even planned to attack the house in which be resided, to pour petroleum upon it, and fire it. But Anthimus got some clue to the plot, and, communica- ting with the Turkish authorities, he obtained a guard of 40 soldiers, under whose protection he retired to Debra. Bert he knows that his death is desired by his enemies, and several prominent inhabitants of Lazaropol were arrested. (An archimandrite is a high dignitary of the Greek Church, an abbot-general having superintendence of many abbots and converts.)

THE question of a Ship Canal from. Ma- nchester to Liverpool is once more to the front, and we do not doubt that, in this- in- stance. it will continue to the front until the Canal is an accomplished fact. Twice beate.n on the scheme upon which they had set their hearts—that of utilising the estuary of the ger-- sey by means of training walls—the promo- ters have turned about, taken their opponents at their word, and are now putting them- selves in a position to disarm the oppositi.on. of Liverpool by the adoption of plans- which will leave the estuary untouched. For some weeks back, both sides of the Mersey have I been surveyed with a view to determining which would best meet the, requirements of the alternative schemes which have from the first been more or less under consideration. It was thought that the Lancashire side of the estuary would find favour, seeing that it would shorten the distance. But there are great engineering difficulties in the way' of crossing, near Runcorn, such a large tidai.. river as the Mersey; and it has been decided, taking all things into account, that it will be best to keep to the Cheshire side of the" river, commencing at Eastham, and crossiog. the river Weaver on the way to Runcorn. From Runcorn to-Manchester the course will be pretty much as originally proposed, so that Warrington, getting, as it will, its twent.f acres of docks, has every reason which formerly had to wish that the promoters nil be successful in their undertaking. It wen' seem that no time is to be lost, for on Tues- day afternoon a large and influential dePata- tion waited on the MAYOR of Miwcitsso.l4 in order to present a requisition asking hira to call a Town's Meeting on the question- Theimmediate object of the meeting is t° obtain the consent of the ratepayers to an.el- penditure of Twopence in the Pound towar."s ithe costs of promoting a new bill in Parlia- ment. This means so far as Manchester as af Corporation is concerned, a contribution £lB,OOO ; but the effect it will have 13 strengthening the hands of the Provision. Committee is incalculable. the Manchester racecourse, it is proposed to buy a considerable quantity of land on the Salford side, near to Trafford-road, thus ob- taining an "excellent communication from the Irwell into the new docks at Pomona in- tended to serve Manchester." Mr. LEADER WILLIAMS, as engineer to the Provisional Committee, made some observations on the he ld, which

new schenie as compared with the old, whici • will certainly set people wondering why the the present scheme should not have been put k forward from the first. He said if the Canal were made as now proposed, vessels would be able to enter it at Eastham at any hour of

able tu the night or day. This would not have been possible at low water, if the estuary had been brought into requisition; and he put it as something against the extra cost. It seems to us that such an advantage is of the highest moment, and certainly worth many times the quarter of a million more which it is estimated the present scheme will cost as compared with that of last year. By avoiding the Garston side, what Mr. WILLIAMS describes as "a magnificient anchorage" can be obtained which would be free from currents and strong winds. It is satisfactory to know that there is unanimity amongst the engineers consulted as to the advantages of the Cheshire over the Lanca- shire side of the river. It is well that this is so; otherwise there might have been a good deal of criticism and not a little heart-burn- ing. With regard to the difficulty of crossing the river Weaver, Mr. WILLIAMS explained that it was proposed to pen up the Canal to a low tide-level by the entrance docks at Eastham. The waters of the Weaver would pass over this level and "escape by means of long regulating weirs constructed in the outer embankment of the Canal. These weirs would not only serve the purpose of passing off floods, but of allowing the tidal water of t, high tides to flow into and out of the Canal." It would thus seem that every contingency is - being provided for; but if there are any " specially weak points in the scheme we may be quite sure that we shall hear of them be- fore long. The one strong point is that it takes the wind out of the sails of the opposi- tion; nothing is to be done which will at all , interfere with the harbour bar; and with Liverpool neutral, if not at last giving sup- port, we do not see what there is to prevent the Ship Canal Bill becoming law when it is next submitted to Parliament.

• "THE Earlestown Church Scandal" has • .assumed a new and better phase. It is un- doubtedly a standing scandal to the Church 11.,,t of England that the Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS, c% of St. John the Baptist Church, should be in ; a position, by an arro7ant exercise of ill- starred authority, to turn organist, choir, curate, church officers, and congregation into the street. But it is a long lane that has • never a turning, and when things get to the worst they begin to mend. They are be- ,• • ginning to mend at Earlestown. It has • taken a time for the good people lately of St. John's to realise the helplessness of the posi- tion in which they stood as supporters of the kJ Established Church. They have done every- • thing that could be reasonably expected of • them to patch up quarrels of the past, and z obtain peace for the future. But the VICAR, ' though a preacher of peace, has shown him- self to be a man of strife. He despised the si olive branch that was held out to him, pre.. ferring to preach to empty pews in the sure and certain hope of "his living" being secured to him. So the parishioners petitioned to the Bishop for his removal, to find, as one • speaker expressed it the other night, that he had his hands tied. He might be an " over- '. seer," but he couldn't remove, to say nothing of discharging one of his men. The Sheep might be scattered; they might go where they listed, and tumble into pitfalls; but as to the Shepherd—once "placed," with hands on the "loaves and fishes," and he abideth for ever. The lesson has been a bitter one, but let us hope that, as with most other things. the after-taste will be sweet. The people are now at any rate on the right track ; they are putting their shoulder to the wheel in the full assurance that God helps those who help themselves. They are for the moment in the rut, but from the way they are going to work they will soon be out and on their way again—this time rejoicing. They met on Sunday evening in the Co-operative Hall, and, though the place was" unconsecrated," and unfit therefore in the eyes of the bishops for divine service, they found that they could, nevertheless, worship in spirit and truth. On Monday evening they continued in good work—it was a consecration, in its way, of the Co-opera- tive Hall—by presenting testimonials of esteem to the late curate and to the organist of St. John's, concluding the proceedings most appropriately by resolving with one accord to have a church of their own. They have had enough, for the time, of State control, and, as men grown wise by expe- rience, they are bent upon keeping the conduct of their own affairs in their own hands. St. John's Church is in the main an evidence of what they can do in the way of finding funds; and with that monument be- fore them they will be careful not to repeat a lamentable blunder. Their aim to raise Loo by Li shares with a view of erecting an iron church is a modest one, and we are sure that, if they steadfastly pursue the path they have marked for themselves,they will succeed in their object. Church matters in Earles- town have attracted more than merely local attention ; throughout the country there are people who have an eye to what is now being done, and if help is solicited they may rest assured that help will be forthcoming. They have put their hands to the plough of a "thorough reformation," and, if they keep a firm grasp and look not back, they will ere long see it happily accomplished.

THE Adjourned Borough Licensing Ses- sions for St. Helens were held on Tuesday, when all the existing licenses were renewed. The magistrates did not, however, take this step without giving a word of warning to the holders of the licenses. In the first instance those who had succeeded to licenses in con- nection with houses as to which there had been a conviction were brought before the Bench, and reminded of the peril in which they stood. It would be hard of course to visit the sins of the guilty upon the innocent, and the Licensing Justices showed no disposition to take such a course. But, as Mr. PILING- TON observed, when they went into a house against which there was a conviction, "they must all know it ; " and he might have added that so far as the owners of the houses were concerned the change of tenant was in most cases made simply because of the conviction. This may seem a rather scrupulous proceeding on the face of it; but as a matter of fact it borders on the unscrupulous, for it means that brewers, &c., are so much afraid of losing a license through repeated convictions against the same offender that they turn tenants out "neck and crop" when there is a "black

mark" against them. It thus happens that a particular house may have a notoriously bad character, and yet, under the present system retain its license, by a change of tenants. This is an evil of the present licensing system which, as it seems to us, calls for a remedy on the part of the legislature. The second batch called before the magistrates was of those who were actual offenders. The CHAIRMAN reminded them that it was the duty of the magistrates to see that public- houses were properly conducted; and he trusted that past punishment would be a sufficient warning to them. He seemed to think, however, that they were not a class likely to be influenced by being preached at, for he added that he was afraid what was said would not have much impres- sion on them. In this we are disposed to agree with him, and we cannot but think it would have been well, in renewing the licenses, to intimate that, in future, the Bench would take into consideration the propriety of refusing, in the interests of the inhabitants, the renewal of licenses for houses against which there was a bad record in the police books. That is certainly the direction in which public opinion is tending. "But suf- ficient for the day is the evil thereof" is the motto of license holders ; and they have a free run in St. Helens for another year.

WARRINGTON has been alike favoured by the PRIME MINISTER on his going to the North and on his coming back. It was at Bank Quay Station four weeks ago that he sounded what proved to be the key-note of his subsequent speeches; that was that this question of the passing of the Franchise Bill was a matter which lay in the hands of the people; and it was at Warrington yesterday that he made known, as one outcome of the second Midlothian campaign, his conviction that the nation has now given ample proofs of its desire that the Bill should pass. With a magnaminity characterstic of him, he still appeals to the House of Lords to repent at the eleventh hour; but at the same time he sounds the note "nearer, clearer, deadlier, than before" that heralds a conflict which may end in their extinction as a legislative body, if they do not stand out of the way. Reform is in the air ; the people are resolved upon achieving, as Mr. GLADSTONE put it, "something that is worthy of achieving," and they are not to be driven back in their righteous purpose by any force which the House of Lords may bring to bear. The PRIME MINISTER, in his brief, but stirring, address made a graceful allusion to the CROS- FIELD family, and "the hospitality he had shared in that house in former years." The name of CROSFIELD was well-known to him, and he could well believe that the town of Warrington could not be more worthily re- presented than by a member of that family— a sentiment which was enthusiastically ap- plauded, and which will have a fitting con- summation when Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD is returned, as he will be, at the head of the poll at the next General Election, as a sup- porter of the great leader of the Liberal party.

Bernwank CHAPEL, Rnnorm Harvest thanksgiving services will be held at this chapel to-morrow. WRECK OF A RUNCORN VESSEL. The schooner Three Brothers, of Runcorn, was wrecked on Thursday morning off Bantry Bay. She was on her return voyage from Bantry where she bad taken a cargo of wheat. HALToN HARVEsT FESTIVAL.—There were good congre- gations at Halton Parish Church on Sunday, when services in connection with the harvest festival were held. The Rev W Allen Whitworth, of Hammersmith, was the preacher. PARISH CHURCH BIBLE CLASSES, WIDNES.—About a hundred members of the men and women's bible classes in connection with the Parish Church Standay School sat down to a good tea at the Waterloo-road school on Monday even- ing. Subsequently addresses were delivered by Messrs Beattie, Foley, Hewitt, and Richards. GOOD TEMPLARISSI AT RUNCORN.—The weekly meeting of the Haste to the Rescue Lodge of Good Templars was held at the new room of the Society, Major Cross-street, on Tuesday evening. There was a good atten- dance of members, and one candidate was initiated and two others proposed. An entertainment was given by Bros C H Smith, Galilee. Johnson, Wood, and Andrews. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.— I The harvest thanksgiving services, which commenced on Thursday evening, were continued on Sunday. There were large congregations at each servic, and the Rev T M Arm. son preached appropriate sermons. Mr E Imison read the lessons. The choir rendered anthems and specially selected hymns in a most creditable manner, under the leadership of Mr Johnson. ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—On Sunday, the annual harvest thanksgiving services in connection with this Church were held. The sacred edifice had been neatly and tastefully decorated with the various products of the soil, and presented a bright and pleasing anpearance. In the morning the Rev S A Spooner, incumbent, occupied the pulpit; and in the evening the Rev B B Prescott, vicar of Latchford, preached to a good congregation. The collections amounted to £II 10J. WIDNES START/ BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The six- teenth appropriation in connection with this society was held in the school-room of the United Methodist Free Church on Thursday evening, and there was a good atten- dance. The Rev J Wright Williams presided. Mr W Handley, of Runcorn, delivered a lecture on the advantages of Starr Bowkett Building Societies. The result of the ballot showed that Mr James Edwardson, junr., was entitled to the use of £2OO free of interest for In years. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN —The first entertainment of the ensuing season in connection with this temperance organisation was held in Regent-street School-room on Thursday evening. The roam was well filled. Mr W Stringfellow presided, and delivered an ap- propriate address. During the evening Mr Joseph Ashley delivered a short speech. A programme consisting of songs and recitations was gone through in excellent style by Misses Annie Nickson, Harriett Rowland, Elizabeth Davies,. Harriett Williams, Florence G Kilcross, Jane Mead, Messrs John Shingler, James Shingler, and Jabez Stubbs, The Choir, under the leadership of Mr James Stubbs. THUNDERSTORM AT WIDNES.—About two o'clock on Sunday a storm of great violence broke over Widnes, and continued for nearly two hours. Rain descended in tor- rents, and vivid flashes of lightning, accompanied by terrific peals of thunder, illumined the sky. Damage was wrought I in several parts of the town. Whilst the storm was at its height the electric fluid struck the house of Mr Wm Twist, in Kaludah-terrace, and carried away the chimney stack, the bricks being hurled In all directions. The lightning then descended into the front bedroom, which it almost wrecked. The mantelpiece was smashed, and the heavy fire grate thrown into the middle of the room, while bricks were scat- tered over the apartment. Passing into the parlour below, the fluid displaced a magnificent marble mantelpiece, which was broken to atoms' and the fire place was hurled into the centre of the room. The door of a cheffonier was wrenched off, chairs were damaged, and the chandelier was melted into a useless piece of metal, and other furniture and fix- tures were injured. The house was filled with smoke and soot. Fortunately neither of the apartments were Gccupied at the time. The inhabitants of the house did not, how- ever, escape unscathed. Mr Twist and his two daughters were in the yard, and by the flash which wrought such havoc in the house they were thrown to the ground with much violence, and were stunned for several minutes. A constable and several persons in the street were also thrown to the ground, and the shock is described as resembling an earthquake. In Waterloo-road the shop of Mr E Wright was struck, the chimney stack and roof being damaged. The ceiling of the back bedroom was destroyed, and Mrs Lydia Wright, who was in the room was stunred. At the shop of Messrs Gill Brothers, in the same locality, the gas pipe was rent, and the escaping gas ignited, but Mr Gill, who happened to be passing the shop at the time, entered to see that all was right, and extinguished the flame before any damage could be done.
