THE OUTRAGE AT WIDNES. James Hughes, charged with committmg a rape upon Mary Ellen Monedell, seven years of age, living in Davies-street, Moss Bank, was again brought before the Widnes magistrates on Tuesday, and committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial. The prisoner was represented by Mr Knowles. WOMEN OBSTRUCTIONISTS AT WIDNES —Elizabeth Hough- ton, Ada Houghton, Margaret Jones, Mary Pendergast, and Annie Kinchley were summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of obstructing the foot- path.—P.C. Cummings said on the 14th inst. be saw the defendants standing at the top of Water-street. They were ' obstructing the footpath along Waterloo-read. He told them to go away, and they simply stood into the roadway and resumed their old positions when he went away. Several ladies and gentlemen complained to him of the defendants' conduct.—On promising not to repeat the offence the defen- dants were ordered to pay costs. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.-0a Wednesday, before Mr G Pilkington and H Gaskell, jun.' Elizabeth Glasheen, Robert Davies, and Margaret Bell (9th appearance) were each fined for being drunk and disorderly.—Catherine Kelly was convicted of committing a breach of the peace in Gi-er- rardestreet, on the 13th lust, and she was bound over to be of good behaviour.—Richard Parkinson, Michel Ryan. and Henry Cosgrove, youths, were charged with gambling. P.C. Savory proved that on Sunday, the 14th inst, at three I o'clock in the afternoon, the defendants were playing cards ! for money in Cairo-street, Simm's Cross. He found lid on the floor.—Each defendant was fined Is and costs 7s 6,1. VIOLENT WOMEN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wedneedav, befoee Mr H Gaskell, jun , and Mr G Pil- kington, Bridget O'Toole, an old offender, was brought up on remand charged with being drunk and disorderly on Monday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Cummings.— Catherine Power, who made her 12th appearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assault- ing P.C. Cheers in the execution of his duty. She was I further charged with damaging the officer's trousers to the extent of 4s. It appeared that about ten o'clock on Monday there was a disturbance in Pear-street, in which the pri- soners were the chief actors. They were both smashing windows with stones, and Powell also seized a brick and a ' poker, both of which she hurled through a window in the vicinity. A crowd assembled, and a row of considerable proportions seemed likely to originate, when Constable Cum- mings and Cheers appeared on the scene. Cummings seized O'Toole, who struggled violently, and so injured the officer that it was probable that he would have to go off duty. Cheers took Power into custody. She kicked him several times, bit his finger, and tore his trousers, which were dam- aged to the extent of 4s.—Each prisoner was fined 53 and las costs for the assaults. Power was also ordered to pay 43. SHAMEFUL CONDUCT OF WIDNES PARENTS. -- At the Wootton Petty Sessions, on Friday, before Messrs Neilson and Barnes, a chemical works labourer named John Giblin, of Lugsdale-lane, Widnes, was charged with deserting his daughter Ellen, aged nine years, and leaving her chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. Mr Hartley, clerk to the Guardians prosecuted, and stated that the pri- soner was employed at Messrs Golding, Davis, and Co's chemical works, at good wages, but he was an idle dissolute fellow, and totally neglected his child, whose mother has been leading an immoral life, but is now in prison. Some time ago the prisoner lived with his daughter in a common lodging-house in Widnes, but he suddenly disappeared, and no trace of his whereabouts could be discovered until a few days ago, when Mr Scannell, relieving officer for Widnes, found he was working at Messrs Golding, Davis, and Co's. The magistrates said the case was one of the worst they had ever neard of, and sentenced prisoner to three months' bard labour. The revelations made respecting the unfortunate child's parents were of a shocking character. • • ^

CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN MILK DEALER —At Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday George Purcelow, Surrey- street, was summoned to answer a charge of supplying milk which was not of the substanca and quality demanded.— Superintendent Leah said about nine o'clock on the morning of the 28th August he went into the defendant's shop. There were two mug,a in the shop, one about half filled and the other quite full of milk. The defendant's daughter said the milk was exactly alike, and she served him with a pint of milk from the mug which was filled. He then pur- chased a pint of milk from the mug which was half filled, and placed each sample in a separate bottle and sealed them. The analyst certified that the milk from the mug which was filled contained two per cent of water, taking a low standard, and the other he certified had been robbed of 25 per cent of its cream. The Superintendent added that he paid lid for each pint.—The defendant admitted that one of the mugs contained skimmed milk. The daughter was called and stated that she did not know it was skimmed milk. She had not sold any of it to any persrin besides the superintendent. Her mother had told her it was for churn- ing, but when the superintendent asked her if the milk in both jars was alike she said they were because she thought he meant whether they both came from the same cows.— The Bench considered there was no intention to defraud,and dismissed the case.

THE OUTRAGE ON WIDNES MEN AT WOOLTON.—At the Wootton Petty Seslion, on Friday, before Messrs H Gaskele P Neilson, and p Barnes, three Irish labourers, named Patrick, Anthony, and Michael Ginley, living in Wootton, were charged on remand with having violently assaulted Alfred Moore and George Stanley, two clerks employed by Messrs W Pilkington and Son, chemical manufacturers, Moss Bank. Widnes, and also with having assaulted Robert Moorst, of Woolton, and John Jackson, a groom, in the ser- vice of Mr Holbrook Glakell.J.P. The circumstances of the cage have been already reported, and as the police desired a remand, only evidence sufficient to justify an adjournment of the case was now given.—Robert Moorst, of Castle-street Woolton, deposed that about half-past ten o'clock on Satur- day night he was walking on the road between Hunt's Cross and Woolton in company with the complainants Moore and Stanley, when he met a party of Irishmen numbering about fifteen. One of the complainants wished the Irishmen "Good night," and the latter then pushed after them and said," We will give you good night, you --." Witness was knocked down and kicked about the head. He recog- nised Patrick Ginley as one of the irishmen.—George Stan- ley of Cuerdley. near Widnes, gave corroborative evidence, and identified Michael and Anthony Ginley.—The com- plainant Jackson also stated that on the night in question he heard a noise as he was walking :along the road, and upon going to see what was wrong he observed a nuneber of Irish- men assaulting the other prosecutors. He interfered with the object of separating them, and was then attacked himself. He identified Michael Ginley as one of the attacking party. —The prisoners were then remanded for a week in order that the police might have an opportunity of producing further evidence. A VIOLENT THIEF AT RUNCORN.—John Taylor, a tramp, was brought before the Runcorn magieerates, OR Monday, charged with felonioesly stealing a pair of trousers and a neckerchief, value 133, the property of Mr Edwin Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street.—lt appeared that the articles were hung cutside the shop window on Saturday night, and about half-past nine George Graham, Mr Imison's assistant, bearing that a robbery had been committed followed the prisoner along Lord-street, and found that he had the stolen property under his coat. The prisoner was taken back to the shop and given into the custody of P.C. Morris. In answer to the charge he said "All right, I did take them," and then struck Graham a violent blow. His conduct now became meat wild and unmanageable, and four constables found it a difficult matter to take him to the police station. —Mr C Reynolds observed, in sentencing the prisoner to a month's imprisonment with hard labour, that to hang articles far from the shop door was ad incentive to thieving. THE ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT SUTTON. Michael Finegan and Martin Finegan, Irish labourers. were brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of having on the 14th inst. unlawfully wounded Griffiths Griffiths, of Sutton. The prisoners were before the Bench on the previous Friday, and discharged, but Superintendent Leah had them immediately re-arrested on the same charge.-0a Monday, Mr Percy Davies, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of the prisoners, and con- tended that the prisoners could not be re-arrested on the same charge after being discharged unless fresh evidence was forthcoming.—The objection was noted by the Clerk, and the case proceeded. The evidence prieviously reported in this journal was repeated.—A. man named Yarwood, keeper of Sutton turnbridge, was called, and he stated that he saw the whole of the disturbance. He alleged that Griffiths was the worse for liquor, and that he was the ag- gressor, being the first to attack Finegans.-On this evidence, Mr F Rigby, the presiding magistrate, discharged the pri- soners. IMPOSING ON A RUNCORN PUBLICAN —kt Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr C Reynolds and Mr F Rigby, Joseph Elopes, a young man, was charged with obtaining food add lodging by false pretences.—Marzaret Morris said she was a widow and kept the Nelson Hotel in High-street. On Saturday morning when she got up she found the pri- soner inside the bar. He told her he had come from Walton Hospital, where he was employed to look after the patients, and that her brother-in-law was getting on very well. Thinking he was whatehe reported himself to be, she gave him breakfast, dinner, and tea, and promised him a bed. He was also supplied with a glass of beer and two penny- eorth of whiskey. If she had known that he was not a warder she would not have given him anything.—P.C. Smith deposed that from what he heard he went to the Hotel on Saturday night and saw the prisoner( who in- formed him that be was a warder in Walton Hospital, and that be was going there next day. From what Mrs Morris told him, he took him into custody. That morning he had charged the prisoner with obtaining food on false pretences. ,He replied, "All right, ball did not get the bed." Later he made a voluntary statement to the effect that he had made a mistake by telling Mrs Morris he was a warder when he was not.—lnspector Roach said he had searched the prisoner and he had no money whatever upon him.—The defendant made a long statement to the effect that he had been seen by Mrs Morris' brother-in-law in the hospital and he delivered a message to Mrs Morris for him. He also told her he bad been in the bar business, and she had said that if he liked he could stop and assist her in the bar in the evening. She asked him to have his dinner with her, or he should have made his way back to St Helens, where he lived, with the money he had in his pocket. He ac- knowledged that he had partaken of Mrs Morris's hospi- tality, and that he had falsely reported himself to be a wieder, and asked the Bench to deal as leniently as they could with the case, as a warning to him.—Mr Reynolds : You would like to be let off on profnising not to offend again.—The Prisoner: If you could see your way.—Mr Reynolds: Well we cannot ; we consider the offence proved. —Samuel John Bertram, assistant to Mr Lea, ironmonger, then described how nine months ago at St. Helens, the prisoner by falsely reporting that he had come from a Liverpool captain had obtained four meals from him.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour, which Mr Reynolda said he richly deserved,

I A HALEBANK FARM LABOURER AND His WAGES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Patrick Murray, a farm labourer, claimed £1 12s 8d from Richard Sutton, far- mer, Halebanlc, for wages due.—The defendant admitted that he owed £1 33 6d.—Tbe complainant said he had worked for the defendant. He claimed .£1 for harvest wages, which the defendant agreed to give him when he was en- gaged, 101 for four days' labour, and 2s 8d for money lent. —Mr Lewin said he could not recover the lent money.— The defendant contended that only 123 was due for harvest money, and he called a labourer named James Allen who said 12s a month was the usual sum for harvest money.— The Bench said the complainant had not proved to their satisfaction that he was entitled to £1 for harvest money, and they made an order for the sum admitted—Ll 33 6d. RUNCORN POLICE NEWS.—On Thursday evening David Robinson went into the Runcorn Police Station and asked Inspector Roach for a ticket for a night's lodging. As the man was most palpably drunk the inspector said it would be an imposition on the Guardians to pay for him a night's lodging, whereupon the applicant made use of various of- fensive epithets, and was ejected into the street. In Bridge- street he acted in a most riotuous and disorderly fashion and he was arrested by P.C. Smith. Yesterday he was brought before Mr W Bankes, J.P, and sentenced to 7 days' hard labour, in default of paying a fine of 5s and costs.—William Taylor, a boy, was charged with stealing a quantity of clover, the property of Mr Fred Savage, farmer, Weston. The prisoner, who was apprehended by PC. Fryer, said he took the clover for his rabl,its, and his worship after hear- ing the evidence, discharged him with a caution. ENTERTAINMENTS AT WIDNES.—An entertainment, ar- ranged by Mr J R Hudson, was held in the Public Hall, Hutchinson-street, on Saturday evening, under the presi- dency of Mr W Shaw, missionary to the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen. There was only a moderate attendance. The band of the Missions was present, and played several selections of music in their usual efficient style, and various members of the band also gave songs and recitations. Messrs W Millington, J Faulkner, and T Wil- son also contributed to the entertainment. Mr J R Taylor was the accompanist. In behalf of the Victoria fife and drum band, an entertainment was given in the Widnes Temperance Hall, on Monday evening. Mr It A Naylor, of Warrington, presided, and the room was well filled. A pro- gramme, consisting of songs, dzc , was gone through in capi- tal style by Messrs Hewitt, Gordon, Scrivens, J Kearns, H Powell, Kennion, S Cook, R Clark, Holt, Pickering, Jessop, White, Wm Jones, Mrs Jones, Mrs Bevin, and Miss Davies. Mr Powell's string band played several selections of music.

ROJIBERIES AT WlDNES.—Before Messrs G Pilkington and H &ask°ll, jun., at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Ann Carney and John Carney (13), mother and son, living at Farnwortb, were charged with stealing 2s 0,1 belonging to Mary Wainwright, wife of John Wainwright, Derhy-etreet, Farnworth.—lt appeared that on Wednesday Mrs Wain• wright gave the boy half a crown in order to buy her half a cwt. of coal, but he did not retarn.—Tbe boy informed the Bench that his mother took the money from him, and Inspector Wood withdrew the charge against him, and &tiled him as a witness —He stated that his mother took the money from his htnd, and that together they had travel- led to Oldham, Manchester, Patriceoft, and Warrington, and were arrested on arriving at Widnes on Suncity night.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.--Eliza McDermott, a married woman, was brought up on remand charged with stealing two yards of linen, three yards of lace, and two sheets, value 3s 9d, the property of Margaret Havey, of 9, Pear-street, IVidnes, on the 17th inst.—The evidence having been repeated, the prisoner was committed to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.--Patrick Kelly was charged with stealing a walking stick, value Is 3d, from a young man named James Knowles. On Saturday night Knowles and a companion were in the Market Hotel, when the prisoner snatched the stick from Knowles' hand acd ran off. Prosecutor followed him and asked him to return the stick, but he refused. A constable subsequently appre- hended him in Sutton's-lane with the stick in his possession. —The prisoner was fined 203, or in default 14 days.

GREAT SANKEY SCYCOOL BOARD —An adjourned meeting of this Board was held in the Schoolroom, Sankey, on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of meeting the late manager of this school, and making arrangements with regard to the carrying on of the school. There were present— Messrs Kerfoot (in the chair), Houghton, Ridgway, Cook, and S Sutton (clerk.) The Rev Mr Jackson and Mr Hatton represented the managers.—The Clerk read letters from the Education Department, stating that that department would be willing to sanction any proper arrangements between the Board and the late managers for either transferring the schools or renting them till they coald provide other accom- modation. It was also stated that the grant for We schools wauld be paid to the Board, but the Education DWpartment would be willing to agree to the portion of the grant for the time during which the school was under the managers should be paid to them.—ln the course of some conversa- tion which ensued, it was stated that the present school was church property, and could not he transferred to the Board, but that the managers were willing to allow it and the fur- niture it contained to be used by the Board eta rental of £2O a year.—lt was agreed, on the motion of Mr Cook, se- conded by Mr Ridgway, that this offer should be accepted. —lt was also agreed, on the motion of Mr Ridgway, that the books, slates, atc., at present in use in the school should be purchased from the managers at a price fixed upon by them and the Chairman of the Beard.—ln the curse of some conversation as to the prob able amount of the precept for the next six months, it was stated that about £l4O or £l5O would be required. to provide which it was estimated that a rate of 61 in the £ Would be requirei.—This was all the business. A SAD DOMESTIC PICTURE AT WIDNES.— Before Mr II Gaskell, junior, and Mr G Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, en Wednesday, Elizabeth Whitfield, a respectable- looking woman, will an infant in her arms, was charged with assaulting Ellen Rotherham. Mr Knowles ap- peared for the complainant, and stated that on Monday, the 22nd inst, Mrs Whitfield went to the door of Mrs Roth- erham's house, and accused her of having told her children that she was a woman of bad character. Mrs Rotherham denied the accusation, whereupon Mrs Whitfield struck the former, knocked her head against the doorpost, and "ran her into the parlour" where both assailant and assailed fell to the ground bringing down the table. All the "children's best hats " were damaged. Since the assault the com- plainant had suffered from pains in the back and head.— The defendant said her husband was the complainant's bro- ther, and he was a man that did not care for his home, and would not keep to his work for more than a few weeks. The complainant had been persuading him to leave her (the defendant) and he had been offering her 63 a week to go away from him. She was dependent upon the neigh- bours for food for her children and herself, and the com- plainant encouraged her husband to stay away from her by giving him meat, and drink, and tobacco, and had even bought him a new shirt. She had been married seven years, and during that time he had removed the family to no less than 14 different houses. That was the sort of men he was; and he did not care for home so lore"' as the complainant encouraged him in the way she did. She (defendant) had had to pawn nearly all her things to keep the home to- gether as long as she could. She had not received a penny to maintain the family for a month, and yet the complain- ant brought her there. She denied assaulting the complain- ant. When she went to the door, the complainant pushed her, and seized hold of her. The complainant then drag- ged her into the house and they fell together. The com- plainant and her daughter held her on the floor while a boy of about ten years struck her. He had marked her face. She would have to throw herself on the parish for she could not live with her husband.—Mr Gaskell said that the Bench thought the defendant had had great provoca- tion, but she most learn to keep her hands off other people. They would deal leniently with her this time by only im- posing a floe of Is and casts, or seven days' imprisonment. The Defendant: I must have the seven days for I have no money,—Mr Gaskell: You must try and get the money. I daresay the police will give you time. The defendant was allowed a fortnight in which to pay the fine. , TONIC SOL•FA CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Mr John nu- ford, teacher of the tonic sol-fa method of notation, in- augurated his winter's classes on Wednesday evening by a concert in Ellesmere-street school-room. There was a large audience, and Mr J Craig presided. The Chairman said in the unavoidable absence of Mr Norman, who had been called away to Chester, he had Peen asked to take the chair. lie was present at the opening of a similar class last year. and he understood that that class was most successful. He bad no doubt that the course this season would be quite as successful. There could be no doubt of the value of music and of singing, and it was one of the most hopeful signs of the times teat the Government were having singing taught all over the land, and having it taught on what was now ac- knowledged to be by far the best method—the tonic sol-fa. He was not a musician, but he liked music, and the thought that the future generations of our countrymen and women would be able to cheer our labours and relieve their burdens with singing was a great gratification to him. They knew that all over poetry there were references to music of a most flattering description. One poet said, " When music, heavenly maid, was young," and another. "Music bath charms to soothe the savage breast," and he was quite cer- tain that an angry man could be calmed in a good temper straight away if they could only sing him the right song. The effect of the right kind of song upon the spirits and upon the mind was marvellous. Seeing that music was such an admirable agency to improve and sweeten the labours of the people he heartily applauded the teaching of it, and particalarly the teaching of it by so able a man as Mr John Holford. (Applause.) He wished him every success. (Ap- plause.)—Mr Holford then explained the principles and advantages of the tonic sol-fa notation, and the method of teaching. He observed that it was very desirable that all Persons ought to learn to sing, and asked those present if they had ever thought how much better it would be for the services of the sanctuary, whether charch or chapel, if every person in the congregation could sing; really and truly and properly sing: If they joined the classes and paid attention to the lessons, in a comparatively short time they would be able to take any part in ordinary psalm singing, and with a little more pains would be able to attain some- thing higher. He spoke of the wonderful mechanism of the throat, and went on to describe at length the tonic sol-fa system.—A choir composed of pupils who attended last win- ter's classes showed the practicability of the system in a'l variety of novel and interesting ways to the great delight of the audience. "Unaccompanied by any musical Instrument they sang at first sight the Lord's Prayer, set to somewhat difficult music by Mr Holford. They accomplished the task in a highly creditable manner, and the audience rapturously applauded. During the evening the class sang several anthems and part-songs with a confidence and ability that earned them several encores.—On the motion of Mr Hollord, seconded by Mr ,Kitto, a hearty vote of thanks was acwzded to she chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

FARNWORTH AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—The receipts at the annual show amounted to upwards of £390, being £2OO M )re than was received the previous year. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—The usual monthly meet- ing of the Provisional Committee was held in the Board- room, Manchester, yesterday afternoon, Mr Daniel Adam- son, chairman of the committee, presiding. Active steps are now being taken to forward the preparation of the de- tailed plans, book of references, and notices, in order to bring the Bill before Parliament in the session of 1885. A eketch plan is in course of preparation, wfiich will give the public a general idea of the lines of the amended scheme., WIDNES POLICE NEWS.—Yesterday, before Mr G Pilking- ton, Elizabeth Travis, a married woman, was brought up charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street on the previous evening, and she was fined lOs and costs 63 131. or 14 days' hard labour.—Catherine Carey, who made her 18th appearance, was sentenced to 14 days' imprison- ment for disorderly behaviour.—John Fury was charged with stealing a bricklayer's hod, value 4s, the property of Dominic Nyland, of 6, Market-street, Widnes. On the 18th April Nyland was labouring at the Widnes Alkali Works, where the prisoner was also employed. In the evening he placed his hod and other tools away, and next morning he discovered that the hod had been taken. The prisoner de- nied knowing anything of the robbery, but on Thursday, the 25th mat, the prosecutor saw the prisoner walking through the streets with the stolen hod on his shoulder He therefore gave him into the custody of P.C. Laing.—Tue prisoner was remanded until Monday. A TICEETLESS TRAVELLER AT WIDNES.—James Dervan. a labourer at Messrs PilkinYron's works, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, charged with travel- ling from Warrington to IYidnes on the Sheffield and Mid- land line without paying his fare, with intent to avoid Payment—lnspector Whitworth, of the detective department Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway, prosecuted. —William Attwell, porter, said he was on duty on Sunday, the 14th inst. On the arrival of the 9-19 p.m. train from Warrington he saw the defendant alight from the rear end of the train and walk in an opposite direction to ths exit of the station, He (witness) called out "This way out," and the defendant returned and mixed with the crowd giving up tickets. Witness went away for a few minutes, and when he came back he heard the defendant say "Do you mean to say I have come by train I"' Witness said "Yes, certainly you have come by train." The defendant then'otTered to pay his fare.—lnspector Beacham gave evidence that the defendant stated he had not come hy train, but wished to go away by train. When the porter came up he offered to pay his fare, but he (inspector) refused to accept it —The Bench fined the defendant, who did not appear, 20s and costs, 8s 6d, or 14 days.

THE BAPTISTS Al' WIDNES. The anniversary services in connection with the Nelson- street Baptist Chapel, Widnes, were held on Sunday, when the Rev W Filling of Hill Cliffe, preached two able ser- mons to good congregations. The collections amounted to upwards of £3. Os Tuesday evening a recognition service and pastors' first anniversary celebration took place in the chapel. The proceedings commenced with a tea, which was served by Mrs Cottain, Mrs J Davies, Mrs CaHand, Miss Cooke, and Miss Morris; and subsequently a meeting was held, presided over by Mr W Clark. of the HoHies, Ditton. There were also present the Revs Hugh Stowell Brown, R Yeatman (the pastor), J Cottam, It Harper (Wesleyan). D Davies (Welsh Congregational), R G Hughes (English Congregationel). Mr Narracott, ikc. There was a good atten- dance.—The Rev R Yeetman, in a speech of considerable length, referred with pleasure to the presence of ministers of other denominations, and went on to speak of his twelve menthe' pastorate amongst the Baptists of Widnes. Looking back upon the period of his first anniversary, he could see that there had been a great deal for which he was very thankful, and he was Very glad that so meny friends had come together to take part with him in raising the Ebenezer stone, and saying" Hitherto the Lord bath helped us." He had been very happy in Widues, and he did not regret be- coming the pastor. (Hear, hear.) Daring the past twelve months there had been added to the church fourteen mem- bers—nine by baptism and the others by letter—and he hoped shortly to baptise four or five more. (Applause.) He observed with gratification that there had been a considerable increase in the weekly offerings. He thought if they could only manage to tide over present difficulties they would have more fair sailing in the future than they bad had in the past. They had received some help from outside. Some time ago their friead Mr Gossage very kindly assisted them without solicitation, and more recently their friend Mr R H Davies had aided them. For this help they were very grateful. The Biptiste were doing their best to prove their right to live and to prosper, by acting to the motto " God helps those who help themselves." They had a fund which they were increasing as best they could for the purpose of building a new chapel. He supposed those present would admit that they were very much in need of one. During the past four months Mr Passey had received VO towards the new chapel fund, and this amount, with the exception of £5, bad come from the members of the congregation. (Ap- plause.) He hoped and they all hoped that success would attend their efforts. (Applause.)—The Chairman then delivered a short and eppropriate address. He was glad. he said, to hear of the success of the first year of Mr Yeatman's pastorate, and he considered it an horenr to occupy the position he did that night. He exhorted the congregation not to rel ix their eff 'lite in the clang of Christ, and to strengthen the labours of their pastor by their continual aid and encouragernent.—The II iv Hugh Site ?fell Brown re- marked upon the importance of singing as an aid to Christian worship, and speaking of Mr Yeatman, he said that gentleman before he came to Widnes had been a con- siderable time at Broad Green, and some of them had oppor- tunities of knowing the character of his work and also the character of the man, which, in his opinion, was more im- portant than the character of ht 3 work—(applause)—and they had reason to repose great cooficlence in hiin. The success of his ministry in Widnes hail increased their esteem for him and confirmed the corifidenen with which they re- ceived his appointment as pastor of that church. He con- cluded by speaking of the duties of pastor and congregation, —The R-iveJ Cottons, D Davies. and R G Hughes and Mr Narracett also delivered short addresses. During the evening the choir rendered several anthems in a very praise- worthy manner. The usual votes of thanks canciuded the meeting.

div.head: PROPOSED INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL
div.p: THE PROPOSED INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL

FOR WIDNES. Mr Stephen Harding Terry, CE, an inspector to the Local Government Board. on Tuesday held an inquiry at Alforde Chambers, into the application of the Widnes Local Board for sanction to borrow £670 to purchase land at Hal- ton View as a site for an Infections Diseases Hospital. There were present Messrs Gossage (chairman). Dr O'Keeffe, Handley, Wright, Midwood, Dutton, Webster (members of the Board). and Dr Hurst, and Mr J F Allen (the clerk).—The Clerk explained that the subject of providing a hospital for infectious diseases was under the considera- tion of the Board about six years ago, but through the oppo- sition then made to all the sites suggested the matter was allowed to drop through. Within the last two years the necessity for an institution of that sort had been forcibly brought before the Board by an outbreak of smallpox, and the matter had again been taken up. There had certainly been some delay through circumstances over which the Board had no control. However, a few years ago, a site was selecte I and approved of by the Board. It was re- commended by the Medical Officer of Health, the Sur- veyor, and the Chairman of the Health Committee, who is a medical gentleman, as being the best site in the whole dis- trict, but there was a certain amount of opposition from various property owners, and the Local Government Board sent down an inspector—Dr Parsons—and on his report they did not approve of the site. It was therefore aban- doned. About 14 or 15 other sites were then offered to the Board, and a committee was appointed to inspect and report upon them. The result was that the site which Mr Terry was asked to report upon was selected unanimously by the Board as being the most suitable. The site was 2,,E acres in extent, and the trustees of the Leigh estate had asked £670 for it. The site was not very far from the cen- tre of the,township. It had good approach roads, and stood on comparatively high ground; and was in an isolated po- sition. If a circle was drawn from the centre of the propo- sed site there was not a house within a circle of 130 yards ; there was only one house within a circle of 170 yards, and only feur houses within a circle of 217 yards. Mr Al- len quoted a report made to the Local Government Board in 1878 to show that a distance of 30 or 40 yards was suffi- cient for a hospital to be from a dwelling.—Tne Inspector remarked that since then wider experi- ence had been gained, but the distances mentioned by Mr Allen offered sufficient margin in this caee.—The Clerk added that there would be no difficulty in draining the site.—The Surveyor said the site could be drained into the present sewer, and he described the course of the drains on the chart.—Mr Webster pointed out that if the site was-drained in the way desaribed by the surveyor the sewage would have to flow through an open ditch.—The Inspector said that would be very ohjec,ionable ; the sewage ought to run into the main outfall.—Mr Allen : That can be easily accom- plished.—Mr Midwood said the site would be best drained I into Bowers' Brook, which was culverted over a great per- I tion of its length. It was also the shortest and cheapest way.—Mr Gossage observed that Bowers' Brook was the strongest stream in the district and belonged to the town- ship. Strong chemicals also ran into it —The Inspector remarked that to drain into Bowers Brook appeared to him to be the best course. He asked if the Board proposed to at once begin the construction of the building If they obtained the site.—The Clerk: Yes, almost. —lt was stated that the population of the township was estimated at 26,500, and that the outstanding loana of the Board amounted to £45,000, exclusive of the . debt on the gas and waterworks, which were not, however, considered in the same light because they brought a revenue. —The Inspector observed that 100 years, the time in which ,the Board wished to repay the proposed loan, was a very long period. Mr Gossage said he thought the leans of the Board ought to be perpetual, and oily pay interest on them. He considered it a great hardship that some of the loans of the Board had to be repaid in 30. years.—The Inspector remarks di that the proposed hospital might not meet the requirements of the people 100 years hence, and they would have to erect another, although they had helped to pay for this one.—Mr Gossage said they would be able to sell the present site at a great profit because it might be desirable for building land then.—ln answer to a question, the Clerk said the Board was purchasing the site at the rate of LB2" per acre, which was very cheap. The usual price of building Land in Widnes was £1,200 an acre.—The inquiry then con- cluded, and the inspector proceeded to inspect the We.
The defence fund for Mr William O'Brien editor of United Ireland, has reached £3,000.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

General Gordon has justified the view of his position consistently taken by the Government. At a time when it salted the Uonservatives to protest that Gordon was in im- minent danger, and shame was cried upon a Ministry that deserted him, Lord Granville; Mr: (Madstone, and Lord td- muod Fitimanrice, and every Minister who spoke on the subject, quietly said that, according to their information, this was not the case. Jost about the time a Conservative paper published a lurid picture of a man (supposed to be Gordon) lying on his back in the desert with heavy top boots on, red tunic and belt, what time a cloud of vultures hovered near, Gordon was writing to say he bad provisions for four months, that all was well at Khartoum, and that " as soon as the Nile rose he would be able to give a good account of the rebels," as he calls the Soudanese. This is a promise he has grimly carried out. He is not only hold- ing his own at Khartoum, but has beaten back the be- leaguers, carried the war into the enemy's country, and kept Berber in a state of deadly fright lest he should appear
before it. His condition calls to mind the old story Of. the

soldier who caught a Tartar. "I've got a Tartar," he called out to his comrades. "Then bring him along," they said. I can't," replied the captor," he's carrying use off." The Soudanese have caught a Tartar in General Gordon, and nothing would oblige them so much on the part ot the man -whom they are supposed to have held in jeopardy, than that he would kindly go away and leave them, taking away whatever men and stores he desired.

An immediate result of this confirmation of the Ministe- rial view of General Gordon's vosition has been the counter- manding of the departure for Egypt of two regiments and a comiderable amoant of stores. But it has made no differ- ence with the forward movement of the army already in Egypt. On Ssturday Lord Wolselev proceeds to the front, and his present destination is Wady Haifa. It will take him a considerable time to reach that point, and there be mast needs wait for three or four weeks till the advance guard of the expeditionary force comes up. Supposing the expedition is left to accomplish its work and to proceed all the way to Khartoum, the new year will be upon us before Wolseley and Gordon meet. But, of course, the affair may be cut short by the action of General Gordon himself. There is nothing now to prevent his leaving Khartoum, striking across the desert from Sbendy, and joining hands with his countrymen at Ambukol. He indicates some such plan in one of his letters, though it is only Colonel Stewart of wham he speaks as going to Berber and after- wards to Dongola. As for himself there is much reason to fear that he is in the same mind as he was when he left England. To conquer the Soudan, trample opposition underfoot all the way to the Equator, and then place a man like Zebehr Pasha at the head of affairs has al ways been Gordon's dream. Tne probabilities are that be will be encouraged in that by the near proximity of a British force. But such a desire on the part of a man who, as soldier and political emissary, owes double dues to dis- cipline. will be promptly put clown. Gordon's well-meaning wilfulness and disobedience of instructions has led to trouble enough, and there will be no more trifling on the sub- ject. The campaign in Scotland may now be said to be closed. Sir S Nertheote has already crossed the Border, and Mr Glad- stone is slowly making his way homewards. At Newcastle, Sir Stafford congratulated Conservatives on the success of their arms in Scotland, which is quit in keeping with the sly humour of the right hon. baronet. Heals° warned them to be ready for the dissolution th it he assured them was im- minent. This is, of course, exactly the point at issue. The Lords claim the right of determining the precise tune at which a dissolution shall take place, a constitutional inno- vation, the monstrous nature of which Mr Gladstone has pointed out. It is with that object that they have thwarted the Commons and are now defying the popular will. Sir Stafford's warning is an assumption that they have triumphed, and that, the Lords throwing the Franchise Bill out a second time, a dissolution will thereupon ensue, There are two fatal errors in this. It is by no means sure that the Lords will throw cut the Franchise Bill a second time. It is quite certain that if they do Mr Gladstone will not be a party to the innovation he has denounced, and play into their hands by immediately dissolving Parlia- ment. He might amongst other things create sufficient peers to turn the scale when, early next session, the Bill i would a third time be sent up to the Lords. Sir John Lubbock is carrying forward his experiments with his dog which he hopes in time to make as accom- plished as the average biped. It is now fully eighteen months since he started with his poodle dog "Van." His idea was that the dog, wanting anything, should ask for it, and as his bark might be unintelligible a series of cards were arranged by which he could make known his desires. Thus a card labelled " Food" is laid within his reach, and when he is hungry he takes it up in his mouth, and brings it to his master. In a similar way, if be wants to go out, he picks up card with the word " Out " upon it, and brings that up. Another and favourite card with him is labelled "Bone," leading, as its presentation does, to the bestowment of a toothsome morsel. The pieces of card- board are about ten inches long and three inches broad. Having successfully triumphed in these early ways, Sir John has recently been carrying out experiments with the object of making the dog distinguish colors. But this, he tells me, has hitherto proved a failure. One circumstance that militates against the success of the education move- ment is the hon. haronet's wedding. Before he was married "Van" used to sleep in his room, and many opportunities for lesson-giving were found. Now "Van " is banished to his own mat, and may possibly feel this slight so much that he turns sulky, and declines to learn. However it be, the color experiments have certainly failed.

Some weeks ago I gave one or two of the stories current in literary and artistic society about Whistler. A friend, who has been on a far journey, in the course of which be accidentally met with this particular letter, supplements the list. Whistler, he tells me, was for some years a denizen of the Quartier Latin in Paris, where, amongst his comrades, was Du Maurier. In those days Whistler was exceedingly impecunious—a condition not greatly varied now when he gets a thousand pounds for what some people would irreverently describe as an indistinct daub. He was one night invited to a ball which he particularly wished to attend. His difficulty was that he had no appropriate shoes, nor had he the wherewithal to buy them. Ile livel in one of the dingy hotels that stand round dimly lit courtyards in this old quarter of Paris. The hotel was full of etudents, artists, brietless lawyers, and others, some of whom had wives. Whistler waited till most people had gone to bed, and then descending the staircase, examined all the boots and shoes at the doorways Finally he came upon a dainty pair that just fitted. (The French grisette, however poorly dowered with wealth, always has well made and well-fitting boots.) This particular pair Whistler appropriated, went to the ball, and when he returned deposited them at the par- ticular doorway. After Whistler left Paris ad began to think of earning his living, he went to America, where at Washington he ob- tained an appointment in connection with the office of the coast survey. He was a topographical draughtsman, a mechanical and precise development of art which, it will be well understood, did not suit his genius. He accordingly was very poorly paid, and his domicile was the attic of a mean little boarding-house. There is, my correspondent says. still extent a sketch of this attic with Whistler making coffee, and standing near him a maidservant of the March- ioness type. On the walls oft this same attic Whistler freely sketched by way of relief from his official labours in the Topographical Department. Doubtless the ruthless white- wash brush has long since gene over the walls, and the Marchioness has married another Dick Swiveller. The manager Of a large hotel. in London tells me of an interesting experiment he has been making. It was de- signed to ascertain which nationality are the best customers, at an hotel. Having a. turn for statistics he went into the matter very carefully, the result of his inquiries being that the Englishman stood at the top of the list as spending most money. Next came the German, then the Frenchman, and finally the American. This last is a marvel, the mere so that many wealthy Americans who come over here iii the season, in some matters, such as dress and jewellery for ex- ample, do not stint themselves. But what runs up a man's bill at an hotel is not what he eats, but what he drinks, and the American rarely drinks anything but water at hie meals. At home he makes up for this to same extent by taking " a smile "here and "an eye-opeaer " there. Just before the dinner hour at any big American hotel the bar is densely crowded with men drinking seductive spirituous mixtures, which must be much more deleterious than a fair c o nbnotoe eye suetof a n beenhotel pm übainiaabgeedr. f A t e k b allowance of good wine. Probably this habit is olsserved in England, and as what the guest takes at the bar is there- upon paid for, and does not appear in the bill, the Ameri- cans may be better customers than they appear to the dis- contented a farthing. Field

fand Tiler are the publishers, and here is the story. Max O'Bell has written a book called John Bull and his daugh- ters. It was to appear in England, but the title leaked out. Your novel must be published to secure you copy right in your title, and this title was going to be stolen, as the publication had not begun. Se the astute publisher put togethera few pages revealing the fraud, and taking the name of "John Bull's Woman Kind" for his title, secured the copy right from the thieves.

div.head: ATHLETIC FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ATHLETIC FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.

With the object of increasing the funds of the Halton Grammar School, an athletic festival took place on Satur- day, on the ground of the Runcorn Football Club, and ft was a gratifying financial success. His Grace the Duke of Westminster, Sir Richard Brooke, Bart, and the local gentry allowed their names to appear as patrons, and Sir Richard Brooke, Lady Brooke, and a party were present in the en- closure during the afternoon. The beautiful weather caused a large concourse of persons to assemble on the ground, and it was estimated that between two and three thousand per- .. . .

A0...:33d, Lunt. oa p e carvers, (Open)—Twenty valuey soss paid for admission,whilst several hundreds watched the sport as best they could from a point of vantage outside. When all expenses are settled, a balance of about £6O will be available for the use of the governors of the school. The- arrang-ments were carried out admirably by a committee, of which Mr J J Yapp was secretary, and everything passed off without a hitch. Messrs E A Chorlton, C L Evans, and W T Weight ably officiated as judges, Mr W Wright beirg- the starter. The handicapper and referee was Mr J R Yeomans, and duties of clerks of the course were discharged by Messrs J Stokes, D T Baguley, F Bate, T Langs'.aw, P Smith and A Woodier. During the afternoon the band of the F and G Companies of the 2nd C.R.Y. played selections of music in their usual skilful manner. For the eleven events which formed the programme there were nearly 200 entiies, and the fields-were very large. The 220 yards flat race for local men produced a good contest, Walter Jones in the final, with four yards start, winning in good style. Considerable amusement was caused in the 100 yards fiat race, for youths under 15 years, by the victory of Jno Joyce, a youth of diminutive build, who showed a clean pair of heels to his longer hat less fleet competitors. The chief wiener of tbe afternoon was G Savage, of Birmingham, who with comparative comfort was first past the tape in the tarn. chief handicaps. George Wright, of Widnes, carried off the first prize in the mile race from 15 competitors, amongst whom were P Shay, rCrellin, Nancarrow, and other Liver- pool cracks. There were 11 starters for the bicycle race. but the track was of so awkward and uneven a eaters that no less than five, riders were thrown, happily without serious result. WARRDiGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

- - SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. BREACH OF Tag PEACE.— Michael Melior, 11, Platt- -street, labourer, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting his wife.—He was bound over to keep the peace for six months, or go to prison for a month in default. MOHDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Alderman Davies, and Mr John Fairclough. DRCNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness :—James Campbell, fined ss, including costs; George Hopkins, fined 103 and costs ; James Jordan, fined ss, including costs; Thomas Fleming, fined 10a and costs; Thomas Gorman, fined 5s and costs; Albert Cook, lOs and costs; Margaret Jackson, fiaed 5s sad costs; Wini- fred Flanigan, fined 55 and costs. A DESERTER.—WiIIiam Howell, charged with deserting from the Royal Welsh Fusiliers, while stationed at Dublin, was remanded to await an escort. _ _ . .

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—William Moran and Patrick Dolan were each bound over to keep the peace for fighting in the Crown and Sceptre-yard.--George Potts was similarly bound over for disturbing the peace by assaulting his wife in Glass-house-yard. THE STONE Tnnowisn NOISANCE.—George Williams, John Henry Williams, Herbert Cleveland, and William Jones, boys, were charged with throwing stones to the danger of passengers.—The two Williams and Jones were fined 2s 6d, including costs, each. and Cleveland, who had given a wrong name which resulted in another bay being thrashed by his father, was fined ss, including costs. TIIESDAT.—There was no business. WEDNESDAY.—The business is reported elsewhere. . .
Tll-11—RSD—AT.—There were no charge; down for hearing.
FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White. DRIINICENNESS.—WaI. MOSOIY, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Sankey-street on the previous evening, was fined 2s ed including costs. _ _ _

NEGLECT OF WOR-E.—Richard Burgess was summoned for lOs compensation by Messrs Fleming and Co., for neglect- ing his work.—lt appeared that he was employed at piece- work „in :the tanning department, and be neglected work, which caused considerable inconvenience. The sum of 7s 9d was due as wages, and with the consent of the prose- cutor an order for that amount was made against him.-- Jno Robinson was similarly summoned, and ordered to pay lOs and costs, 14s in all.—A representative of Messrs Flem- ing, who was present, said that the money ordered to be paid by the defendants would be put in the Infirmary box. —Margaret Plinston (15) was summoned by Wm Hock- euhall for neglecting work.—The defendant said that the master called her offensive names.—The case was adjourned for the defendant to call evidence in support of her state- ment—Mary Ann Richardson was summoned for non- payment of 93 ordered to be paid by her to Mr Welsby for breach of contract.—The CASO was adjourned for a fort. night on her promise to pay 2s a week. Ansautr.—Betsy Ryan was ordered to be bound over in her husband's recognisances of £5 to keep the peace for six months for assaulting Bridget Macnamee on the 22nd Sep- tember. _ _ .
Titz USE OF THREATS —Jane Riley was charged by Mir- garet Hines with using threats towards her on the 22nd Zeptember.—She was fined 5s and costs, or 14 days.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr C Reynolds and F Rigby. MISCELLANEOUS.—Margaret BaSnett Was on the evidence of P.C. Bryan fined £1 and costs 9s 61, for being drunk and clisordilay In Cooper-street on the 12th inst.--Joseph Carter was summoned for being drunk in the Derby Arms on the 13th inst, and refusing to quit when requested by P.C. Mor- ris. He was fined lOs and costs.--For drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Penketh-lane on the 20th lust, Sarah Blower was fined £1 and costs 7s 4d. P.S. McMichael proved the case.—Ann Grattan, a woman of ill-fame, was convic- ted of being drunk and disorderly, and she was fined lOs and costs Ss 4d. _ . _ . . .

_ AssermTs.—Samuel Lydiate, a middle•aged man, pleaded guilty to assaulting Ralph Prescott, an old man, living in Pennington's-row, on the 13th September.—The complainant said he was coming down Doctor's Bridge on the dav named when the defendant ran at him and "knocked him senseless and threatened to kill him and his son." A fine of 103 and costs was imposed.—Martha Lunt, of Whisky-row, Wes- cbarged Margaret Kilgrees, her peighboprt with Reuni- ting her on tile gi;iit's:r.ti3r. It appeared that the de- fendant's sister had washed her flags and left a quantity of flirt near the complainant's door. The complainant then "swilled her flags," and the refuse went against the defen- dant's door. The defendant then seized the complainant, shook her, and "placed her knuckles in her neck." Mrs Griffiths and Mrs Inglesfielel gave evidence. Defendant al- leged that the complainant had swilled her flags twice that day, and she asked her if it wartight. She denied that she had used violence, and she called Mrs Sarah Fisher in cor- roboration. The Bench fined the defendant is and costs 17s. VAGRANCY.—Patrick Dan, who stated he worked for Mr Barber at Budworth Heath, was charged with begging. P.C. Wallace proved that the prisoner who was nearly drunk, went into the Blue Ball Inn, and asked for alms because he was "hard up."—The prisoner said he never begged in his life that he was aware of. The Bench sentenced him to seven days' hard labour.
