div.p: ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr J C Gamble and Alderman .1 Harrison. _ .

CHIMNEY ON FIRE.-63;11.i-Varley, of Eccleston, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 19th inst.—He was fined 68 ad and costs. BAD LANGUAGE. Robert Metcalf, of Windle was sum- moned for using obscene language in Corporation-street on the previous afternoon, and was fined 2s ed and costs.-- A like penalty was imposed on Michael Mavrin. of Sut- ton, for using profane language on Monday night. UNBIIOTHERLY CONDUCT.—OMM Mooney and Edward Mooney, brothers, were summoned for committing a breach of the peace. Edward Mooney did not appear and a war- rant was issued for his apprehension.—P C Cbrystal deposed that be saw the defendants fighting in Gerard-street on the previous Monday evening. The defendant, Owen Mooney, pleaded not guilty, and plaintively inquired, "What do two brothers want fighting for ?" The Chairman : You must decide that for yourself.—The cass was adjourned for the defendant to produce witnesses. A TREFT.—John Rothwell was charged on remand with stealing lie Bd, the property of Margaret Atherton, at Red Cat Village. The prisoner lodged with the prosecutrix, who missed the money from her house. The prisoner was sus- pected, and he was apprehended.—He was committed to prison for a month.

RELEASE OF AN Irma Coxvirr.—The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland has directed the immediate release of a convict named Kilmartin, who was not long ago sentenced to penal servitude for life after conviction on a charge of shooting at and wounding a he'll!! on Aran Island. Recently a " confession " was made in America by a man who accused himself of the crime, and after a lengthy investigation his Excellency has felt able to exercise his prerogative in Kit- martin's favour. REDisrmouTiox.—The October number of the National Review will contain an article by Lord Salisbury on "Redis- tribution." His Lordship says his object is to refute a calumny directed against the Conservative party, that they really dread both Franchise and Redistribution, and are only desirous of delay. He gives statistics to show that the Con- asrvatives have every reason to desire extension of the Franchise, and that the Conservative party are now weaker in the Rouse of Commons by eighty-nine votes than they would be with a true distribution and the proposed enfran- ekisement.

A DISASTROUS Tax.—Dnring Oliver Cromwell's Protectorate Jamaica was taken from the Spaniards and ever since has been a British possession. At our advent on the Island. there were sixty-five cocoa walks. each walk or plantation comprising thousands of trees—the Theobroma Cacao. On Charles the Second's return we hear of, M Bt. James's street and else. where. chicolate-houses as well as of coffee-houses, both one and the other being the mode. and answering to the West-end clubs of to-day. Later on we find coffee-houses standing on a broader basis, and gr.dually adapting their prices to meet the means of all classes. but we find no such records of the pro. grass of chocolate: yet it needed not to go far to And the wherefore. In Bryan Edward's " History of the West Indies," 3 vols., published in 1793, we find the duty on cocoa made into cakes was twelve guineas per cwt., besides lie lit d paid at the Custom House. t.e., 480 per cent. and this rate of duty continued down to the end of the 18th century, cocoa becom- ing, for the English market, a production not worth the grow- ing, and Jamaica's plantations were let fall to decay. When we again come upon a record, it is in 1832. and the duty which had been standing at 6d per pound, with an importation of under half a million pounds per annum, was forthwith reduced to 2d, and not long after we find, as a coincidence, that the bomceopathic doctrine of medicine was introduced into this country, and that cocoa was specially advocated as a drink by the physicians adopting that mode of treatment, aa outcome ef which being that the first established homosopatbic chemists in England (James Epps and Co.) produced a special prepara- tion, which only needed boiling water or milk to be at once ready for the table. In 1842, the duty was again reduced to a penny per pound, and we find the consumption making such way that the output alone of the manufacturers above alluded to reached in the year jnst passed away between axe and six .milliorts of pounds,—" Tits Brarier,"-44e1.
TERRIBLE DISASTER ON THE IRISH
COAST. SINKING OF THE GUNBOAT WASP.-50 LIVES LOST.

Information was on Tuesday— afternoon received at the Admiralty that her Majesty's gunboat Wasp had been totally lost at Tory Island, off the coast of Donegal, and that only six men had been saved out of a total complement of 58. The brief despatch reporting the disaster added :—" The Lieutenant commanding and other officers are not among the survivors." _

Almost simultaneously with the receipt of this mes- sage the following telegram came to band from Lloyd's agent at Innistoffin, dated Dunfanagby, September 23,.3 12 p.m. : Her Majesty's gunboat Wasp wrecked Tory Island. Only six men saved. On Monday morning, three o'clock. Not practicable to proceed from mainland in open boat." It has since been ascertained that one officer was absent on leave, and a seaman was in sick quarters at Westport. The loss of lives is thus fixed at 50.

The Wasp is a composite gunboat carrying four guns and 465 tons butthen. Her engines are 470 horse power. She was commissioned at Devonport on December 1, 1881, and was engaged on particular service, which at the time of the disaster necessitated her coasting round the north- west of Ireland. Her lieutenant and commandant, John D Nicholls, was commissioned on January 1, 1883, the other officers appointed being Navigating Lieutenant Frederick A Warden, Sub-Lieutenant Thomas S Guppy, Engineer Wm. Hudson. and Gunner John W Kerrigan. The north coast of Donegal is of a wild and rugged character, studded with numerous little islands, of which Tory Island is the most important. Both headlands and precipitous cliffs render the coast very dangerous for navigators in stormy weather. Tory Island is about two and a half miles long and one mile broad, and has a lighthouse on the north-west end. The north side presents a range of cliffs 100 ft to 3001 t high. Toward the south the laud slopes down and the shore is fiat. The lighthouse stands 1221 t above the sea level. There are about 70 families on the island, depending chiefly noon fishing. Inistoffin is an island about one mile from the mainland, and has a coast- guard station. The islet is about a mile in circumference 'About three months ago the Wasp was set apart for special 'service on the north-west coast of Ireland to proceed with the several Commissioners of the Harbour Fisheries Board round the different harbours and rivers, where statistics and 'other information were being collected relative to the fish- eries and navigation. In addition to the officers above men- tioned Surgeon Otway P Brown was appointed this year to the Wasp, but he was not on board, being away on leave. When the news of the wreck reached the Admiralty Admiral Sir Cooper Key, who is fulfilling Lord Northbrook's duties ad interim, was in the office, and be instantly telegraphed to the nearest available responsible officer to proceed to the spot and report upon the disaster. Meantime a fur- ther telegram was received from one of the crew con- firming the earlier news, but giving no additional facts. The Wasp belonged to the Queenstown division of the British squadron on the Irish coast. The fact that there were so many souls on board the gunboat is accounted for by her being engaged on special service and having pro- bably a number of coastguards for transfer as well as the commissioners on board.

A telegram from London, on Tuesday evening, states that the gunboat Wasp was coming round to Moville for the pur- pose of taking the Sheriff and an evicting party to the Islet of Innistrahul, situate at the mouth of Lough Foyle, where a number of persons were to have been removed from their dwellings. The Admiralty state that Her Majesty's ship Valiant, (Min Batillnullen, has been sent to Tory Island to render assistance and to obtain particulars of the wreck of the Waap. Rathmullen is on the Donegal coast, in Lough Swilly, a distance of about 40 miles by sea from the scene of the disaster. The Valiant is on coastguard service, her usual station being at Bantry. A later te'egram says none of the officers are among the survivors. Those saved are greatly exhausted, and they re- main in Tory lighthouse. The rock upon which the Wasp struck is within 40 yards of the lighthouse, and the top- masts of the vessel are visible. There is groat tlifficulty in getting details, as the place is remote and not easy of access. The Wasp left Westport for Moville on Sunday last. The following is a list of the officers, as printed in the "Navy List" for September :—Lieutenant and Commander John D Nicholls; Lieutenant (N.) George H King; Sub-lieuten- ant Thomas S Guppy; surgeon, P Browne; engineer, William Hudson; gunner, John W Kerrigan. Her crew is returned on the list as consisting of 58 men, so that suppo- sing that there were no coastguardsmen or others on board being conveyed from one place to another, the loss of life would be about 50. The service on which she was employed was principally coastguard. The resident Clerk at the Admiralty states that the Fisheries Commission was not on board the Wasp. Thursday's " Freeman's Journal" states that the morn- ing of the wreck (Monday) was marked by drizzling rain. All on board, save the watch, were in bed, and the com- manding officer in the cabin ; but the navigating lieutenant was on deck. Precisely at five minutes to four the gunboat ran upon a reef. The first bump was so violent that the bottom was broken in, and the vessel filled rapidly. The commander ordered boats to be got ready and lowered ; but tefore this could be done the vessel bumped again, and within 15 minutes she sank in 20 fathoms of water, with a loss of 50 souls. The quartermaster of the watch and the man on the lookout were saved, as well as the man at the wheel, who was the last to leave the doomed vessel. The wreck was not seen by any islander, or by the lighthouse- keeper, and the six survivors, who clung to a spar, were greatly exhausted before they were thrown upon the rocks and saved. They all suffer from wounds they received. Her Majesty's ship Valiant reached Tory Island on Wednes- day. A London correspondent has received particulars of the wreck of the Wasp from one of the survivors. The gun- boat was under sail at the time of the disaster, and was hugging the shore far too closely. The captain himself set her course. When she struck an ineffectual attempt was made to get up steam. Three boats were launched, but all were dashed to pieces in the surf. A tremendous wave then washed away the bridge and all the officers. Great confusion followed, each man struggling for him- self. Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary were, on Thurs- day, posted along the coast, keeping a sharp lookout for any wreckage. Various opinions were expressed in the locality as to the probability of the appearance of any bodies along the northern coast of Donegal. Surprise is ex- pressed by those acquainted with the coast that the Wasp shoeld have hugged Tory Island so close. The following telegram was received on Thursday morn- ing by Admiral Lethbridge from Commander Marrack, of the Valiant, from Rathmullen :—" I succeeded in embarking the six survivors of the Wasp on Wednesday afternoon from Tory island, and returned to Lough Swilly at 11 p.m. The names ef the men saved are Jones Hutton, R Rattenbury, quartermaster; Philip Andrews, second captain forecastle; W H Dunne, A. 8.; A Brotnhead, private Royal Marines; and E Styles, private Royal Marines. They state everybody else perished except the surgeon and engineer (Hudson), who were on leave, and James Eva, A. 13., who is left behind at Westport, breaking his leave. No bodies have been washed up. Request instructions as to:the disposal of the survivors." Mrs Hutton, wife of the cook, who resides at Queenstown, received at midnight, on Wednesday. the following telegram from Father O'Donnell, Dunfanagby:—Mr Hutton very well; only a few scratches. He can return immediately. Tie Valiant is now at the island. It is stated that the navigating lieutenant caused the Wasp's sail to be shortened just before the disaster, which occasioned her to run on the rocks. The survivors were taken to Dublin on Thursday, and then proceeded to Portsmouth, where a court-martial will be held on board the flag ship Duke of Wellington. It is now stated that the navigating lieutenant of the Wasp, Mr Down, was comparatively inexperienced as to the dangers of the coast. He was on dace when, on Monday morning at four o'clock. the ship struck on a reef, being then, it is remarked, "too near the island." Warning of the position is said to have been given by the man at the wheel, who received as answer to a communicatiom made to the captain that he must steer the course directed by his superior officer. The Wasp was proceeding under sail. and her furnaces were banked up, and the attempt to get up 'steam which appears to have been at last decided on came

div.head: EXAMINER, SA_TURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA_TURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27. 1884.

too late to carry the ship out of danger. The first bump on the rocks completely broke in the bottom of the vessel, which filled rapidly and went down in 20 fathoms of water within a quarter of an hour. Had it been possible to place the Wasp's boats upon the water they must have been dashed to pieces. The six survivors clung to a spar and were thrown,upon the rocks. The Valiant arrived in Lough Swilly on Thursday after- noon with the six survivors of the Wasp on board They are nominally under arrest, but are allowed full liberty in the vessel. They have almost recovered from their injuries, I which apparently were not of a serious character. At three o'clock in the afternoon five of the survivors were asleep I below, while the old grey-haired cook Hutton, was walking briskly on deck chatting with the crew. The whole circum- stances of the disaster are being communicated to the Admiralty. One of the officers of the Valiant stated this afternoon at Rathmullen that just before the Wasp struck, and while all her officers were on the bridge, an im- mense wave broke over her and carried the bridge and its occupants slang with it. Immediately afterwards the gun- boat was dashed on the rocks. The following special tele- gram has been received from Duefanaghy :—"The Wasp is , still in the same position. No bodies have been washed ashore yet. The sail boat which came with the intelligence I of the disaster went off to the island on Thursday, but has not returned!'

the parishioners, who willingly subscribed towards the testimonials which were presented on Monday. Some time ago a committee was appointed to consider the advisability of erecting a new place of worship, and they have since considered several schemes. They are at present in communication with the London and North-Western Rail- way Company with respect to a plot of land in Earle-street, adjoining the stores of the Co-operative Society, and it is confidently expected that the site in question will be ulti- mately secured. It will be remembered that some time ago the committee made an effort to secure the large room of the Viaduct Institute, in which to temporarily hold Sunday ser- vices; but in this they were unsuccessful. Last week, how- ever, it was announced that a church of England service would be held in the Co-operative Hall, and that it would be conducted by the Rev H E Smith. Before Sunday, how- ever, the rev, gentleman named was informed that he would incur a risk as far as his position in the Church of England was concerned, in preaching and conducting a Church of England service in an " unconsecrated " building, and con- sequently he sent word that he found it advisable not to fulfil his engagement. The evening service was I held, however, and the hall was crowded to its utmost extent; a large number of persons being unable to obtain admittance. The service was conducted by Mr M Birkhead, late vicar's warden, the psalms and hymns being sung by the late choir of St. John's, and the late organist, Mr Darman, accompanied on the harmonium. The res- ponses of the congregation were remarkably hearty, and the whole service was gone through in a vigorous and spirited manner which formed a strong contrast to the " dumb " services which are still carried on by the small residue of the congregation now attendisg St. John's Church. The sermon was preached by a local evangelical preacher. Whilst this service was going on, the attendance at St. John's was remarkably scanty, there being fewer than twenty persons present. On Monday evening, the Co-operative Hall was again filled, when the presentations to the Rev H E Smith and Mr Darman were made. The chair was occupied by Mr George Appleton (who, it will be recollected, was appointed people's warden at the last vestry meeting), and he was supported by Mr B Corlett, Mr H J Durman, and other gentlemen. There were also upon the platform the members of the late choir of St. John's Church. The proceedings were com- menced with the glee "The stars are with the voyagers," which was nicely given by the choir; Mr Darman presiding at the pianoforte. Shortly afterwards Mr George Wright gave in capital style "I fear no foe." The Chairman then said that they all knew what they were there for that evening. It was to present Mr Smith and Mr Darman with testimonials of their good wishes and kindly feelings towards those gentlemen. They were all in the unfortunate position of being "Out of a shop." (Laugh- ter.) In that respect they were similarly situated, but Mr Smith and Mr Darman were being victimised, as they were practically out of a situation. Bat they (the parishioners) were not in that strait. He did not know that they. could do much for them in any way so far as finding them situa- tions was concerned, but he was sure they were all sincerely sorry that they were in the position they were at pre- sent. (Applause.) The Rev H E Smith here entered the room and was re- ceived with loud and prolonged cheering. When the ap- plause had subsided Mr Birkhead was called upon to ad- dress the meeting. Mr Shithead commenced by humorously remarking that it was usual for a person placed in the position he was to start with a good many apologies, and to say that they were very unfit for the task and thoroughly unequal to it. (Laughter.) But be (Mr Birkhead) did not exactly be- lieve in that; and others sometimes regretted that they had not selected a better man. (Renewed laughter.) But he (Mr Birkhead) did not feel that at all—(hear, hear,)— because somehow or other he thought they could hardly have got a better rnan. (Applause.) He was quite satis- fied with the man they had got, and he hoped there would be no grumbling on their part when he had got through his work. He was at a loss how to treat the subject. Squab- bles and scandals were things bad of themselves when in a private family or in private individuals, bat when they came to churches it required a very delicate handling. He did not want to say much about the bother they bad got into, but wished to say as little as possible about it. The question for them was that having got into a mess, how were they to get out of it as comfortably as they could. During the time the anpleasantness had been going on he (Mr Birkhead) became acquainted with Mr. Smith, for previously he had had no introduction to him. Sine* that time the introduction had brought out the bright, honett, and sterling qualities of Mr Smith, and showed him to be as he (Mr Birkhead) believed a gentleman and a Christian. (Applause). There sec ra two sides to the dispute—both a comical side and a seri- ous side. It had broeght out the good sterling qualities of some and had shown the weakness on others; but besides that it had done something else' and nobody living would ever be able to tell what it had done to the rising generation, because just now the young folks in the parish were receiving their impressions. Mr Smith had been placed in a very unpleasant position, and like others had been placed in hot water, and when the water got tnwartil they mild net long remain In It. (Luughter and applause.) SO far as Mr Smith WU Concerned he had always acted as a Christian gentleman. He had been charged with disloyalty to his chief. Disloyalty in some instances was a very dirty sort of thing to handle, but he (Mr Birk- head) thought Mr Smith was only disloyal to a bad princi- ple—(bean, hear)—and on that account they honoured him. (Applause.) Mr Smith was loyal to his church, as far ae he could understand, and loyal to the people committed to his charge, and they believed he was loyal to his God— (hear, hear' and applause)—and for that loyalty they honoured him, and they highly esteemed his presence amongst them that evening. They were not a very wealthy class, and had not much of the aristocracy about them, but what little they were doing for Mr Smith was given with the goodwill, the blessing, and the wishes of those who were giving it. (Applause.) If they bad bad more they would willingly have accorded it, but as it was Mr Smith had the prayers and good wishes of his former congrega- tion, and they desired to acknowledge the valuable services which he bad rendered to them. (Applause.) He (Mr Birkbead) hoped before long Mr Smith would have a good church, and as loyal and faithful a people as he had had at Earlestown. (Cheers.) He had the greatest pleasure in handing to Mr Smith an illuminated address, along with a purse of gold, on behalf of the parishioners of St. John the Baptist Church. (Applause.) Mr Birkhead then read the address as follows

To the Reverend Henry Elwell Smith.—Reverend and Dear Sir,—We. the undersigned, desire on behalf of the congrega- tion till lately worshipping at St. John the Baptist's Church. Earlestown, to tender to you this expression of our heartfelt appreciation of your ministrations and Christian conduot dur• log a time of unexampled trial. We also wish to bear record to the fact that, amidst all the diffloolties with which you had to eontend. we tawny, found you doing the work of the good Shepherd 'that sohttereth not His sheep," and to assure you that in parting you carry away with you the best wishes of all. Our earnest prayer is, that whatever sphere of usefulness you may hereafter be engaged in, the Divine blessing may be with you and crown your every effort; and when at last called to give an account of the flock committed to your charge, you may be able to say "Here am I Lord, and the people Thou haat given me." That health, happiness, and every temporal blessing may be your portion here; and that when your earthly pilgrimage is finished, you may attain to that heavenly calling whioh is far batter," is the sincere and heartfelt prayer of—Yours very sincerely, The Committee.

The Chairman ren.arked that he need not say anything about Mr Smith after what Mr Birkhead had said. He, too, was sure that all appreciated him, and they were all ex- ceedingly sorry now that they had to part with him. He hoped that when Mr Smith had left he would go to a place where he would be much better appreciated by those in authority over him than he had been at Earlestown. He had only to say that Mr Smith had been 'got shut of," as it were, by the Vicar on a very off-hand way, and he only wished the parishioners could get shut of the Vicar as easily (Laughter and cheers.) Mr J Worsley, a young man, then stepped forward, and said his pleasing duty was to present the Rev H E Smith with two testimonials subscribed for by his late senior class in the Sunday school. He could not express the regret of the scholars at being so suddenly separated from Mr Smith. He had the greatest pleasure in handing to Mr Smith an album containing the portraits of his late class, every mem- ber of which loved and respected him; and also with a silver pen and pencil case. (Cheers.) He hoped before long they would have a new church or school in which they would be able once more to hear the good story of the Shepherd and his sheep, and where the scattered flock of St. John the Bap- tist could once again gather together for worship as in the past. (Applause.) The album was what is known as a "Floral Album," and was a very handsome one. It bore the following inscrip- tion :—"Presented to the Rev H E Smith, on the 22nd day of September, 1884, as a token of respect and esteem during his ministry at St. John the Baptist Church, Earlestown ; also a silver pencil and case, by the scholars of the first Bible class, of whom the Rev H E Smith was our beloved teacher." The male voices of the choir then excellently gave the glee, "The sailors' chorus." The Rev H E Smith then rose amid cheers to acknow- ledge the gifts. He said he knew not how to find words to thank them for the gratifying testimonial and kind presents which they had made him, but he could assure them that when he had the honour of fulfilling the various offices, to which as curate of that important office he was appointed, he endeavoured faithfully to discharge the duties pertaining to those offices, and it was the consciousness of that that made him more fully appreciate the testimonials. When he looked at the beautiful illuminated address and the album they had given him he would ever think of the time he had spent among them with pleasure, notwithstanding the little rough passages in the pilgrimage they had bad to pass through. It was always a sad hard task to bid good-bye to friends; and could they wonder that it was very difficult for him to utter the earnest expression of vrhat he felt in ad- dressing those from whom he had received so warm a wel- come that evening and such generous kindness that he would always speak and think of them as his best and dearest friends. He had no idea that they were getting up the tes- timonials until they were nearly completed. With all due respect to Mr Birkhead, he must say that he did not deserve it. They knew he had not visited them as he wished, or as he would have liked; but there were strong reasons why he had not done so, and for those very reasons he had been condemned. lie did not want to form any clique. (Hear, hear.) He wished to be very Cautious in what he said; far be it from him to say anything against anyone; but he did not want the pastor of the parish to be able to say that he was forming a clique. (Applause.) He, however, was now sorry that he had not visited them, for theylhad proved to be his best friends. He had to thank all present for the social welcome : so genial and Bo heart- felt, which he would ever cherish with affectionate regret ;

the remembrance of the scenes of that evening would ever be aesociated with their generous kindness. (Applause.) He was sorry to allude to anything that had passed, but before closing he must vindicate himself. (Hear. hear.) The three letters of his, which Mr Matthews published. were written when he was very ill, suffering bodily and mentally, and he thought he would have to give up minis- terial life for sometime. A clergyman asked him to address the Sunday School children for him, when he (the Rev HE Smith) was absent on sick leave; and the week before he did his best not to do so; and Mr Matthews then asked him to take his holidays. The clergyman pressed him to address The scholars, and the only reason he did so was because he (the cleryrnan) was 'going to preach else- where, and consequently he did address the scheol children. The reason why he left was what happened at the Sunday school, on the Sunday after his return. They all knew the young men whom Mr Mathews said were absent 44 times bad only been absent three or four times. ("Shame.") That was the very cause. The Bishop could not have turned him away; nobody could have tamed him away. But when he came back he saw the sheep had 'led, the organist had gone, their good choir, who had a famous name like Mr Durman had, and who ways did their work well and encour- aged him (Rev H E Smith), had all gone away. On the Sunday that he was told to close the service after the banns of marriage in the absence of the vicar, some of his (Mr Smith's) friends told him that they were determined to have a service, and what was he to do ? Who was he to obey? Was he to obey Mr Matthews and break the law, or obey the law and his bishop? He had promised to obey his bishop, but only in things honest and lawful; but he was afterwards told that be had broken some contract with the bishop. He, however, had broken no contract with the bishop, but Mr Matthews had broken one with him. Because he thought, and he would speak boldly, that Mr Darman was perfectly right in not turning their friends Mr Wright and Mr Platt from the choir—(applause)—he had been charged with the origin of the disturbances that ensued. But it arose from the vicar's pew. The bishop's letter to him was most kind, and a copy of it he believed was sent to the vicar. They all knew that he knew nothing of their inten- tion to build an iron church. (Hear, heir.) He was told from high quarters to remain until the let August, and that was the time that he signed up to; but on the Bth August Mr Matthews said he was in Earlestown doing he knew what. Mr Matthews yet owed him £lO for his six months' notice. (" Shame.") With reference to his priest's orders. he never knew when he had to go up for them; but he had suffered quite enough. He was in deacon's orders, and many men in the church had been in deacon's orders longer than he had and had held far higher offim than he could ever hope to fill. The people of Earlestown were a sam- ple of true English people, and he was sorry he could not come and preach to them on the previous day. It was his own doing end be did not want to blame any of his kind friends. They must be very cautions in what they did for he believed the Bishop was on their side. But they would still have ministrations although they had been cast out by Mr Matthews. (Applause.) Mr Matthews had charged him with secession from the Church of England, but he could assure them he never did it. He loved his dissenting friends and would shake hands with them, but at the same time he was a far better churchman than Mr Matthews. (Cheers.) Let him tell them too that the Established Church was a church for everybody, and as a clergyman of the Church of England he (Mr Smith) did not call anybody dissenters. (Hear, hear.) They might call them Methodists or Congregationalists, but he would not call them dissenters. They must be careful to work on church lines, and if they wrote to the Bishop he (Mr Smith) thought a place would be licensed for them, if Mr Matthews would not feed the sheep. (Hear, hear.) He did not want to be too strong on Mr Matthews, and far be it from him to Fay anything that would injure anybody' but Mr Matthews had injured him. Wishing no ill to any, he would leave his case and all con- cerned in it in the hands of Him who ordereth all things right. (Loud applause.) The Chairman then remarked that the next item on the programme was a presentation to Mr Darman. (Applause.) He fully sympathised with the parishioners in presenting Mr Durman with a token of their good wishes. He felt, he could say, as much as most people with respect to the suc- cess Mr Darman had attained during his connection with the perish. They might look at the enormous concerts they had had, and haw Mr Darman had broughe up and trained such are efficient choir for the services of the church. The success which Mr Durman had attained had created a certain jealousy on the pert of the vicar, by being thought well of instead of himself. There was no doubt that Mr Darman was fully entitled to everything they could say about him, and they were well satisfied with the result of his efforts in the parish. (Applause.) He (the chairman) could not at the same time wish to forget the services of Mr Smith.

- The Rev H E Smith here rose and said the chairman could not speak too well of Mr Durman, and he (Mr 6inith) was glad Mr Darman was associated with him on that pre- sentation. He thought the world of Mr Durman, and if that gentleman went to Liverpool and took his choir with him he would be bound to say some tbouiands of people would go and hear them, for they were well liked in Liverpool. Tbey had been together charged with telling falsehoods, but feel 3poke for themselves, The newspapers had educa- ted the people of Liverpool and other places, and they now all knew who were at fault. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman (resuming) said Mr Durman commenced without a choir, but before long he got together a choir which was second to none in Lancashire. (Applause.) He (the chairman) was the first to start the movement for securing an organ, by offering a subscription of £2O, and they all knew what had been the result of Mr Durman's services. Mr Durman's reputation extended further than Earlestown, but he along with Mr Smith had been victim- ised. ("Shame.") It was jealousy on the part of the Vicar for the good they were doing in the place. (Hear, hear.) Nothing could have gone on better. There was no church in England better supported than the Earlestown church by the working-classes, and if they had been properly treated by the Vicar, who had shown a great want of com- mon sense, he believed they would have had as successful a place as any in England. (Applause.) Bath the gentle- men he had named had lost their places because they had done good, and the parishioners regretted that they were los- ing them. They had lost the church, they had lost the choir and the curate, and they had nothing but the Vicar, and another such vicar did not exist in England. (Laugh- er.) He was a vicar who cared nothiog about his con- gregation, but said be could preach to the wall—it was im- material to him whether he preached to the people or not. It had been said that that the church had not been built by Earlestown people. It was true they had been liberally supported by outsiders. He alluded to the exertion of Mr Tootil, of Etrlestown, in the establishment of the choreal, and added that he thought Mr Tootil was entitled to the thanks of the whole community for his assistance. The speaker afterwards commented upon Mr Durman's services, remarking that in everything he had undertaken lie had had a run of continued success. He did not think there was a better organist in Lancashire, and no one could have been of more use and benefit than he had been. (Applause.) Miss Bertha Jackson and Miss Harrison, two girls, then stepped forward, and handed to Mr Darman a large copy of the Bible, handsomely bound. Miss Jackson, speaking to Mr Darman, said : We have been appointed by the juvenile choir to ask your acceptance of this small token of our love for you as our teacher. We are much obliged to you for your kindness towards us, and we trust the lessons taught in this Book may benefit you both in this life and that which is to come. (Applause.) Miss Harrison then read an inscription on the cover of the Bible, which was as fol- lows:—" Presented to Mr H J Durman by a few of the little folks who took part in the cancert given in connection with St John the Baptist Church, Earlestown. September, 1884." There were also handed to Mr Darman by the Chairman four volumes, comprising the oratorios of "Elijah," "St Paul," "Redemption," and " Judas Mac- cabaus." One of the books bore the following words Presented to Mr H J Darman by the parishioners of St John the Baptist Church, in recognition of his services as the organist and choirmaster for a term of five years." Mr H J Durman was received with loud applause. He thanked them very sincerely for their kind and generous ex- pressions of their good feelings towards him. He did not know that he deserved them, but he was sure he had realised pleasures sufficient to recompense him in the work in which he had been engaged. It had been his privilege to be amongst them for nearly six years, and it had been a pleasure to him to be identified with almost every movement in connection with the church during that time. (Applause.) It was very gratifying to him to know that what little he had done met with their appreciation, and.he was only sorry that circumstances prevented him from being amongst them in the same capacity as heretofore; bathe trusted before long they would be able to gather together for worship in the good old fashioned way. (Applause.) He was much obliged to the little people for their present, and if ever there was a work in which he delighted to take part it was in being amongst the little children—(hear, hear,)—and it was a pleasure to know that one was beloved by children. He sincerely thanked all for their kind expressions of respect. (Applause.) Mr J Spragg, who designed and painted the testimonial presented to the Rev H E Smith, next sang "The Old Sexton," and the male voices of the choir gave "Comrades in arms."
This concluded the presentation proceedings. THE PROPOSED NEW CHURCH.

The meeting afterwards considered the advisability of erecting an iron church or other structure in which to hold services. Mr Benjamin Corlett was first called upon to make a statement in relation thereto. He stated that on the last occasion when the parishioners met together, a promise was given that the question of having a new iron church eh mid be gone into thoroughly after they had made an effort to remove the Vicar by a petition to the Bishop. They had done so, but the Bishop had written stating that any arrangements for an exchange by Mr Matthews could only be initiated by himself. He (Mr Corlett) did not think that was a satisfactory reply; they ought to have the Bishop's sympathy. No doubt he considered himself within the strict letter of the law ; but if it was the law that one man should drive 700 or 800 of a congregation away from a church, the sooner it was reformed the better. (Applause.) With regard to the new iron church, they had made an application to the London and North-Western Railway Company for a patch of land near the Co-operative Hall, and a reply was expected from .them every day. He coneidered by putting their shoulders to the wheel they would be able to raise a very decent structure for about £4OO, which could be easily raised by £1 shares. They would not Ask for the pound at once, but it would do if it was paid at the rate of Id per day. (Laughter.) He dared say they would wonder bow they proposed to support the church when it was built. They estimated they would on an average have a congrega- of 200 in the morning and 400 at night, irom whom they would collect about £l5O in the year if each person gave

a penny to the offertories. Then by quarterly collections or subscriptions they would raise ths amount to £2OO per year. He thought if they paid a clergyman £l3O per year it would be as much as some received from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and they would use the remainder for other expenses. He would like to ask how many of those present would voluntarily assist by taking shares. It depended on them whether they would have a new church or not. His plan was to have a church on Reformed principles, and they could then please themselves whether they had a minister or not, and it would not be under state control. He would like the meeting to say whether they would go to the old church or have a new one.—A Parishioner: What is the use of the old one? (Applause.)—Mr Corlett asked those in favour of a new church to signify it by holding up their hand.—All present heartily responded amid applause.—Mr Corlett stated that the decision having been unanimous they would require a committee to carry out the movement —A A Voice: Get rid of the vicar, the old place will do very well. (Hear, hear.)—Mr Corlett remarked that if they only made a start with regard to the new church they would soon get plenty of support. Mr M Birkhead said that on the previous evening they were almost like the children of Israel for they had a taste of the "promised land." (Applause.) They had had a service in that hall and if he could judge from the counten- ance and the manner in which they entered into the service they thoroughly enjoyed it. It was a monstrous thing that a whole parish should be driven out of their place of wor- ship by the obstinate and self-willed stubborness of one man —(applause)--and any church which allowed such conduct as that required a thorough reformation. (Cheers.) If he had any say in regard to the new church it must be on a different foundation to that. (Applause.) They must have a say in regard to the services and in the appointment of the man who should minister to them. Did they want a church of that sort? ('‘ Yes" and applanse.) They wanted a minister over them who would lead and not drive them —(hear, heir,)—and one who would visit and comfort them. He remarked that the Bishop had been condemned in some quarters for his action in regard to the parishioners, but they must remember that the Bishop had his hands tied ; that he could not do anything he liked. He (Mr Birkhead) believed they had the Bishop's sympathy at heart. If they pat up an iron church arid held services in it for a year there was no telling what changes might take place. They might have an opportunity of going back to the old place, and then they could sell the new church for old iron—they would get half price for it. (Loud laughter and applause.) If they did not want to demolish it and sell it as old iron they could use it as a school. (Applause). Mr F Blundell then excellently sang (in character) "Robinson Crusoe," and received a deserved encore. Miss B Jackson afterwards gave " Beautiful voices " in a nice manner.

The Rev H E Smith, in moving a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, remarked that Mr Matthews had brought everything about himself. He thought the Bishop of Liver. pool would licence them a new place for worship, for he believed he (the bishop) felt for them. There were many ways of raising funds to start a new church, such as by lectures, sermons, dic. His duty that evening was to ask the meeting to show their appreciation of the services of Mr Appleton, as chairman by hearty applause. (Applause.) The Chairman briefly responded, after which the meeting concluded with "Softly falls the shades of evening," apiece by the choir.

LOCAL HARVEST FESTIVALS. ALL SAINTS', THELWALL.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held at All Saints' Church, 'Thelwall, on Saturday and Sunday, the offertories being in aid of the S.P.G, and the Diocesan Institutions. On Saturday evening the Rev F Slater, MA, vicar of St. James', Latchford, preached to a good congregation. At 8-30 on Sunday morning there was choral celebration of Holy Communion, ond at 10-30 matins and second celebration, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev Gibson Smith, MA, Boteler Grammar School. In the afternoon a serrnen was preached by the Rev E W Lomax, MA, curate of Lymm, and the Rev C J Winsor, M.A, of High Leigh, preached in the evening. EMMANUEL CHURCIL—OR Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held in Emmanuel Church, Bold-street. There had been no special attempts at decoration. There were large congregations both morning and evening. The ser- mons were preached by the pastor, the Rev W Mules, from the texts "Giving thanks always lor all things," Sic., Ephe- dans, 5, 50; and "The harvest is past, the summer is ended," Jer. 8, 20. The collections amounted to nearly £7. CHRIST Crtunctt, PADGATE.—Harvest thanksgiving ser- vices were held at this church on Sunday, when sermons were preached by the vicar, the Rev W H Williams, to large congregations. Special anthems were sung by the choir, under the leadership of Mr Harding, the organist, and the church was artistically decorated. The collections realised £lO. Amongst the workers and donors of fruit, vegetables, and flowers were Mrs Williams, Misses Crawford (3), Misses Appleton (2), Miss Sansome, Misses Turner (2), Miss Yates. Miss Wrightson Miss Walmesley, and Messrs Houghton, Hatton, and others.

PENEETH WESLEYAN CHAPEL-011 Sunday a harvest festival and anniversary sermons were preached in the Wes- leyan chapel, in the morning at 10 30 by the Rev G E Cutting, and in the evening at 6-30 by the Rev J Howell Jones, the newly appointed ministers to the Warrington circuit. There were good congregatiens, and the sermons were highly appreciated. Collections were made on behalf of the trust funds. The altar was profusely and tastefully decorated with fruit, grapes, pears, marrows, bops, dm, the work being undertaken by Misses Garnett,Moses, and Brie- coe. Plants were kindly lent for the occasion by R Garnett, Esq, Hall Nook, Penketh.

CHRIST CHURCH, CROFT.—On Sunday morning and afternoon harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above church. The congregations were rather large, that of the afternoon, however, being smaller than is usual on such an occasion owing to the rain, which commenced early after the morning service. The Rev W Wilson, vicarlof Burtonwood, officiated at both seryices. The texts were the 59th verse of the 110th Psalm and the 3rd verse of the 14th chapter of St Mark, and the sermons based on them were unusually appropriate. As regards the decimation of the structure of the church, which gives very little scope for such a purpose, the effects produced were excellent. Most of the designs were very tasteful, and one prominent and praiseworthy feature throughout was the lightness of the decorations. At the bottom of the chancel window, which was prettily latticed almost to the top, was the text "Gather the wheat into my barn " (a wheat sheaf, however, being substituted for the word), the letters being worked out in corn, and placed upon a background of moss and ferns. The flowers on the Communion table, and throughout the church, in fact, were the choicest of the season, and were very attractive indeed, consisting of asters, dahlias, lilies, gladioli, roses, stocks, everlasting flowers suoflowers, which were kindly contributed by some of the members of the congregation and the members of the choir. Outside the Communion rails which were elegantly trimmed with oats, wild clematis, the., were two small round tables, one at each side, on each of which was a very line ice plant; several other choice plants kindly lent for the occasion were also placed near the Communion rails, and were greatly ad- mired. Before leaving the chancel one could not avoid noticing the display of fine fruit, which was very neatly arranged under the two tables. Itie pulpit, reading desk, and the choir stalls were very skillfully ornamented, the designs adopted for each being very suitable. The window sills, of the sides of the church, each had a pramework of oak or ivy leaves, and were tastefully trimmed with flowers and fruit. Great pains- taking and much labour had been spent on these, there being no less than ten in number. At the west end was a minia- ture stack of corn and some gigantic vegetables' die.. kindly contributed by some of the farmers of the parish. The font was ornamented in a very simple but artistic style. Moss covered the whole et the top, but this was relieved by a beautiful circle of asters; this, together with the chain Sus- pending it, which was decorated with fuchsia sprigs, had a very pretty effect. In the windows near the font was the appropriate phrase "Corn of Heaven" nicely worked in corn and surrounded by some rare flowers. The other part of the decorations was also a source of attraction, viz., the three festoons,which were attached to one of the cross beams, and to which three baskets of flowers were suspended. The following are the ladies who carried out the principal part of the work of the decorations, viz.;—Mrs Kirkman, Mrs Owen (the brewery), Miss Ball, the Misses Bate, the Misses Birchen, the Misses Southern, and Miss Robinson, who were kindly assisted by a few of the other members of the con- gregation and the members of the choir. The services were full choral, special hymns appropriate for the occasion be- ing sung, and the anthems "Thou crownest the year with Thy goodness" (T Smith), and "Praise the Lord, Oh, my soul" (W Marshall), which were rendered by the choir in a highly efficient manner, under the conductorship of Mr Ball, the organist and choir master. The collections, which were in support of public worship, amounted to £8 15s. ST. PA 7L'S CHURCH, WARRINOTOST.—On Thursday even- ing a harvest thanksgiving service was held at St. Paul's Church, Warrington, when the sermon was preached by the Rev Canon Rycroft. The rev gentleman remarked that he supposed that the present harvest was one of the finest that the country had experienced for several years, and it was quite proper for people to show their gratitude for the good things that had been vouchsafed to them. The chancel, pulpit, font, and windows were very prettily decorated, and the congregation was large. Special hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung.

A Redcar smack-owner named Jackson was remanded on Thursday on a charge of having smuggled about I,Boolb. of manufactured tobacco and cigars into this country. The convict John Sullivan, who was last week sentenced to death for the murder of his child at Poplar, has been respited. At the trial the jury recommended him to mercy. The Russian tailor Eiverstaed, who on Saturday night murdered a woman in Liverpool by stabbing her to the heart with a dagger, was on Thursday committed for trial on the capital charge. At Sheffield. on Wednesday, Thos. Atherton, tobacconist, was fined LSO and costs for allowing his premises to be used for betting Purposes; and Edwin Jones was fined £lO and costs for betting there. The magisterial inquiry into the charge of conspiracy in connection with the Whalley will ease was concluded on Thursday, at the Bow-street Police Court, and the prisoners —Charles Thomas, Thomas W Nash, and Edward Gunnell —were committed for trial. Lord Rosebery, who was thrown from his horse on Tues- day, and fractured his collar-bone, was on Wednesday im- proving a little, though confined to bed. In the evening be was visited by Mr and Mrs Gladstone on their arrival at Dalmeny House.

div.head: EARLESTO WN.
div.p: EARLESTO WN.

Wonitainie's OUTING.—The men employed in the "Erecting" shop at the Vulcan iron foundry held their annual picnic on Saturday. The party left Earlestown early in the morning, and pleasantly spent the day at Halton Castle and the neighbourhood. GOOD TEMPLAR'S GATHEHING.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters held a meeting on Monday evening, when Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. After two new members had been initiated, the proceedings were of a novel character. The members pro- duced an assortment of miscellaneous articles, and they were disposed of to the highest bidder, the W.C.T. officia- ting as auctioneer. The proceeds of the sale were given to the funds of the lodge. There was a good attendance. THE VULCAN WEsLETANS —The closing of the Vul- can Wesleyan Sunday School, under circumstances previ- ously reported, has caused much inconvenience to the Wes- leyane of the district. The Government Inspector ordered the removal of the Sunday school furniture to make room for materials required in the day school ; and this fact in- fluenced the decision of the Wesleyan body to give up pos- session of the building. It is stated, however, that they in- tend to take steps to erect a new school and chapel, and subscriptions with that object are being solicited. THE RARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—OrI Thursday evening a meeting was held in the .Wesleyan schoolroom, Cross-lane, to consider the advisability of for- ming a senior band of hope society for the school in addi- tion to the present juvenile band of hope. There was a large attendance, and Mr It Higgins occupied the chair. A very interesting discussion took place, among the speakers being Messrs J El Graham, W Pearson, T Hipwood, 0 Pick- ett, U Clarke, W Clare, A Marrow, J Moss, J U Jones, and others; and it was decided to form a temperance society for adults. It is intended to arrange for papers on dif- ferent subjects to be read for the instruction and education of tb,e members and Mr W Pearson was elected secretary pro tem. THE TEMPERANCE TONTINE SOCIETY. A specially summoned meeting of the members of the Earlestown Tem- perance Tontine Society was held at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, on Tuesday evening. A large number attended, and Mr Crompton presided. After the transaction of the ordinary business of the society the question of hold- ing a concert was discussed, and it was ultimately decided to have a concert; a committee to make the necessary ar- rangements being appointed. The rest of the evening was spent in a social manner, refreshments being partaken of, while several members gave a selection of songs, recitations, Lc. Among those taking part in the entertainment were Messrs Thomas Gorse, William Sephton, George Sumner, A Allison, and others. THE EARLESTOWN SONS OF TEmPERANCE SOCIETY.— A special meeting of the members of the Earlestown Sons of Temperance Society was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Legh-street, on Wednesday evening, when Mr 0 Pickett, W.P., occupied the chair. Delegates were ap- pointed to attend the session of the Grand Division of the Society at Liervpool oe the following Saturday, and a com- mittee was also appoieted to arrange for the holding of an anniversary tea party. An announcement was made that Mr S Arro wsmith, an old and respected member of the society, had somewhat suddenly expired; and it was resolved that as many members of the society, as possibly could do, be invited to attend the funeral of the deceased to-day (Satur- day). This was the principal business. DEATH OF MR. SAMUEL ARROWSMITIL—The some- what sudden death of Mr Samuel Arrowsmitb, of Legh- street, Earlestown, on Wednesday, created a painful impres- sion among his numerous friends and acquaintances. Mr Arrowemith had officiated as the librarian of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, was a member of the chapel choir, and was in other respects a hard workisg and useful mem- I ber of the society. A considerable time ago he suffered from bronchitis and pleurisy, but he apparently recovered, and resumed his customary duties. His old ailments again attacked him again about a fortnight ago, however, and were intensified with bad inflammation. Notwithstanding the attentions of Dr Handyside the deceased gradually grew worse, and he expired on Wednesday. He was 47 years of age, and 'ewes a wife and four children. EARLESTOWN CoNSEEVVATIVB CLUB: FORDEs.T/ON OF A Discussion CLASS.—The officers of the Newton Polling District Conservative Club, whose premises are situated in Earle-street, Earlestown, have recently had under considera- tion the question of forming a discussion class for the bene- fit of the members, and to test the opinion of the members a meeting was called for Thersday evening. The gathering was held in one of the roams of the club, and there was a good attendance. Mr N Slinn presided. It was explained that the meeting had been called for the formation of a de- bating class for the members of the club, and the dismission 9f any eubiect, political or non-political, would hi allowed. The meeting seitm4 very favourable that the suggested elass should be at once proceeded with; and one of the members intimated that at the next meeting he would read a paper on "One of six plain reasons why the House of Lords were justified in rejecting the Franchise. Bill." SERIOUs ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN RAILWAY STA- TION—William Naylor, a young man, residing at St Helens, and employed as the night foreman at the Earles- town station, met with a serious accident while following his employment on Saturday night. While the 9-45 p.m. train to Wigan was standing near the station, Nayler got on the carriages for the purpose of placing the " communi- cation cord" along the top. He was so engaged when the train moved into the station; and when passing under the iron footbridge his head came into violent contact with the framework. The poor man had his head cut, and otherwise injured in a shocking manner, and was rendered insensible. Fortunately he fell on the top of the carriages, and there remained until other railway officials lowered the body to the station platform. Naylor, who was in a dangerous con- dition and remained unconscious throughout the night, was removed to the house of Mr John Singleton, Wargrave. On Sunday forenoon the injured man, who still remained in a serious state, was conveyed to his home at St Helens.

FOOTBALL ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN A PLAYER'S LEO BROKEN.—Earlestown was thrown into a state of ex- citement on Saturday afternoon and evening by a rumour that one of the principal players of the Earlestown Football Club bad bad one of his legs badly smashed while playing in a football match that afternoon. Unfortunately the re- port proved too well founded, and when it became known that the injured individual was Joseph Cameron (or" Joe" Cameron, as he was popularly called), much sympathy was manifested for him. It appears that the first teams of the Earlestown and Bootle Wanderers clubs were playing on the ground of the Earlestown Club at Wargrave, and there was a good attendance of the supporters of the local eleven. The game had only been proceeding about five minutes when Cameron, who was playing on the left wing, had the ball passed to him. He started to dribble it down the field, when one of the Bootle players rushed towards him at full speed, and made a" jump" in his effort to "scotch " the ball or throw Cameron to the ground. The Bootle player alighted with his feet against Cameron's right leg, and Cameron immediately fell. Several of the Earlestown players ran towards him. whereupon he exclaimed "My lees broken," and such was found to be the fact. The game was stopped, and the officials of the club immedi- ately sent for medical assistance. In the meantime Cameron was carried from the field to the Sunbeam Inn, the head- , quarters of the club. Here he was shortly afterwards at- tended by Dr J N Patterson, who ascertained that the bone of Cameron's right leg had been smashed a little above the ankle. After the broken limb had been "set" he was con- veyed to his home in Mercer-street, Newton. Cameron is a favourite with the Earlestown footballers, and his enforced abermce will be a great loss to the club with which he was connected. He is 19 years of age, and previous to the accident was employed as a paper cutter at the printing works of Messrs George McCorquoiale and Co. Those pre- sent on the field on Saturday afternoon, after he bad been carried away, evinced their sympathy by a ready response to an appeal for funds on Cameron's behalf, and nearly £2 were collected. The club have also decided upon a benefit match on Cameron's behalf.
THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL. PRESENTATION TO THE LATE CURATE AND ORGANIST.

The Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, was crowded wit-h. an enthusiastic audience on Monday evening, when there was held a meeting of an important character arising out of what has been known as the Etrlestown Church Scandal. The circumstances under which the dispute arose so long ago as November last are familiar to our readers. The sequel has been a church _without officers; a highly trained choir and efficient organist discharged; a respected and bard-working curate compelled to sever his connection with parishioners to whom he was attached; and a large congregation, num- bering on the average from three to four hundred persons, sent adrift. There has ever been a remarkable unanimity of opinion among the parishioners that the principal cause of the disturbances has been the conduct of the vicar (the Rev T R Matthews) in relation to the church and its go- vernment, as well as in the ordering of its services. The scattered flock, however, have not manifested a disposition to allow matters to take their own course, but have latterly been taking steps towards securing fi building in which they could hold services b their own liking; and also at the same time marking in a tangible shape the thanks due to the late curate (the Rev H E Smith) and the late or- ganist (Mr H .1 Darman) for their services in the parish. div.p: HINTS FOR THE HOME.

SUCCESS IN BUSINESS.—Learn your business thoroughlii Observe system and order in all that you do and under- take. Do not take too much advice, but rather depend upon yourself. Never fail to keep your appointments. Be ever generous in thought or deed—help others along life's thorny pathway. Make no haste to be rich; re; inember that small and steady gains give competency aD tranquility of mind. Never put off till to-morrow who you can do to-day, and never burden others with Your complaints.

-- REST AND RECREATION.—The refreshment of rest and cool air, the enjoyment of fine scenery, the intercourse with nature in her varied forms, are valuable not onlY for their direct influence, but also as affording an entirely new Bet of circumstances around us, giving us new things' to observe, to think of, and to do. Continued monotoni in any direction grows irksome and distasteful, 6,13_,.°' beyond certain limits, intolerable. To discover these limits are and rightly to provide for them ii consult not only our happiness, but our value to society. -- Pies FOR FATTENING.—In selecting a pig to fatten, ft' is well to remember that fineness of bone is rarely disappointing. A broad, dished face, with snout short and turned up, indicates an aptitude to fatten, and le 031 of the surest indications of a good pig. No hog shoal have bristles, as these have been bred away from &lithe good breeds, and will not be tolerated at present on snY respectable farm, for they indicate coarseness, restless: ness, and preponderance of offal. He should no? be a squealer, nor should he be restless. He should eo quietly, and after his hunger is appeased should patiently* lie down, without even travelling around his pen.

-- Boiled vegetable marrow is a well-known dish, but ,iet t"; is rarely served as it should be. Do not cut or pare marrows before cooking, unless they are inconvenient large, in which case they must be cut, but they shell not in any case be pared until after they are cooked. Belt quickly in a smallish quantity of water and a liberi" allowance of salt. Small marrows will require boilinsg about 15 minutes, and large ones 20 to tr, minutes, and it is a point of some importanee ~,; have them slightly crisp or underdone, as then '"'" flavour is delicious, and the substance firm, and they are in every way more creditable to the cook. When taks? up drain and press them slightly, then remove the rind and seeds, dish them on toast and send to table with gld melted butter. When young and fresh, marrows shou be served a little underdone; they are too often over- done, and then they are poor watery things.

LIGHTICING-RODS.—The following are the essential re quirements for the construction and erection of lightning. rods. (1) Make them of round iron five-eighths or three fourths of an inch in diameter. (2) Give them a fel° sharp iron points at the top. (3) Have them continuous throughout. (4) Let them go several feet down inte.t" earth to soil which is wet or moist in the driest ton- These constitute the whole essentials. It may be addr that round iron is best, simply because it is essli handled; square or flat would do, if as heavy. Sharpeu.„„e iron will remain sharp as long, as the rod stallu:' and silver, copper, or other points are only a waste of ef, pense. A blacksmith can do all this work, and make rod into one piece by welding the joints. No nisttls how long it is, it may be all in one piece and be dragg - home on the ground behind a waggon. It may be fas tened to the house or barn with staples or in any other way, projecting well above all. Glass insulators are Per° fectly worthless. Every man may erect his own rod at small cost, and it will be as good as the best if the abe" four essentials are observed.

GOOD GRUEL—GrueI is a thing which is very ofteS sadly neglected in the way of preparation. Solos people shudder at the very mention of it, simply bectuf: they have known what it is to drink it when badly made; but, with care and a little trouble, it can be made ye, palatable indeed. To prepare it nicely, proceed sti, follows :—Put one table - spoonful of fine oatmeal with into a basin, and mix it quite smoothly two table-spoonsfuls of cold water. Stir this int* a pint of boiling water which you have readY on the fire. It must boil for at least half-an-hour, being stirred every now and again. Gruel simply by itself ja very insipid, but it is quite pleasant when nicelY flavoured. A little ginger, or grated nutmeg, is a great improvement. Sometimes beer is put into it, while ()the! persons prefer a spoonful of vinegar. This latter is especially good, if the object of taking the gruel S t ° cause a free perspiration. To make it as tempting as possible it ought always to be served as neatly as one 4. can manage it. In a nice china basin, on a tray witl.l,„ clean white napkin over, it looks quite another thing altogether to what it does when rudely or careleselY served.—Saturday Magazine.

USEFUL LIVES.—How useless our lives seem to be sometimes! How we long for an opportunity to perfofol some great action! We become tired of the daill routine of human life, and imagine we could be fer happier in other scenes. We think of life's gi eat battle- field, and wish to be heroes. We think of the good we might do if our lot had been cast in different scenes. We forget that the world bestows no titles as father, mother, sister, or brother. In the sacred precints of home we have many chances for heroism. Tb e daily acts of self-denial for the good of , loved one, the gentle word of soothing for another's troubles, the care for the sick, may all see'? as nothing; yet who can tell the good they accomplish Our slightest word may have an influence over another, for good or evil. We are daily sowing the seed which will bring forth some sort of harvest. Well will it be for if the harvest is one we will be proud to garner. If some of that dear home circle can look back in after years, and, as they tenderly utter our name, say, "Her word° and examples prepared me for a life of usefulness—to her I owe my present happiness," we may well say, I have not lived in vain.—Household Words.

He attributri+ this to maidenly reserve, for it never occurred to him that she was not in love with him. 'He cautiously pre- , faced his declaration with a few questions, for he had n° intention of "throwing himself away." Did she love hint well enough to live in a cottage with him? Was she good cook and washer? Did she think it a wife's duty t° make home happy? Would she consult his -tastes afld. wishes concerning her associates and pursuits in life Was she economical? Could she make her own clothe°, &c.? The young lady said that before she answered questions she would assure him of some negative virtue; she possessed. She never drank or smoked; never owed a bill to her laundress or tailor; never stayed out n night playing billiards; never lounged on the pier au° ogled pretty girls; never indulged in wine suPPe* 'Now," said she, rising indignantly, "I am assured. b.t, those who know that you do- all those things, *0 it a; rather absurd for you to expect all the virtues Ut while you do not possess any of them yourself. never be your wife." And she bowed him out, and him on the doorstep, a madder if not a wiser man. She is the child of the Great and to her applies the Royal law according to the SeTS, ture, -" Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyseb•e• This law, which is the highest of all,, surely politeness. If we are bound to love our neighbour° 7,7. ourselves, we are bound to treat them courteenelf. at any rate. This is one of the first and ..„%r most rudimental of our duties to them. rc'er servant, madam, is your neighbour—the neare4 of y,°,5„ neighbours. She has a right then under this R0Ya115,,, —which is itself the spirit of all just laws—to be, soli teously treated by you. It is no more condescension I.(t)b you to use respect and gentleness in your intercourse WI, her than it is for her to sweep your floors and build r?'"'; fires. You are entitled to no more credit for gr. 3-1.1• kindly to her than you are for not stealing her handkerchieb If you do not govern yourself in all your conversation her, by the same laws of courtesy which you observe ;,‘ your conversation with the callers in the parlour, 3t00.1"; a very vulgar person. Mr Leader Williams, at the request of the Mayor, ex- plained the mode by which it is proposed the canal shall pass the river Weaver at the junction of the latter with the Mersey. It was proposed, he said, to pen up the canal to a low tide level by the entrance locks at Eastham. This level would by dredging and excavation allow of 2dlt of water being maintained as a minimum, or over 301 t at high water of spring tides. Over this level the waters of the Weaver and ether tributaries of the Mersey would escape by means of long regulating weirs constructed in the outer em- bankment of the canal. These weirs would not only serve the purpose of paseing off floods but of allowing the tidal water of high tides to flow into and out of the canal. Mr Daniel Adamson having stated that the prcmoters would hold the Corporation free from any of the respon- sibilitits of the carrying out of the scheme, the proceedings terminated.

MANCHES l' ER SHIP CANAL -NEW SCHEME ON THE CHESHIRE SIDE. The promoters of the proposed Ship Canal, acting on the recommendation of their own engineer, Mr Leader Wil- liams, and of Mr Bateman and Mr Abernethy, who had been called in to advise, have unanimously agreed to apply for Powers to cut a Ship Canal on the Cheshire side of the Mersey, from Eastham to Runcorn, instead of one on the Lancashire side, from Garston to Runcorn Bridge, and there crossing the Mersey to Runcorn. The difficulties connected with taking a canal, 2a feet deep, across a river subject to floods, and up and down which the, tide flows twice every twenty-four hours, were found too great for a navigation intended to be used night and day. Hence the decision in favour of the Cheshire side. It may be stated that the Mer- sey Dock Board have submitted a scheme by their engineer, Mr Lyster, for the construction of a Ship Canal from Eastham to Runcorn. It was prepared by Mr Lyster as an alternative to the training walls of the last , Ship Canal Bill. Why is a washerwoman like a navigator P—Because she spreads her sheets, crosses the line, and goes from pole to pole. When Sheridan was asked if he had ever undergone an Operation, he replied that he had had his hair cut and that he had sat for his portrait. OF WHISTLERB.—It is said the whistling man is one who thinks little. But he makes others think; and, oh, what fearful thoughts they think! A reader in a much-frequented public reading-room pen- cilled this petition on the margin of a popular evening news- paper—" Don't read all the advertisements to-night. Other People would like a glance at this paper." BOYlSlL—Tourist, to boy fishing: "How many fish have you caught, my man ?" Boy: "Oh, I couldn't count em !" Tourist:" Why you have'nt caught any, you little vaga- bond." Boy: "That's why I can't count 'ern!" COMPLIMENTAL/Y.—" Gentlemen of the jury," said a Tecumseh (Neb.) lawyer the other day, " there were just thirty-six hogs in the drove. Please remember the fact— just three times as many as in the jury-box, gentlemen." SEASONABLE.—Student: "Heat expands and cold con- tracts." Professor: "Correct. Give lan example." Student: "During the summer the affections of city people for their country relatives expand, and in winter they con- tract." _ . .

OF Two EVILS Cmaosmo min LESSER.—CIerk "Pri- soner at the bar, are you guilty or not guilty ?" Prisoner: "Not guilty." Judge: "Who is your counsel?" Prisoner: "I have none; lam unable to employ a lawyer." Judge: "Mr. 8., I appoint you to defend this man." ' Prisoner, after looking at his lawyer: "Well, then, I plead guilty." Mr. Howard Paul is credited with a neat mot. A rhymester button-holed him as he emerged from the Vaude- ville Theatre, and said, " Have you heard my 'Song of the seven Senses'?" "I have not. Pray, repeat it." The poet obeyed. "Very good," said Mr. P. at the finish; "but there is one sense you have utterly ignored." "Which is that ?" "Common sense" And then silence fell upon the twain, as They glided off in opposite directions. The ften of a deceased officer in India was one morning invited to mess with his late father's regiment. Not having time to return home, he told his old coolie servant to inform his mother' and, as that menial was rather forgetful, he wrote the following message on a piece of paper:—" Gone to dine with my father's old corps.' At dinner-time, noting her son's ahence, the mistress said, " Where is Mr. John, Tippoo ?" "Ali," said Tippoo, fumbling for the paper, "the sahib's gone to die with his father's old corpse !' WHAT H SAID.—" How many of your parents, children, say grace ?" asked the teacher. "Please, mum, what's them?" asked an overgrown girl in a last year's hat. "Why, Maggie," exclaimed the teacher, "is it possible you don't know what grace is? Doesn't your father say something before you begin to eat ?" " Oh!" responded the girl, with a glow of intelligence. "Yes, mum, he does; he always says, Don't make pigs of yourselves; that's all the butter there is in the house.'" . .

WHAT BECOMES OF THE TAXES.—A country voter ob- jected to send any member to Parliament on the ground that, whoever was sent, he always made a lot of money by it. The candidate urged, on the contrary, that a seat in the Douse meant money out of pocket instead of in. "Come," said the voter, "I'm not going to believe that! Don't you see in the paper &tan enough cries of Divide, divide'? Now, do you think th.y'd cry 'Divide, divide!' if they'd got nothin' to divide? No, no; they just take the taxes and divide them amongst themselves—that's what they do!" Personally Rochefort was amiable, generous to prodigality to his comp tnions, and absentminded. He was one of those whose brains are winging in the clouds while their boots may be gathering slush in the gutters. It is said he was so for- getful that he went to Brebant's one evening in response to an invitation to dinner. On arriving, the name of his host had quite escaped him. He explained his dilemma to the landlord. "There is but one way out of it, "said the good- natured Brebant ; "we must pass in review all the diners in the house; but, as our visit might appear intrusive, put a napkin over your arm and come with me as my head waiter." The notion suited Rochefort down to the ground, and they made an inspection of all the private rooms and all the tables in the dining-room; but in vain. Rochefort did not find his Amphitryon. Suddenly he slapped his fore- head and exclaimed, "What an ass lain! The appointment was for Saturday last! " A CASE IN Poinr.— Young Johnny Jarpley was inclined to be a good boy, and his mother spent much time in in- structing him in the enormity of the sin of telling false- hoods, and, to impress it upon him wound up by telling him that people who told lies choked to death. When the Rev. Mr. Muckle and his wife were taking dinner at the Jarpleys' on a "return call " the next day, Mrs. Jarpley asked her guest, "So, Mrs. Mackie, you like my cooking ?", "It is splendid. Mrs. Jarpley—splendid !" enthusiastically responded the Rev. Mr. Muckle's lady. "Mr. Jarpley is for- tunate in the possession of such an excellent cook as your- self." Just as the lady concluded, she took a sip of water, and a few drops "going the wrong way" caused her to cough. "There she goes! There she goes, mother !" ex- claimed young Jarpley, in great excitement. "I heard her oay to Mr. Muckle, when you was out of the parlour that she wished it was all over, as one of your dinners was enough to I kill a mule ; and she wondered how your husband had ever lived so long !" One day the lion. Thaddeus Stevens called upon President Lincoln with an elderly lady in great trouble, whose son had been in the Army, but for some offence had been court- martialled and sentenced to death. There were some ex- tenuating circumstances, and, after a full hearing, the pre- sident turned to the representative, and said, "Mr. Stevens, do you think this is a case which will warrant my inter- ference? " "With my knowledge of the facts and the parties," was the reply, "I should have no hesitation in granting a pardon." "Then," returned Mr. Lincoln, "I will pardon him ; " and he proceeded forthwith to execute the paper. The gratitude of the mother was too deep for expression, save by her tears ; and not a word was said be- tween her and Mr. Stevens until they were half-way down the stairs on their passage out, when she suddenly burst forth in an excited manner with the words, "I knew it was a copperhead lie!" "What do you refer to, madam ? " asked Mr. Stevens. "Why, they told me he was an ugly-looking man!" she replied with vehemence. "lie is the handsomest man I ever saw in my life! "
