div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

THE JUBILEE SINGERS.—Two services of sacred song were given by the Jubilee Singers (from North Carolina), in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, on Sunday, and were largely attended; and on Bbnday and Tuesday evenings a large audience assembled to hear their popular concerts of sacred music. . . _

I THE WATER SUPPLY.—A special meeting of the Frodsham Parechial Committee was held in the Town Hall, Prodsham, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., presided. A telegram had been received from Mr. Bancroft, engineer, that he was unable to attend the meeting. The Chairman stated that he had visited the works during the afternoon, and found that the boring was 101 feet deep, and the well 29 feet deep, the yield of water from well and boring being about 500 gallons per hour. This was insufficient, as the minimum quantity required was thirty thousand gallons per day. After some discussion it was decided to adjourn the meeting and meet the engineer and contractor on the ground at Five Crosses.l

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.
A RUNAWAY COUPLE.—There was a rumoured elopement of a voting girl with a married man from this village dur- ing the wakes, but they have since returned, sadder, if not wiser and better.

DRUNKENNESS, Sic.—At the County Police Court, Strange- way, before Sir John I Mantel!, on Tuesday, the 23rd inst., James Taylor, Cadishead, was fined 5s for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday, August 16th. John Taylor, of Fir. lane, Cadishead, was fined 5i for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday, August 23rd. Also J Shaw, W Shaw, J Iles- ford, Isaac llampson, James Hampson, W Whitfield, and William Taylor, all of Cadishead, were fined Is each fo playing pitch and toss at Cadishead, on Sunday, August the 24th. Police-constable Jones (1,178) proved the cases.
The Dundee whaler Narwhal, with a full cargo of whale- bone has been totally wrecked in the Arctic Seas. The crew were saved.

It is proposed to confer the freedom of the borough of Dundee upon Mr John Bright, who is at present enjoying a holiday in the North. It is stated to be extremely probable that the Queen will call at Edinburgh on her way south from Balmoral, and that she will stay at Holyrood Palace. The police of Scotland have issued a warning to the effect that counterfeit half-sovereigns are being circulated whole- sal e in Edinburgh and other towns. Captain Boycott, who defiance ef the Lend League, caused so much stir at the time, and introduced a new word into the language, is about to do something which will cause no end of surprise. In short, he has so completely changed his way of thinking in reference to Irish mat- ters that be is about to stand as Nationalist candidate for Mayo.

Ii SAD CASE.-At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, a youg woman named Eliza Elazlehurst, was charged with leaving an illegitimate child chargeable to the , Warrington Union. It transpired that the father of the child, against whom a warrant has been out for twelve mouths, could not be found, and the young woman had left the child in the care of a person living on School Brow, and had then deserted it. It was in consequence taken to the Workhouse. She now said that the had not been able to earn enough money to keep it. The Bench re- manded the case for a week on her promise to go into the Workhouse, Mr Shearer remarking that it that course was adopted the case would not be pressed.

div.head: Tl4te FXANITNER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 27. 1884.
div.p: Tl4te FXANITNER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 27. 1884.

THE PREMIERS HOMEWARD JOURNEY. SPEECH AT WARRINGTON. Shortly before nine o'clock yesterday morning the Prime Minister, accompannied by Mrs and Miss Helen Gladstone. drove from Dalmeny House to the Caledonian Station at Edinburgh, where be left by the ten o'clock train, ea route for Bawarden Castle. The party, on arriving at the sta- tion at a quarter to ten, were he‘rtily cheered by the large crowd that bad assembled outside the station. Mr. Glad- stone was received by Mr. John Cowan, of Beeslack, the pre- sident of the Midlothian Liberal Association, and other members of the Executive Committee, and conducted to the train. As be stepped into the saloon carriage reserved for the party, Mr. Gladstone was again enthusiastically cheered by the crowd who had succeeded in forcing their way through the barriers. Mrs. Gladstone was presented with an exquisite bouquet of flowers by Miss Cowan, and those present having once more indulged in a hearty cheer, and a general waving of hats and handkerchiefs, Mt Gladstone addressed them from the window of the carriage as follows:—" Gentlemen, I wish to thank you for thus continuing your kindness to the last moment. Nothing could exceed the goodness of the manner, the extreme indulgence of the manner, in which you re- ceived me when I came into Midlothian, and I have the pleasure of assuring you that the encouraging feeling mani- fested here has been shown in the same fervour all through the country through which I have traversed. I well know that it is not owing to anything due to myself personally, but is on account of the great cause in which we are en- gaged. I desire to bid you before the train starts a grateful farewell." Although he was looking in excellent health and spirits, the right hon. gentleman's voice was somewhat hoarse. rhe crowd once again lustily cheered when he re- sumed his seat —Mr Cowan then announced that he was pleased to be able to state that the Earl of Rosebery was making capital progress. Punctually at ten the train steamed out of the station amidst the enthusiastic cheering of the crowd, in response to which the right hon. gentle- man frequently bowed.
CARLISLE, 12-30.

As the train steamed slowly past the railway Works just after leaving Edinburgh station, loud cheers were given for the Premier by the workmen, most of whom were assembled on the side of the line. The first stoppage was at Baltock, which was reached at 11-30. Here a small group of persons had assembled, and when the train drew up at the platform Mr Gladstone was greeted with cheers. Mr S Smith, M.P., who is at present the guest of his brother at Moffat, was amongst those on the platform, and he remained in conver- sation with the right honourable gentleman until the train started again, when the cheering was renewed. Lockerbie, the next halting place, was reached at 11-53, and here a similar demonstration took place. At Carlisle, the next sta- tion of importance, a considerable crowd had congregated on the platform, and the cheering was very hearty. Mr Gladstone, in answer to an address presented by the Carlisle Liberal Association, and speaking in the pre- sence of a large concourse of people, said the enthusiasm which he had met with in Scotland prevailed also in Eng- land on the present crisis. What the House of Lords ought to study was the best means of providing that the House should not fall, and that was to be done by their acting with mo- deration and prudence. The question came to be was it prudent or moderate on the part of a small number of gentlemen in themselves irresponsible, to stand against the voice of the whole country and the demand of the House of Commons by refusing to enfranchise two millions of people. Their honour and consistence did not require them to re- ject in October, with enlarged knowledge, that which they rejected in July with contracted knowledge. At Lancaster, where a great crowd assembled, Mrs Davis presented to Mrs Gladstone a very choice bouquet, and the Rev B Davis handed to the right hon. gentleman an address on behalf of the Reform Club. Mr Gladstone, in reply, said: I am very much indebted to you, sir, and to those on whose behalf you attend here both for your personal kindness and for affording me an additional proof of the feeling which seems to prevail throughout the whole country with respect to the controversy in which we are engaged. I found in Scotland an enthusiasm greater than I ever saw before, and I find on crossing the border exactly the same kind of feeling prevailing. (Cheers.) The train moved off while Mr Gladstone was still speaking. At Preston, Mr Gladstone, in reply to addresses, said: Gentlemen, I have not had the opportunity of reading the addresses you have been good enough to present to me, but I have no doubt that they are in conformity with those that have been placed in my hands in every quarter of the country I have visited during the last few weeks; and, gentlemen, their character is to indicate the fixed convic- tion on the part of the people that there ought to be with- out further delay an adoption of the Fianchise Bill by the Government and the country. According to the opinion of the country, or at all events according to the opinion of tbe enormous masses of people whom I have seen in every quarter, the Franchise Bill was unfortunately rejected by the House of Lords. (A voice: Over with them.) It is said by those who approve of that unfor:unate action that the bill was not rejected, but that the ac- ceptance of it was based upon a condition that the Redistribution Bill should be passed with it. (A voice: "Nonsense.") Now, gentlemen, it would have been much better in my opinion if it had been rejected honestly and outright—(hear, hear, and cheers)—in the good old English manner, gentlemen, in a manner which prevailed in this country when men were not afraid to show what they were about. (Hear, hear, and a voice: "That's it.") It is idle, gentlemen, to say that the condition attached to this Bill was not equivalent to a rejection. (Hear, hear.) The condition was that we should pass the Redistribution Bill. Well, now, I think I have shown that the Franchise Bill was a very simple measure. (Hear, hear.) Everything was done by the Tories that they could to make it complicated. (Hear, hear.) Why, gentlemen, what did they do? They tried to bring in a Women's Franchise ! (Laughter.) What was the object of that? Do you suppose that they are so very fond of a Women's Franchise (No.) If they were fond of a Women's Franchise, why did they not bring one in when they were in office for six years. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) No, gentlemen, the object was to weight the Franchise Bill, and make the ship, as I said, carry such a cargo as would swamp it. (Hear. hear.) Still more is that the case with regard to Redistribution, because with respect to that it is perfectly clear that that is a complicated sub- ject in itself ; and as the Franchise Bill took 25 days so it would have been absolutely impossible to pass any measure which had Redistribution attached to it, because the time made it perfectly out of the question. [lt this point one of the inspector's came to the front, and informed Mr Gladstone that the train was ready for starting.] Well, gentlemen, unfortunately we are pinched in point of time. I had believed that we should have had a longer stay in Preston than appears to be the case. I must, therefore, -confine myself to thanking you for the address you have been good enough to present to me, and I hope when the proper time comes you working-men who have got votes will ask those who appeal to you whether they will or will not withold those votes from their brethren in the counties of England. (Loud cheers, amid which Mr., Mrs. and Miss Gladstone were escorted to the saloon). RECEPTION AT WARRINGTON.—SPEECH AT BANK QUAY STATION.

In good time yesterday morning the announcement was made public that the train in which the Premier was journeying homeward would reach Warrington at 4-10 in the afternoon, and arrangements for according him a fitting reception were at once taken in hand. A number of the prominent Liberals of Warrington held a meeting, and de- cided to present Mr Gladstone with an Address on his arrival at Bunk Quay station, and Mr H Roberts, secretary of the Liberal Association, and Mr Ziba Armitage, J.P., took charge of the arrangements. The Liberals of Mid-Cheshire were eqnally active, and also prepared a suitable address for presentation to the right honourable gentleman. In antici- pation of a large number of people taking advantage of the I visit, tickets for the railway platform were issued, and there was an eager demand for their possession, the subject of the visit forming a prominent topic of conversation in the town. For some time before the hour at which the train containing the Premier was expected to reach Warrington, the high level platform at Bank Quay wore an animated appearance, and it is estimated that the people assembled numbered very little short of a thousand. Indeed, the platform became so crowded by about 4 o'clock, that many were unable to gain entrance. The train at last steamed into the station only one or two minutes behind time, and its approach was the signal for a tremendous burst of cheering from those nearest, which was quickly taken up by those behind. On the saleon in which the right hon. gentleman and party were seated being brought to a standstill, in a siding, the cheering was resumed, the Premier meanwhile repeatedly bowing his acknowledg- ments. Amongst those assembled on the platform were Mr Cheetham, M.P., Sir Joseph C Lee, Mr W Crosfield, J.P. (Liberal candidate for Warrington), Alderman Burgess, Alderman Holmes, Councillors Barker, Platt, Broadbent, and Dixon, Mr Ziba Armitage Mr H Roberts (secretary of the Warringtoa Liberal Association), Mr F A Roberts, Mr J Walker, Mr It J Mentha Mr W Long (Thalwall), Mr W Milne (Bowdon) Mr Claude .1 Morris, Mr J T Branna, Mr J Plinston, Mr It Shaw (Runcorn), Mr F Milne (Sale), the Rev J Mclurk, Rev W Males, Mr Browne, Mr W Wynne Ffonlkes, jan., Mr M Bowden, Mr E J Guest, Mr J Wieser, Mr W Barn, Mr P Newall, Mr Brewtnall (Thelwall), Mr W Roberts, Mr Percival, Mr W Hall, Mr T Knowles, am Tbe crush near the saloon was very great, but excellent order was maintained, Inspector Spinks, Sergeant Rowbotham, and several constables being stationed near the train, and the railway officials under the superintendence of Mrl Ashurst, the stationmaster, facilitating matters in every way practicable. The representatives of the Press with some difficulty secured positions directly in front of the saloon, and close by were stationed the more prominent members of the two Liberal Associations represented. Mr Gladstone, who appeared to be in excellent health, was, as the crowd was forming into compact order, the subject of the greatest enthusiasm. The cheering having subsided, Mr CHEETIUM, M.P., addressed the Premier. Be said : I have the honour and the pleasure to present to you Mr Croefield, the Liberal candidate for Warrington. (Applause.) He is charged with an address to you from the Liberals of the constituency, which at no distant period he is destined to represent. I have also a similar honour and pleasure in making known to you Sir Joseph Lee and other members of the Executive Committee of the Mid-Cheshire Liberal Association. I can only add that from what I know of the feelings of Liberals in the constituency that it will be no fault of theirs if, whenever the next appeal is made to the country, they do not succeed in breaking into that dead

uniformity of Tory representation which is at present the unenviable distinction in Mid-Cheshire. (Cheers.) Mr W CELOSFIELD, who was received with cheers, said that he had the honour to present an address which bad been entrusted to him. He then read the address as follows To the Right.lionourable W E Gladstone, Her Majesty's

Prime Minister. Sir,—We, as representing the Liberals of Warrington, wish to convey to you our high appreciation of the invalu- able services which you have rendered to the people of this great country. Throughout a long and busy life your powerful aid has been given to the cause of freedom and for the elevation and happiness of the great masses of your fellow-men. We heartily rejoice in the knowledge that your recent holiday has proved of great benefit to your health and we sincerely hope that during the present great crisis you may be sustained in your determination to "make the bounds of freedom wider yet," by the enfranchisement of two millions of our fellow subjects. The remarkable enthusiasm which your presence has everywhere evoked in Scotland is, we believe, only typical of the heartfelt confidence which the Liberals of all ranks throughout the kingdom repose in yourself and your col- leagues. Trusting that you may be long spared to lead our party to other and greater victories, We are, on behalf of the Liberals of Warrington, Joins BURGESS, Vice-President. F A ROBERTS, Deputy Chairman of the Executive. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, Liberal Candidate. Z IBA ARMITAGE. WILLIAM PIERPOUPP. HENRY ROBERTS, Secretary. Sir JOSEPH LEE, amidst applause, proceeded to present the second address. He said: On behalf of the Liberals of Mid-Cheshire I have great pleasure in presenting you with this address. I have only to express great gratitude to Al- mighty God that He has brought you safe home again. and the hope that you may long be spared to fulfil those duties which you have with such pains performed. He then read the address, which was signed by Sir Joseph Lee, Mr Wil- liam Milne. and Mr P G Menthe, and was as follows:— To the Right Honble. W. E. Gladstone, M.P., First Lord of the Treasury, &c., Sir,—We gladly avail ourselves of the opportunity of your short stoppage in Warrington to welcome your return home, and to exprs.ss our heartiest congratulation upon the marked enthusiasm which your journey to and from the Highlands has everywhere evoked. Whilst the bracing atmosphere of Scotland is peculiarly favourable to the principles of progress with which your life is especially associated, the responsive cheers of your constituents, and their neighbours, have been echoed throughout the length and breadth of Great Britain. To the Liberal party of Mid-Cheshire your resolution to pass the Franchise Bill is particularly acceptable. There are few constituences (if any) which will gain more largely by it than ours ; as it is estimated that it will raise the number of electors on our register from 10,000 to 23,000. We earnestly join, therefore, in the appeals which have been made to you to "hold fast that which is good " by Insisting upon justice being rendered, as quickly as pos- sible, to the 2,000,000 of unenfranchised capable house- holders. _ _

With the sincere prayer that you may be permitted, in health and strength, to continue the magnificent services of Your life to the well-being of the country, we beg to sub- scribe ourselves, dm. 26th September, 1884. Mr. GLADSTONE said: Gentlemen, I am very much obliged to you personally for your kindness in presenting these addresses. But I feel that thete are other considera- tions much higher than what is personal, that have brought you hither to-day, and they, as I believe, are governing your conduct at the present time. (Cheers.) It is true— , and perhaps before I go forward let me express my ardent hopes that the local wishes which have been stated to-day with regard to the representation of Mid-C;heshire and War- rington—(hear, hear)—may be fulfilled when the time comes. (Applause.) The name of Crosfield is well known to me. (Rear, hear.) I have shared the hospitality of that house in former years, and I can well believe that the town of Warrington could not be more worthily re- presented. (Loud cheers.) Gentlemen, we have before us now no doubt a very serious affair. ale the real question, depend upon it, is whether it is the desire of the nation that the Franchise Bill should be passed. (Applause.) If it is the desire of the nation, and for my part my mind is made up that it is, and the proofs of it are ample, well then, the Franchise Bill will be passed. (Cheers.) We are united, gentlemen, in feeling. In the first place I can assure you that we are a united Government. There has never been in the Government the slightest hesitation or doubt as to the course to be pursued in the various stages of this serious question. (Cheers.) But I believe the Government enjoys the confidence of the liouse of Commons, as well as of the Crown. I hope this controversy may terminate quickly, , because I, for my part, de not want to mix up other matters with it, and I say plainly if it continues other matters will and must be mixed up with it. But there is no help for it. for it is impossible to suppose that an hereditary assembly can nominee to urge persistently their views, without any responebility whatever, against the representative chamber and against such a feeling as pre- vails in this country without committing a great impru- dence, from which it may find very serious consequences to ensue. (Cheers.) For my part I desire to avoid all these things.. I wish to get the Franchise Bill, and! wish the

Franchise Bill to followed at once by a reasonable and just and ample measure for the redistribution of seats— (cheers)—and I believe, if it pleases God to enable es to being that result about within a limited time, so as not to open further questions of controversy, we shall have achieved something that is worthy of achieving—for the benefit of the country, for the liberties of the people, for the stability of the Throne, and the greatness and unity of the empire. (Loud and continued cheering.) The train was then shunted amid great cheering to the middle platform prior to departure. Mr Gladstone again briefly addressed the assembly, and said that he very hear- tily thanked the stationmaster (Mr Ashurst) for the admir- able arrangements that had been made, and the successful way in which they had been carried out by him and the staff under him, The arrangements had been admirable all through at the different stations, but especially so at War- rington. He was pleased to see the great concourse of people that had assembled to welcome him, and remarked that such had been the case all along the line. The Premier was again heartily cheered, every hat being uplifted, as the train left the station on its way to Chester. It may be added that while the saloon was in the station, Mrs. Gladstone kissed her hand to the little son of Mr. G. Holford (who was with his mother), and gave him a few grapes. Mr Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs and Miss Helen Glad- stone, arrived at Hawarden shortly after six o'clock last evening, and was loudly cheered by the crowd which had assembled to welcome him. He will remain there a fortnight, and then proceed to London to attend the meetings of the Council.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held yesterday, at the Board's Offices, Bridgewater-street. The Rev Canon Barclay pre- sided, and there were present the Rev Father Fennelly, Messrs P Briscoe, T Norman, J Pritchard, G 8 Hazlehurst, and F Rigby (clerk.)—The following letter was read from the Education Department :—"I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 25th instant. My lords regret the delay which has occurred to your letter of the 4th ultimo, which has been referred to Her Majesty's inspector, who writes as follows: I agree with the Board that there was a deficiency of accommodation for girls, and that the Mill Brow Board School was overcrowded. I agree, therefore, in their conclusion to build a girls' school, and to turn the Mill Brow School into an infants' school. Looking also to the special difficulties of the place as the head- quarters to the canal boat children, I agree with the Board that it would be advisable to build a large first standard school for girls and boys. I do not remember that the Board wished to build for boys. The question was raised, and I think at that time the opinion of the majority was against the proposal. Bat the lower standards in each school are crowded into small class-rooms, or into inconvenient corners, to make room at the desks and benches for the higher standard. I think if the Board will build their mixed junior school for 200 or 250 boys and girls this will relieve the pressure, and will leave the boys' school not over-full. The girls' school shows much overcrowding, and the con- version of the Mill Brow School into an infant school will increase the deficiency. I think the Board may with safety build for 200 girls, but I do not see any necessity for the boys' echo .I.' lam to inquire if your Board is disposed to accept this view of the requirements; if so lam to request that plans may be prepared accordingly, and forwarded to this department for approval.—Signed, J Mil- ler."—After some conversation it was moved by Mr Nor- man, seconded by Mr Briscoe, and carried, that the sug- gestion of the Education Department contained in the above letter be adopted, and provision for 450 children only be mole for the present, with a view to further extension at some future time.—lt was also agreed that the solicitor should be instructed to take such steps as might be neces- sary to determine the validity of the title to the site in Greenway-road, and to prepare the requisite con- veyance. It was further agreed, on the motion of Mr Hazlehurst, seconded by Mr Pritchard, that the clerk be instructed to apply to the Public Works Loan Commissioners for a loan not exceeding £5,500 to be repaid in a term not exceeding 30 years; and that the architects, Messrs F and G Holme be directed to prepare.—The Clerk stated that the grant this year for Mill Brow school amounted to £9l 7s, as compared with £65 lsa 6d last year. The inspector, it was further stated, complained of the cold and 'cheerless sp. pearance and the inadequate accommodation of these schools and subsequently the schoolmistress was called into the room, and arrangements made with her by which the num- ber of infants in the school would be redaced.—This was all the business of public interest.

RUNCORN REVISION COURT. The annual revision of the Parliamentary register of voters for the townships of Runcorn, Clifton, Weston, and Halton took place at the Royal Hotel, Runcorn, on Mon- day, before Mr Langford F )ulkes, barrister. Mr Pattison (registration agent for Mid-Ch-shire), and Mr 0 Leak (local Liberal agent) appeared for the Liberals, and Mr Lance Bentley (registration agent for Mid-Cheshire), and Mr J W Lightburn (local Conservative agent) represented the Con- servatives. The overseers of the various townships were present. AN UNWELCOME CHANGE.—The overseers of Runcorn objected to the claim of Dr Bagnall on the ground that he was not on the rate book and that his annual rental was only £l2.—The Revising Barrister remarked that if he was ob- jected to his name would be erased from the list.—Mr Bent- ley : I don't see that, I think you take what evidence we can give.—Mr W Handley (overseer) : He is not on the rate book.—Mr Bentley : That doesn't follow.—Mr Pattison: I submit, sir, that the question as to fixing the amount of the rateable value rests entirely with the Re- vising Barrister. He has uncontrolled discretion.—The Revising Barrister said the Act stated he might, but did not say he must. Prima facie he would take the over- seers rateable value which was in accordance with the Act of Parliament. The Assessment Committee was composed of gentlemen having a knowledge of land and of the locality, and he did not see why he should call into dispute their decisions. He knew nothing about land or the locality.— Mr Pattison : Of coarse you will bear in mind that you have in past years allowed people to go on the register who pay a gross rental of £l2.—The Revising Barrister : Yes, I was wrong; that is the only answer I can give.—Mr Bent- ley : In future you will accept the rateable value as given in the rate book except other evidence is brought to show that it is wrong.—The Revising Barrister: That evidence must be of an exceptional sort, and not anybody jumping up and saying this men pays so and 130.—Mr Pattison : Mr Bentley will you agree with me that it is necessary for our own sakes that some definite rule should be laid down and we shall know where we are.—The Revising Barris- ter : Take the overseers rateable value in the rate book.— Mr Pattison and Mr Bewley intimated that they were agree- able to this course.—The Revising Barrister said to be con- sistent he ought to strike out the whole of the names that were on the list through a £l2 rent qualification; but if they were all agreed to leave them on the register he did not see any reason why he should take any notice of them any more than another man. —Mr Pattison said the Revising Barrister would observe that in past years many of these £l2 rent claims had crept on the register. The overseers in various districts had adopted various plans for dealing with them. In some cases they had been put on the list because they had been there before, but in some cases they had been omitted, and in these latter cases Mr Bentley and himself had claimed for them. As far as Mr Bentley and himself were concerned, they had agreed not to object to any £l2 clauses which had been placed on the register before.—The Revising Barrister: I quite assent to that —Mr Pattison: As regards new occu- piers, it is a different thing altogether.—Mr Bentley: Then we may take it that where a man has been admitted by you last year, and through an omission of the overseers has had to reclaim this year, you will pass him 7—The Revising Barrister said he was not supposed to know anything about the claims unless they were objected to. It would be time enough to take notice wheo the objection was brought be- fore him.—For all new purposes he would take the valua- tion from the overseers' books, and with regard to the "twelve pounders," if there was nothing said about them he should say nothing about them.

A MORAL RIGHT.—The overseers of Halton objected to the name of Thomas Hatton on the ground that the bout- daries of the township had been altered and the property qualification was now in the township of Runcorn. Mr Bentley argued that the vote ought to be allowed because the overseers' objection published in the ordinary way was not sufficient notice to the voter.—Mr Pattison contended that the overseers' lists were notices to the world, and he held that the property being no longer in Halton the claim ought to be struck out.—The Revising Barrister thought the claimant had a moral right to his vote, although in prin- ciple he ought to be struck out.—Tbe vote was allowed,— Several claims were allowed under similar circumstances.
THE RESULT.

Mr 0 Leak, the local -L-ib-er-ara-g-ent, has supplied us with the following statistics :—New Liberal property claims, 18; sustained 9; new Conservative property claims, 12; SLIP tained, 10; Liberal objections to old register. 10; sustained, 8; Conservative objections, 3; sustained, 2; Liberal occti- piers' claims, 12; sustained, 4; Conservative occupiers' claims, 13; sustained, 0.

SUSPICIOUS DEATH OF A WOMAN AT WIDNES. A DROWNING MYSTERY. On Tuesday, at the Arch Hotel, Mr W T Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest touching the death of Catherine Brennan, who was found drowned in the West Bank Dock, Widnes, on Sunday morning. Mr Buckley was present on behalf of the Hutchinson Trustees, and Mr Stone was foreman of the jury. Patrick Lynch, a chemical labourer, living in Pear-street, said the body the jury bad seen was that of Catherine Brennan. He had known her for about ten years. She came from Ireland about a month ago. About five years ago he lived with her for about a couple of years in Peel-street. She was the widow of James Brennan, and he understood she was about fifty years of age* She was of intemperate habits. She left his house between five and bix o'clock on Saturday evening. She had been wash- ing in Newtown and he thought she was going for her money. She was not quite sober at the time as she had had two glasses of ale with him. He next saw her at the Arch Hotel. She was dead. He never heard her say anything about suicide or anything of that sort. He knew nothing bad of the woman while she was about his place. He was a married man and his wife lived with him. The deceased was a lodger. He did not know that anybody had a quarrel with the deceased. Her body was found in West Bank Dock,about a hundred yards from his house. She had no business to take her to the dock. She might have strayed there or been carried there by others.—Alice Griffiths, wife of Owen Griffiths, a labourer, living at 33, Dock.street, de- posed that she had known the deceased for four years. She did not know what she did for a living, but she (witness) always saw her knocking about the corners of the streets. At ten o'clock on Saturday night the deceased asked her the way to Newtown. She directed her towards Mr Inison's pawnshop. Soon afterwards the deceased was knocking at the door of an empty house in Dock-street, and two young men were standing near. She was not sober. She told witness that the men had been "laying" on her, meaning that they had been striking her. The young men then commenced "haggling "at the deceased, and threatened to strike her. She (witness) went away and left them. One of the young men had his hand raised. The deceased followed her to the door of her house. She did not say she was frightened of the two men, but witness thought she appeared to be so, as she ran down the street when she left her. One of the young men was " middling" atout-looking in the face, and appeared about 20 years of age. The other was dressed in dark clothing, and seemed to be a working-man. He was rather tall and dark complexioned. She did not know either of the men. She did not know what the men and the deceased had been quarrelling about. Her house was about 200 or 300 yards from the place where the body was found.—By Sergeant Clarkson: She did not see the young men following the deceased.—By the Coroner : She was not a woman whom her husband would allow her to take in as a lodger, if she took in lodgers.—Dr W Lennan said he had made a post-mortem examination of the body that morning. The deceased appeared to be about 50 years of age. The body was well nourished. There was well marked post-mortem rigidity of the limbs and foaming at the mouth. • The skin had the appearance of what was called "goose skin." At the back there was post-mortem discolouration. Internally he found the lungs dilated full of frothy mucous,

and on dissection water freely escaped, leading to ' the conclusion that the woman was drowned. The other internal organs were apparently healthy. The brain was slightly congested, and on the surface and in the ventricles was a small quantity of clear fluid of the normal character. The fluid on the brain was generally caused by taking too much alcohol. There was no doubt whatever 1 that drowning was the cause of death, and the condition of ' the brain pointed to the fact that she was under the influ- ence of drink at the time of her death. A gentle push into the water would not cause any external marks —James Limb, of 52, Nelson-street, Runcorn, said a little after one o'clock on Sueday morning he brought his flat into the West Bank -Dock. He saw something in the water against one of the pillar guards of the bridge. Thinking it was a dog he took no further notice of it but went to bed. At seven o'clock next morning his son, aged about seven years, drew his attention to two men dragging the body of a woman by the side of the bank by one of her hands. They did not stop there. They appeared to be working-men in their Sunday clothes.—The Coroner, in summing up, said it was evident that the deceased was drowned, and that she was in drink at the time of the occurrence. A woman in her condition could have been put into the water with a very gentle push. but whether she was so pushed they could not say. He did not see that the jury could return any other verdict than an oven one of found drowned. Whether anything more would come of it he could not say. .• It would be for the police to ferret these men our. It was impossible to say whether there was any connection between the men who were with the deceased and those who pulled her out of the water on Sunday morning.—The jury then returned a verdict of found drowned, and the Coroner added , that the police (night to leave no stone unturned to discover the men concerned, because so long as that matter remained in doubt a certain amount of suspicion would be attached to it.

Woodworth: I contend—The Revising Barrister : You cannot contend yet, wait until I get evidence.—Mr Dennett said the letter arrived in the Liverpool bag due at Widnes at seven o'cicck in the morning. That was too late for delivery in Farnworth or Bold, and consequently it would be sent to Farnworth at four o'clock in the afternoon. It would [be too late for delivery that day, and would be stamped ' the following morning. The letter would not therefore reach Bold until the 21st, as the village was five miles from Farnworth.—Mr Woodworth: Is there no direct com- munication with Widnes.—Mr Dennett : No; only in the morning.—The Revising Barrister held that the notice of objection was a bad one, and the vote was granted.—Mr Powell (to Mr Woodworth) : We will have special arrange- ments made for you by the Liberal Association. (Laughter.) —Mr Woodworth: We will have different arrangements at the post office.

32. HE CENTRAL HOTEL —Mr William Robert gowler, of the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, claimed a vote in respect of the Central Hotel, Victotia-road, Widnes.—Mr Fowler, in answer to Mr Powell, stid the property was leasehold. He purchased it from Mr W Evans, brewer, Prescot, after he had been tenant two years. Originally the land belonged to the Hutchinson Trustees, but it was purchased by Mr John Hunter, of Stockport, and he now paid ground rent to that gentleman.—Claim allowed.
_ The other clainis possessed no features of general in- serest.

STATISTICS—The Liberal objections to the old register and new claims amounted to 141, and the Conservatives to 43. The Liberal claims on the £l2 list were 55, and the Conservatives 6, while the Liberal property reclaims num- bered 47. Although unable to state definitely the result of the revision it was evident during the proceedings that the Liberals were making a considerable gain, and that the ob- jections laid by the Liberals were not frivolous or vexatious, though so numerous, is shown by the fact that they only paid 2364 costs.—The Conservatives had no costs to pay.

div.head: Xettero to the OhUttar.
div.p: Xettero to the OhUttar.

THE "NEW INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY." Sir,—Your correspondent, Mr H Whitham, in an interest- ing letter, refers to the "New Industrial Inquiry" that is about to be held. I confess I cannot agree with him in thinking that this inquiry 'ought to lead to something definite." To me it seems to be foredoomed to failare by the very sentence in which its object is set forth. It is said to be for the purpose of pointing out "What are the best means, consistent with equity and justice, for bringing about a more equal division of the accumulated wealth of the country, and a more equal division of the daily products of industry between capital and labour." A Scotch gentle- man, it is slid, has given £l,OOO to promote this inquiry. I do not know whether or not this Scotch gentleman is the owner of half a dozen depopulated deer forests or the auto- cratic lord of the destinies of a few hundreds of poor crofters; but I must say he has taken a most effective way of drawing a false scent across the true path of those who wish to bring about "a more equal division of the accumu- lated wealth of the country." Capital and labour are the two things which in this inquiry are to be considered an- tagonistic to each other. Land, or economically speaking, rent, the third great divisor of the "daily products of in- dustry," is to b 3 comfortably left out. I cannot help thinking that this continual cry about the conflict between capital and labour is a most pernicious one—pernicious in itself, and still more pernicious in that it draws away inquiry' from that quarter in which inquiry can alone be profitable. It is a lapwing cry by which landholders assisted by their conscious or unconscious satellites attract attention from the evil consequences of their own huge monopoly. For after all what is the share of the "daily products of industry which goes to capital? Is it not clearly and exactly indi- cated by the current rate of interest? Whatever above that any particular capitalists may get for their capital, pure and simple, is in the shape of compensation for the risks they run. And where is the working-man who has been thrifty or fortunate enough to save a hundred or two hundreds of pounds, who will say that the two or three or four per cent. he will get for a perfectly safe investment is too much reward for the abstinence he has exercised? And what is a perfectly fair return for a small capitalist cannot surely be unfair for a large one. . . .

To show in as forcible and cmcrete a manner as possible, the true antagonists of the working classes, I will quote an item qf news which appeared in your columns a fortnight ago. It is this:—" Many of the Glasgow ironmasters have intimated that they intend to limit production unless the landlords agree to reduce royalties and the railway c,ma- panies establish lower rates. It is stated that the business is carried on at a loss, and that this cannot be wholly taken out of wages." Here we are in the most significant and unmistakeable manner brought face to face with that which keeps wages down and continually tends to make them less. It is clearly not capital, for the capitalists have been carry- ing on business at a loss. It is primarily the royalties, or in other words the rent, demanded by the landlords. Reduce the royalties and you increase the wages; increase the roy- alties and wages are gradually reduced till it is possible to reduce them no further and it is impossible to even carry on the business. To make my contention still clearer let us suppose that the Glasgow iron trade was to spring into sudden prosperity. What woald then take place ? Doubt- less the ironrnasters would make better profits, and no doubt the workmen would earn better wages, but would they get the full benefit of the sudden prosperity? Not at all. The landlords would step in and say "Now you are getting high prices for your manufactured iron; you cannot have manufactured iron unless we let you have the raw material, and therefore we must have a larger price for the raw mate- rial." This demand could not be resisted, for iron ore can only be had from the bowels of the earth, and as things are the bowels as well as the surface of English earth at all events is the exclusive property of private people. And if the prosperity continued for some time the share of the better prices which went to the landlords would be rapidly increased, through com- petition for the raw material, until ultimately the Condi- tion of both capitalist and workman would be little, if any, improved. For the reasons I have given, and others which might be urged, I say that an "Industrial inquiry," which leaves the question of rent out of its scope, will be not merely useless but pernicious in its results.

There is another limit to this inquiry prominently set forth as to which I cannot help feeling somewhat curious. The inquiries, or at least the conclusions come to, have to be consistent with " equity and justice." Now. I should like to know what is to be the standard of' equity and jus- tice " which is to be set up, or who will be the determlna- tors of what is "consistent with equity and justice ?" Is it the legal standard which is to be set up ? Surely that cannot be, for every anomaly that at present exists, or has ever existed, is or has been "Consistent with equity and justice" in the eyes of the law. Then, as to determinators, if there are to be such, will they be those persaras who main- tain that the process by which holders of lanl have been transformed from tenants of the State -into full or at least practical owners, was consistent with " equity and justice," and yet denounce a similar process which would lead back to State ownership as confiscation and robbery. Or, finally, are the principles of equity and justice which will guide this inquiry to be themselves coasistent with the grand maxim, "The good of the people is the supreme law ?"—I am, sir, JACQUES.

div.head: HUMBLE_REPLY TO MR. FRED. R. ROBERTS.
div.p: A HUMBLE_REPLY TO MR. FRED. R. ROBERTS.
Sir,—! sit down in fear and trembling to reply to the severe and scathing letter of your able correspondent which appeared in your last issue, and I am thankful that I still survive it.

_ Was it condeseension on his part to agree with me re- specting the Corporation's action in the matter of chapel . letting? I feel that it wes -, and I cannot be too grateful, for his master mind could easily have differed from me. ; But now comes a dash to my happiness. Mr Roberts tells , me I have made some remarks of doubtful taste about the Rev John Yonge, and that I ought to know it is " the minister's duty to combat sin in every shape and form wherever found." There is a sense of satire in this, when , we remember that it needed a platform buffoon like Murphy and a blatant disturber of the public peace like Booth to accomplish some such ends here—even if they prove to be only evanescent. And the question then comes— Are the ministers doing as Mr Roberts says they ought to do? Echo's answer is " feeble to a degree." Then I am told there is confusion in my mind respecting tshat is "legal" and what is "legitimate." This is ironical for this reason: in these very lines the "confusion is worse confounded," and I defy even Mr Roberts to clear up the Serbonian bog of his diction hereabouts. But with all this, I still hold that a publican's trade—when properly conducted —is as legitimate as that of the butcher or baker. and I defy anyone to contradict it. I am told that there are many trades having legal sanction which I might not think so unobjectionable. It may be so, but I sincerely hope yonr correspondent will spare me from his superior knowledge of those questionable trades. Then I am taken to task for sarcastic allusions to the "philanthropic" tradesman, and told I would forbid in them all political and social ambition. I would do nothing of the sort; but I would still have them "do as they would be done by." There are more ways than one of doing good and eschewing evil ; hut your "philanthropic" tradesmen always take the most offensive course, asd lay themselves justly open—at any rate on the publican's businoss—to the charge of meddling and muddling. Mr Roberts says "Our deep regret should be that so few of his (the tradesman's) class do demonstrate the possession of a soul at all—a fact that must be infinitely pleasing to " Pendennis." This is too scathing; and, as an assumption of knowledge in regard to my feelings, is a striking example of good taste. lam too modest to accept, even if it were offered, a re- tainer to defend one who is much more able than I tarn to defend himself, and so I leave the " Captain " to deal with the latter portion of this letter ; but before closing, let me assert that I believe Mr Roberts knows as much about public-houses as I do about books that I never read • and therefore is as qualified to judge of the one as I am of the other. But critics must have something to do, as they had in Dean Swift's day, when he wrote : " Rail, Critic r thy labourious pen May carp at Dick—his wooden wit; But how trifling 'tis for grown-up men To mark how little children—spit! " PENDENNIS. 26th September, 1884.

PROSECUTIONS UNDER THE VACCINATION ACTS. Sir,—l have read the report in your last issue of the dis- cussion at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians as to the conduct by Mr J C Sutton, their clerk (who is not a solicitor), of prosecutions under the above Acts. Mr Sutton, in his pride of legal knowledge, ^s amusingly arbitrary. Had the magistrates decided not to hear him, he

ASSAULTING i PoticstrAie —At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, a man named John Heath was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, and with assaulting P.C. Johnson. That officer said that at 11-30 he saw the prisoner in the Market-place wishing to fight with one of his companions. He endeavoured to per- suade him to go away but he could not, and finally prisoner became very violent, and kicked and struck witness.—He was fined £5 and costs, or a month in default.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board's Offices, Victoria-road, on Thursday. Mr T S Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev Father, Finegan and Clarke, Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs Bradshaw, Deacon, Shaw, Imison, Glover, Davies, and Danby (clerk.) DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE —This committee re- ported that during the month of August (four weeks) there were 57 applications for school fees, and 249 persons were summoned before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 52 cases. There were 53 persons prosecuted before the magis- trates, and 51 were convicted.—The report was adopted, on the motion of Mr Deacon. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE —TIIO School Manage- ment Committee recommended that Miss Dodsworth be ap- pointed head mistress, Senior Girls' Department of the Warrington-road Schools (vice Miss Strickland), on pro- bation at a salary of £BO per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board. They also recommended that Mrs M A Hughes be appointed caretaker and cleaner for a further term of three months on trial.—The minutes were passed, on the motion of Rev Father Finegan._

MR GLOVER TAKEN TO TASK.—THE OVER-WORKED TEACHERS.—The Chairman asked the Rev Father Finegan if the School Management Committee had taken any steps with regard to the alleged over-work of pupil teachers in the Board schools.—The Rev Father Finegan replied that the committee would consider the matter at their next meeting, and would make a recommendation to the Board next month. They must not forget that they had instructed the masters to see that the law was carried out in all cases which applied to pupil teachers. Whether the masters had done this or not it remained for them to say, but he was inclined to think they had not.—Mr Glover said it might be help,nl to the consideration of this question if they were to have informa- tion how the prominent school boards in the United Kingdom succeeded in cc-7ring out the requirements of the depart- ment—say London, Liverpool, Birmingham, Manchester, and Bradford.—The Chairman thought the information would assist the committee if it could be got.—The Rev Father Finegan observed that they must not fly so high. He could not forget that he lived in Widnes, and not in London, Liverpool, or Manchester. They must compare Widnes with a town of equal propor- tions.—Mr Glover did not know why they should follow the least intelligent instead of the most intelligent School Boards. He did not know why ratepayers of Widnes were not entitled to the very best arrangements for the teaching of their children and for the training of their sons and daughters as those in London, Liverpool, or Birmingham.— The Chairman: It is quite competent for you to move for any returns you like, but this is not the time. Father Fine- gan bad simply answered a question put to him.—The Rev Father Finegan: I am entirely in the bands of the com- mittee.—The Chairman observed that Mr Glover's sugges- tion was a good one, and he had no doubt it would be acted upon.—Father Finegan said this discussion arose at the last meeting on a motion put upon the agenda paper by Mr Glover, who he thought had gone out of his way to show the committee the way in which it should be done. He should now say in his presence what he then said in his absence. He certainly would not sit upon a committee if they were to be told how they were to conduct their business. If the committee bad not done their work properly it was for the Board to make a change. He had been a member of the School Management Committee for a period of four years. and he could look back with a certain amount of pleasure to the work done by the committee. It was work that would bear investigation, both as to efficiency and economy in the management of the Board schools. He thought it was rather hard after four years' service to be told they were doing their work wrong and to be instructed to do certain things, as though they were children. He thought these remarks were called for.—The Chairman: We had better pass on now.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £403 193 24. The school fees re- ceived for August were—Simms Cross, £69 178 5d ; War- rington-road, £29 7s 94; West Bank, £55 4s id; managers of national school for instruction of pupil teachers, £5; to- tal, £159 93 9d. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr Shaw.

div.head: RECALCITRANT OVERSEERS.
div.p: RECALCITRANT OVERSEERS.

Mr Shaw moved "That the Finance Committee be em- powered to take legal proceedings at once against the over- seers of Widnes to compel the payment of £l,OOO, the balance due upon the last precept issued upon them, and due March 31st, Mg." It was with great regret, he said, that the Finance Committee found it necessary to take this action. It was a great pity they had to take legal proceed-1 logs, which could only fall upon gentlemen personally for ' refusing to pay money that had really been collected for the specific purposes of the Board. The poor rata had been collected, and the money ought to have been paid eight mouths ago, but they had tried to obtain instalments as they required them, and they had made repeated applications for this large payment without any effect. He was stare they I would agree with him that it was ribt pleasant to be obliged to take proceedings, which would cause gentlemen to have to pay costs for money that might have been paid long ago.—The Chairman: I take it, Mr Shaw, that you want the money, or you would not ask for this resolution.—Mr Shaw: We are considerably overdrawn at the bank, and we cannot pay our treasurer any interest.—The Chairman: You won't act upon this resolution precipitately. You will sand a copy of it to the overseers.—The Rev Father Clarke: He will give them another chance. (Laughter.)— Mr Dauby said he had that morning seen an overseer, who had informed him that the overseers had passed the amount, and a cheque would be forwarded to the Board. (Laughter.) —Rev Father Finegan remarked that Mr Goff, the assistant overseer, had been absent on his holidays for the past three weeks, and now that he was at home the overseers would pay their way immediately. (Laughter.)—Mr Shaw said the Board was in this position. Supposing the treasurer re- fused to advance any money, they would not be able to pay the teachers' salaries as they fell due. They had not got any money in the bank to pay the accounts passed that day, but they were considerably overdrawn.—The resolu- tion was passed. _ _

MR GLOVER ON THE WEONO ficEbrr.—Mr Glover asked if there should not be at least seven days' notice given of a meeting which involved business such as they had trans- acted that day. He quoted from a book he held in his hand in support of his question—The Chairman said Mr Glover had got hold of an old Act of Parliament. The Board were meeting in a perfectly right and legal manner.— This concluded the business.

div.head: WIDNES REVISION COURT.
div.p: WIDNES REVISION COURT.

Mr Batler, revising barrister, held a court at the Sessions Uouse, Widnes, yesterday, for the purpose of revising the list of voters in the Widnes polling district. The Liberal party was represented by Mr T P Croaden Powell, Mr Maior, and Mr H B Shores; and the Conservatives by Mr W t _Husband, Mr W Woodnorth, and Mr R Whiteside.

A Nova'. POINT.—On the name of Mr William Berry, Ball-lane, Ditton, being called, Mr Husband said notices of objection had been sent by the Liberal party to several Con- servatives who claimed a vote. The notices were dated from St. Helens on the 19th August, Warrington on the 20th August, and Widnes on the 3rd September, and the notices were not delivered within the time specified by the Act of Parliament. He therefore contended that the notices were invalid.—Mr Powell pointed out that the notices were posted in St. Helens in time to be delivered within the specified period in the ordinary course of the post. Besides the people were present to answer the objections.—Mr Husband said they were there to tell the court they did not receive the notices in time.—Mr Powell said they had no right to be there.—The Revising Barrister asked how it was there was such a difference in the dates.—Mr Shores re- plied that the postmaster said that the letters were forwarded from Warrington on the 20th in a bundle, which bore a label with the name of Mr Hunt upon it. All the letters were delivered to Mr Hunt, and as that gentleman did not return them for several days they were not delivered until the 3rd instant.—Mr Powell pointed out that the Act of Parliament said that it should be sufficient notice if posted in time.— Mr W Dennett, the postmaster, was called, and stated that in the ordinary course of the post a letter posted at St Helens on the 19th ought to be delivered on the 20th—the following morning. He confirmed the statement made by Mr Shores.—The Revising Barrister held that the notices of obiections were good, and the various claims involved were inquired into. Tnacanso THE TORIES.—Dr Ferdinand Hurter, chemist at Messrs Gaskell Deacon and Co.'s Works, claimed a vote in respect of his residence. The Conservatives had lodged an objection.—Mr Powell contended that the notice of ob- jection had not been posted in time to catch the mail for service at Widses.—Mr Woodworth: I am certain it was. —The Revising Barrister said the notice was stamped Liver- pool August 20th, Widnes August 20th, and Farnworth August 21st. He wanted to know if this would reach Dr I Hurter in time in the ordinary course of the post.—Mr

div.p: would not "hays bowed to their dec;sion," but would no doubt have carried the case to the House of Lords. It is a pity that he did not "refer to the orders and statutes relat- ing to the subject "before he "laid down the law" for the Flom! Secretary. He appears to have lamentably mistaken the situation. He cannot, on objection being taken, claim to act as an advocate, for he is not a "counsel or attorney." BY the 12th section of 11 and 12 Vict., chapter 43, which regulates proceedings before justices of the peace, it is enacted that "every complainant or informant . . shall be at liberty to conduct such complaint or information respectively, and to have the witnesses examined and cross- examined by counsel or attorney on his behalf." The " complainant "or " informant " is the vaccination officer acting on behalf of the Guardians, and he may engage a "counsel or attorney" to represent him, but not the town crier or clerk to the Guardians, unless such crier'or clerk is a "counsel or attorney" also. Moreover, the clerk cannot prosecute under the Vaccination Acts. The conduct of prosecutions under those Acts is distinctly thrown on the vaccination officer by the 16th article of the General Order of the 31st October, 1874, which was issued by the Local Government Board under the authority of the Acts. It runs thus:—" The Guardians shall in all cases cause proceedings to be taken, dm., and for this purpose shall give directions autharising the vaccination officer to institute and conduct such proceedings." Neither the Acts nor the General Order contain a single word empowering anybody else but the vaccination officer to institute or conduct proceedings, ex- cept a deputy appointed under the 13th article of the Order, "with the permission of the Local Government Board given on the application of the Guardians." The talk about "non- legal minds," "legal acumen," and "a legal education" would seem to have been somewhat idle, and I think that Mr Forster may yet "score off" Mr Sutton. The " express authority given by the statute under which the cases were tried" only exists in Mr Sutton's fertile imagination But, really, is not the administration of the Vaccina- tion Acts very much of a farce? Here are a Board of Guardians and their clerk, who under- takes to keep them in the„right path, ignorant of the mode in which prosecutions should be conducted, and it would ap- pear that the justices and their clerk have allowed a gross irregularity to pass unchecked. And what is the effect of the Acts? Do they tend to induce a respect for the law. or the contrary ? The numbers of prosecutions instituted are increasing every year, and in one town alone there are more than a thousand persons who should be prosecuted to- morrow if it had not become absolutely impossible there to carry out the Acts. The recusants are told by the vaccin- ationists that in vaccination a real disease is imparted, the issue of which admittedly cannot be foreseen, and is it to be wondered at that they will run great risks rather than the acknowledged risk to which they are asked to submit their children ? And what has the practice of vaccination ef- fected ? There were in London in the 10 years, 1871-80, 15,359, and in the three years, 1881-3, 2,931 deaths from smallpox: and this year, 1884, is again an epidemic year. Against these numbers place the deaths in the three previ- ous periods of 10 years each, 1841-50, 1851-60, 1861-70,1 namely, 8,416, 7,150, and 8,347 respectively, and where is the diminution of mortality in London as the result of vac- cination? The boot is rather on the other leg. And the figures as to England and Wales tell the same tale, though not according to Sir Lyon Playfair, whose method, however. is unique. He chose In Parliament in June, 1883, to con- trast 18 years, 1853-71, with 9, 1872-80, so just , managing to include in the earlier period the 23 062 deaths of 1871 and to exclude from the later period the mortality of the epidemic time 1881-2. The Act of 1867 applied coin oulsion as we have it now, and he might have compared equal periods of 15 years each, namely, 1853-67 with 1868-82, but by so doing he would have refuted his own argument. Vaccination has in fact nullified the enormous advance made by the medical faculty during this century to a rational treatment of small-pox patients, and also the vastly improved sanitary conditions• under which we now live. Dr. Alfred Carpenter (a vaccina- tor who has said that he would take the child by force, if need be, and vaccinate it, and keep it away from its Parents till the operation has taken effect), on August 19th, 1882, wrote thus :—" Let anti-vaccinators support true sani- tary work, such as the abundant supply of pure water, the immediate removal of all excreta from our midst; make en- gineers understand that stinking sewers are wrongly con- structed, &c., and the time will come when vaccination will become an unnecessary work." And I join with Dr. Car- penter in saying that with improved sanitary conditions no one should take small-pox, provided only that the prac- tice of vaccination is ab indoned, as inoculation has been ; for the Lancet of August 2nd stated that " experiments have clearly shown that vaccinia and small-pox are one and the same disease." The Vaccination Act, 1867,. enacts that " Any person who shall produce the disease of small-pox in in any person shall be liable to be proceeded against sum- marily, and upon conviction to be imprisoned for any term not exceeding one month." I wonder whether Mr. Sutton's "legal acumen" is equal to "drawing the inference " from the Lancet's statement and the enactment !—Yours. ctn., The Park, Highgate, N. F. D. ASKEY.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

In consequence of recent heavy rains, a large portion of the province of Buenos Ayres has been, floodel, causing enormous damage to property. At Dover, on Friday, General Newdegate, commanding the Eastern District, presented medals for distinguished bravery to the men of the Lancaster Regiment who were present at El Teb and Tamai. At a meeting of the Anglesey Conservative Association, held at Bangor, on Friday, a letter was read from Captain Rayner declining to become a candidate at the general election, and it was resolved to invite Major Henry Platt to contest the county. EXPLOSION AT A ROYAL GUNPOWDER FACTORY.—A quantity of gun cotton in a drying oven in a detached building of the Royal Gunpowder Factory, Waltham Abtey, exploded on Friday morning, doing a great deal of damage to property but none to person. Pieces of copper from the drying oven were picked up 250 yards away. SHOCKING DEATH OF A COLLIERY UNDERLOOKER.-011 Friday morning John Makin, 40 years, an underlooker, was killed in Ashtons Green Colliery, near St Helens. There had been a fall of earth on the wagon-way during the pre- vious night, and the deceased, who had charge of the part, was superintending its removal when another mass of dirt and coal, estimated at six tons, fell and buried him. The earth was removed as quickly as possible, but an hour elapsed before the body was reached, life being extinct. GREAT FIRE AT AN OILWORKS.—Between twelve and one o'clock on Friday morning a destructive fire occurred at the well-known oilworks of Messrs Craig and Rose, Leith. The flames seized upon some hundreds of tanks of varnish, and the whole district around was brilliantly illuminated. Great excitement was caused by the probability of an explosion, but the firemen, at great personal risk, covered the explosive material with wet sacks. The damage is estimated at several thousands of pounds.

div.head: DISASTER ON THE IRISH COAST.
div.p: THE DISASTER ON THE IRISH COAST.

The Central News correspondent, telegraphing from Dun- faaagby on Thursday night, says :—The tempestuous weather which has prevailed since Monday morning calmed down somewhat this morning, enabling the two boats which ventured from Tory island en Tuesday morning to re- turn to the island.

Telegraphing from Letterkenny, a correspondent says that five Admiralty divers have passed through that town on their way to the scene of the wreck. The weather, how- ever. is so stormy that it is impossible to say when they will be able to reach Tory island. The six survivors of the Wasp left the Valiant at Rathmullen on Thursday morning, and have just reached Londonderry by train. A great crowd awaited their arrival at the station, their coming exciting intense interest. The men appear to have almost recovered from their injuries, though their bands are badly cut and one of the marines has a very bad foot. Mrs Huttoo, wife of the cook of the Wasp, has received a letter from her husband, who said he haa a terrible struggle for his life, but escaped miraculously with slight injuries,

THE SALVATIONISTS IN SWITZERLAND. GENEVA, FRIDAY.—A meeting of the Salvationists held yesterday at Nyon, in the Canton of Vaud, was distur- bed by a crowd of persons who assembled outside the build- ing. The windows were broken, the doors forced in, and the furniture destroyed. THE SOUDAN EXPEDITION.

div.head: DEPARTURE OF TROOPS.
div.p: DEPARTURE OF TROOPS.

The various detachments from the brigade of Guards which form the Guards contingent for the Camel Corps, left Victoria Terminus, London, on Friday morning, for Portsmouth, where the men embark • with the Cavalry con- tingent for Egypt. Their departure was witnessed by a large number of persons, including several staff officers, who loudly cheered the troops as the train moved off. The bands of the Coldstream and Scots Guards were in attendance, and played several lively airs. Portsmouth dockyard was all alive with excitement on the occasion of the embarkation of the members of the Camel Corps for the Soudan.

A Central News Assiout telegram says :—Several boats for the Khartoum expedition have arrived here and are be- ing sent forward. Lord Wolseley reaches here on Sunday on his way up the Nile. A large draft of the second battalion of the Berkshire Regiment left Chatham on Friday morning for Egypt to strengthen the first battalion.

Two life belts, or cork jackets, per boat are ordered to be added to the equipment of the Nile Expedition, and 2,000 of these articles are now being delivered at Woolwich Dock- yard for conveyance to Egypt. The arrangements for sup- plying the troops with wholesome water have been supple- mented by a supply of 3,000 pocket filters with tubes attached, through which a man may safely slake his thirst from even a muddy ditch or stagnant pool. On Friday morning, a party of about sixty of the Army Service Corps left Woolwich en route for Egypt. The pressure of busi- ness at the Stores Departments at Woolwich may now be said to have ceased, and notices have been posted outside stating that no more hands are required.

Flour Mill Building on the new process of grinding the wheat has become a great industry throughout the whole world. The old mill stones are replaced by chilled iron rolls, which have a great many important advantages over the for- mer, and owing to their adoption on the American and European continent, large quantities of foreign flour, of superior quality to home made, are ceing imported into this country, and thus the millowners of the United Kingdom, of which there are about 11,000, recognise that in order to be able to compete with foreign ft ur, manufactured on the new system, they must at once re-model their mills, and adopt the new system—but of the above 11.000 mills over 206 ihave already been altered. Roller Mill System.—These rolls are used exclusively in con- nection with greatly improved dressing and purifying ma- chinery, and the flour and bran roduced thereby are of a supe- rior quality. The introduction of the above improved system of milling in various mills In the United Kingdom has proved in every case a financial as well as a commercial success to the respective mill-owners, and Messrs. Fiechter's are now well known as among the best mill builders In the United Kingdom, and certainly their well-studied system of Gradual Reduction Milling, based upon great experience and practice, is second to none. The new Company proposes to continue the manufac- ture of the Spirial Plow Mill Machinery, so far made by Messrs- John Fieeht er and Bone, at their works in Liverpool, and the erection of entire Flour Mills, &c. ; and to increase the capacity oif the firms, so as to be able to cope with the great demand for F:echter's Machinery System and general Mill- wright work, a large portion of the work will be done in War- rington, at the Bewsey Mill Works, which are well fitted up and arranged for the purpose The Company will also under- take to execute, as betore, orders for Messrs. Jones and Sons' well-known Boilers, Engines. &c. The Directors have, furthermore, made arrangements with the inventor, Mr McNeill, for the manu"acture of a new Tram Motor, driven by gas. The first Car is already in hand. This new invention promises to bemme a great success It is esti- mated that the cost ot the Motor will not exceed that of a set of horses to work an ordinary tramcar, while the saving will be from eight to nine pounds per week per ca". The Motor is self-prope ling, and may be worked continuously any length of time or distance without stopping, except for a short time once a week for cleaning purposes.

_ - LYNX. AN UNLICENSED HAWKER. At the Lymm Police Sta- tion, on Saturday, a vagrant named William Forrest, who" said he came from Runcorn, was -charged with hawking without a license on the same day. Sergeant Bosson proved the case, and the presiding magistrate (Mr T P Norris), sent Forrest to prison for one month. CONGREGATIONAL CI:MECH.—The anniversary service of the Lymm Congregational Sunday School were celebra. ted on Sunday. Both morning and evening the Rev Joseph Moore, of Congleton, preached to large congregations irons the words: "For we are labourers together with God " and "Which is the manifest token." In the afternoon a service of song entitled "Elijah " was rendered, the choir perfor- ming the musical part with skill and judgment, whilst Mr R A Naylor, of 'ihelwall, gave the connective readings. Mr Albert Leather officiated at the organ. The proceeding' throughout the day were highly interesting, and collectione made at the close of each service in aid of the school fund, realized over £l9. With other donations likely to be forth- coming, this amount will be raised to about £24. At Newmarket on Wednesday the Great Eastern HandiCaP was won ha- Mr Manton's Energy, the Duke of Beau. fort's Ishah being second, and Mr W Gilbert's DesPaic third.
